If you need it longer, it isn't that 'the medicine isn't enough' — it's **time to find the cause**. The medicine used depends on whether it's reflux oesophagitis, a stomach ulcer, or Helicobacter. Your doctor decides whether treatment to get rid of Helicobacter is needed.

In particular, **heartburn that is new or long-lasting after age 40** (Korea's national stomach cancer screening also starts at 40), trouble swallowing, weight loss or black stools should not be covered up with medicine — ask about an endoscopy.

faq.q: Why is it worse when I eat before bed?
faq.a:
When you lie down, the stomach and oesophagus are at the same height, so **acid flows back up more easily.**

**Finishing dinner 3 hours before bed** and raising the head of the bed 10–15 cm (not piling up pillows but **putting blocks under the bed legs at the head end**) often helps as much as medicine. Lying on your left side helps too.

heartburn.clinic: **A medicine that strongly reduces stomach acid** for 4–8 weeks. If there's squeezing pain, **a medicine to relax stomach spasms**, and if food doesn't go down well, a medicine that gets the stomach moving; for pain, acetaminophen.
heartburn.pharm: Deal with **burning and pain separately**. For burning, **a medicine that reduces stomach acid**; for squeezing pain, a medicine that relaxes spasms. Both are at the pharmacy. Antacids only help a little.

insomnia.lead: Pharmacy sleep aids (diphenhydramine, doxylamine) borrow the drowsiness of an antihistamine, so they're **for a night or two** — after a few days you build tolerance, you feel foggy the next day, and over 65 there's a risk of seeing things that aren't there or falling. The first-line treatment for insomnia lasting more than 3 weeks is not medicine but **cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia**, and in Korea melatonin is prescription-only.
how: Take just 1 dose 30 minutes before bed. Don't take it if you plan to drive the next day.
Never take it with alcohol.
pharmacy: Mention your age (65 or older), glaucoma or prostate problems, any cold or motion-sickness medicine you take, and whether you're pregnant.
**Show your list of medicines.** Sleep aids are among the medicines most often linked to falls in older people.
selfcare: Get 15 minutes of sunlight in the morning, and keep naps under 20 minutes.
Turn off the TV and phone 1 hour before bed, and keep the room dark and cool.
If you can't sleep, don't lie there trying — get up, do something quiet, and lie back down when you feel sleepy.
avoid: Taking a sleep aid with cold medicine doubles up the antihistamine.
Don't use alcohol as a sleeping pill. You may fall asleep, but you wake up before dawn.
Don't take a sleep aid every day for more than 2 weeks.

plan.title: Sleep hygiene — first
plan.why: Fixed wake-up time, no caffeine after 2 p.m., bed only for sleep, get up if sleep won't come.

plan.title: A night or two only — diphenhydramine 50 mg
plan.why: Jet lag, the night before a big day. Within 2 weeks; avoid if 65 or older.

plan.title: 3 weeks or more — see a doctor (behavioural therapy, prescription)
plan.why: Long-standing insomnia needs the cause (depression, pain, sleep apnoea) sorted out and cognitive behavioural therapy. Prescription sleeping pills if needed.

notWorking.title: If you still can't sleep on medicine
steps: Don't increase the medicine — see a doctor. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia has longer-lasting effects than sleeping pills.
If you snore heavily or are very sleepy during the day, get tested for sleep apnoea.

faq.q: Can't I buy melatonin at the pharmacy?
faq.a: In Korea it's a prescription medicine (prolonged-release melatonin), and ordering it from abroad is also banned. The evidence for jet lag is strong (analysis pooling several studies), so if you need it, see a doctor.

faq.q: Is it bad to keep taking sleep aids?
faq.a:
Pharmacy sleep aids (diphenhydramine, doxylamine) are for **a few days**. Taken for long, tolerance builds and they stop working well, and **in older people they linger into the next morning, causing falls and foggy memory**. They're also a classic example of a medicine with a heavy anticholinergic load.

If you haven't slept well for more than 2 weeks, it's not a matter of changing medicine but **time to look for the cause** — sleep apnoea, depression, restless legs or pain are often hiding behind it.

faq.q: But I sleep well after a drink?
faq.a:
**You fall asleep faster, but sleep quality gets worse.** Alcohol breaks up the deep sleep in the second half of the night so you keep waking before dawn, and it makes snoring and sleep apnoea worse. That's why you don't feel refreshed the next day.

And **taking a sleep aid together with alcohol is dangerous.** Your breathing can become shallow.

insomnia.clinic: **Treatment that fixes sleep habits (cognitive behavioural therapy) lasts longer than pills.** If medicine is needed it's used briefly, and if there's snoring or breathing pauses, a sleep study is done.
insomnia.pharm: There are sleep aids **only for a night or two when it's urgent**. Older people need to be careful because next-day dizziness can lead to falls. Don't take them for more than 2 weeks in a row.

rhinitis.lead: If clear runny nose, sneezing and itchy eyes come back in the same season every year, it's allergic rhinitis; if it comes with fever and aches and lasts a few days, it's a cold. The first-line treatment for allergic rhinitis is not an antihistamine but a **steroid nasal spray (prescription)**, and pharmacy antihistamines are good for runny nose and sneezing but **weak for a blocked nose**.
rhinitis.planLabel: Antihistamine for runny nose, decongestant for blockage
how: In allergy season, take loratadine 10 mg once in the morning (or cetirizine before bed). Starting before the season begins works even better.
On nights when your nose is badly blocked, use a nasal spray once in each nostril — for 3 days only.
Rinse your nose with saline 1–2 times a day.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “It's mainly runny nose and sneezing” or “It's mainly a blocked nose.”
Mention high blood pressure, prostate problems, glaucoma, pregnancy, and whether you drive.
selfcare: Rinse your nose with saline and wash your bedding often. In pollen season, keep windows closed and run an air purifier.
Indoor humidity of 40–50% is best.
avoid: Using a decongestant nasal spray (such as xylometazoline) for more than 3 days makes your nose more blocked because of the medicine.
Taking cold medicine and allergy medicine together doubles up the antihistamine.
If you have high blood pressure, don't take pseudoephedrine (a decongestant) for long.

plan.title: Runny nose and sneezing — 2nd-generation antihistamine
plan.why: During the day, loratadine or fexofenadine (almost no drowsiness); if effect comes first, cetirizine (at bedtime).

plan.title: Blocked nose — nasal spray / combination cold medicine
plan.why: A decongestant nasal spray (xylometazoline) is fastest, but use it **for no more than three days** (longer causes medicine-induced rhinitis · the package insert says not to go past 7 days). By mouth, pseudoephedrine works well, but **on its own it's prescription-only** in Korea, so at the pharmacy a combination cold medicine containing pseudoephedrine is used instead. Be sure to mention high blood pressure, heart disease, an enlarged prostate or glaucoma.

plan.title: Ongoing rhinitis — steroid nasal spray (prescription)
plan.why: First-line treatment that reduces blockage, runny nose and sneezing all together (2020 guideline). It has to be used every day to work.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't helping much
steps: It's normal for allergy medicine (antihistamines) not to clear a blocked nose. A prescription steroid nasal spray is the answer.
If only one side is blocked with blood or a bad smell, or your face hurts and yellow discharge lasts more than ten days, other causes such as sinusitis need to be checked.

faq.q: I've already used a nasal spray for more than a week.
faq.a: **Medicine-induced rhinitis**, where the medicine itself blocks your nose, may have started. When you stop, it's more blocked for a few days, but it passes. If it's hard, switching to a steroid nasal spray prescribed by a doctor makes it easier. You can also stop one nostril at a time.

faq.q: Which allergy medicines don't make you drowsy?
faq.a: Loratadine and fexofenadine are the least drowsy. Cetirizine works well but makes some people sleepy, so take it **in the evening**. 1st-generation ones (chlorpheniramine, common in combination cold medicines) cause a lot of drowsiness and dry mouth, so people 65 and older should avoid them.

faq.q: Does nasal rinsing (saline) work?
faq.a: Yes. In allergic rhinitis, saline nasal rinses reduce symptoms and the need for medicine. Always use **sterile saline or water that has been boiled and cooled**. Plain tap water is not OK.

rhinitis.clinic: **A steroid nasal spray** is the main treatment for rhinitis. It's different from pharmacy decongestant sprays — it isn't habit-forming and is used long term. Allergy tests are done if needed.
rhinitis.pharm: Split it up: **oral antihistamine for runny nose and sneezing**, **a spray for a blocked nose**. Decongestant sprays for three days only — longer makes the blockage worse.

toothache.lead: The real treatment for toothache is the dentist. To get through until your appointment, the strongest evidence is for taking **ibuprofen 400 mg + acetaminophen 1,000 mg together**. In an analysis that pooled several studies of pain after wisdom-tooth removal, this combination beat either medicine alone, and in an emergency-room study it worked as well as opioid painkillers.
toothache.planTitle: The backbone of dental pain prescriptions
toothache.planLabel: Dentists prescribe it this way too
how: After a meal, take ibuprofen 400 mg and 2 tablets of acetaminophen **together** (the package insert says not to take it with other painkillers — in the clinic they are sometimes used together, so check with your pharmacist whether to combine them). Ibuprofen up to three times a day (1,200 mg); acetaminophen every 4–6 hours, up to 8 tablets a day (4,000 mg).
After a tooth is pulled, take the first dose **before** the numbness wears off — it makes it easier to get past the worst of the pain.
Holding cold water in your mouth calms nerve pain, and a cold pack on the outside of your face for 20 minutes also helps.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I have a toothache. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen, please.”
If you are bleeding after a tooth was pulled, be sure to say whether you take a blood thinner.
selfcare: Rinse gently with warm salt water (if a tooth was pulled, start after 24 hours).
Avoid hard or hot food for a few days.
Don't use a straw over the spot where a tooth was pulled. The blood clot can come loose and the pain gets worse (dry socket).
avoid: Don't put aspirin directly on your gum. It causes a chemical burn.
Don't take two anti-inflammatory painkillers at once.
For 24 hours after a tooth is pulled, avoid smoking, alcohol and straws.

plan.title: Ibuprofen 400 mg
plan.why: Toothache and pain after an extraction are inflammatory pain, so an anti-inflammatory is the key. Ibuprofen 400 mg is better than acetaminophen 1,000 mg (analysis pooling several studies: it worked 1.5 times as well).

plan.title: + Acetaminophen 1,000 mg
plan.why: Taken together, 73 in 100 people had their pain under control 6 hours later (52 with one medicine alone). The standard dental combination.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues.

plan.title: If it's an infection — antibiotics (prescription)
plan.why: If the gum is swollen with pus or fever, painkillers won't do it — the dentist needs to give antibiotics and drain it.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't helping much
steps: Are you taking an anti-inflammatory and acetaminophen **together**? Toothache is a pain one medicine alone often can't handle.
Swelling, fever, or trouble opening your mouth are signs the infection is spreading. Go to the dentist that same day.
If it gets worse 3–4 days after an extraction, it's dry socket. Going back to the dentist brings relief quickly.

faq.q: The painkiller isn't working — can I take more?
faq.a: Rather than raising the dose, take **two kinds together** — ibuprofen 400 mg + acetaminophen 1,000 mg. Don't go over the daily limits (over-the-counter ibuprofen 1,200 mg, acetaminophen 4 g — for people 65 and older, doctors advise 3 g or less). If it still doesn't work, the inflammation has reached the nerve, and the answer is **the dentist, not more medicine**.

faq.q: Will taking antibiotics early help it heal faster?
faq.a: No. Most toothache is inflammation of the nerve inside the tooth, which antibiotics don't clear. Antibiotics are what a dentist prescribes **when there is swelling and fever** — taking leftover antibiotics from home only builds resistance.

faq.q: When do I start the medicine after a tooth is pulled?
faq.a: Taking the first painkiller **before the numbness wears off** makes it hurt much less. For 24 hours avoid hot food, straws, smoking and alcohol, and if it gets worse 3–4 days later, it's dry socket — go back to the dentist.

toothache.clinic: Doctors use **an anti-inflammatory painkiller at an adequate dose**, and add an antibiotic if there's pus. The root fix is dental treatment, so the cause is checked first.
toothache.pharm: **Ibuprofen 400 mg + acetaminophen 1,000 mg together** will control most toothaches. In principle the leaflets don't recommend taking them at the same time, but for toothache clinics often use them together like this — keep each medicine's own dosing interval and daily total.

wound.lead: The rule for small wounds is **rinse under running water → moist dressing**. Antibiotic ointments (fusidic acid, neomycin combinations) are only for signs of infection like pus or spreading redness — using them otherwise just builds resistance. For burns, 20 minutes under running cool water (not ice water) is all it takes — no ice, toothpaste or alcohol.
how: Rinse under running water, pat dry, and put on a moist dressing. Change it every 1–2 days.
For a burn, cool it under running cold tap water (not ice water) for 20 minutes, don't pop blisters, and cover with a burn dressing.
If redness spreads or there is pus, apply antibiotic ointment 1–2 times a day, for no more than 1 week.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “No signs of infection — a moist dressing, please” or “There's pus.”
Mention diabetes, conditions that weaken immunity, and whether you take a blood thinner.
selfcare: Rinsing with running tap water is the best disinfection.
Check whether you've had a tetanus shot within 10 years — especially for a dirty wound or an animal bite.
Even after it heals, keep it out of the sun. That stops the scar from darkening.
avoid: Don't disinfect every time with hydrogen peroxide, alcohol or iodine solutions. New skin grows back poorly.
Don't put ice, toothpaste, alcohol or potato on a burn. Cooling it under running cold tap water (not ice water) for 20 minutes is right. Within 3 hours of the injury it isn't too late.
Don't pop blisters.
Don't habitually put antibiotic ointment on wounds that aren't infected.

plan.title: Rinse under running tap water
plan.why:
Removes dirt and germs. Hydrogen peroxide and alcohol damage tissue, so they're no longer recommended.

**For a clean scrape, water alone is enough.** Only if there's soil on it or it looks like it may get infected, wipe once around the edges with **povidone-iodine**. Putting it on daily actually slows healing.

plan.title: Moist dressing / petroleum jelly
plan.why: Keeping it moist helps it heal faster, without a scab and with less scarring. For **deep or gaping wounds, or wounds with a lot of fluid**, get them cleaned at a clinic and ask whether to use a hydrocolloid dressing.

plan.title: Only with signs of infection — antibiotic ointment
plan.why: Pus, spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain. Fusidic acid and mupirocin are equal (analysis pooling several studies).

plan.title: If it hurts — acetaminophen / ibuprofen
plan.why: For burn pain, ibuprofen also fights inflammation.

plan.title: If you're worried about a scar after it fully heals — scar gel
plan.why: Use it **after the wound has completely healed**. Heparin–allantoin gels are better than putting nothing on, but **there's no evidence they beat other scar care such as silicone gel.** Sun protection alongside keeps the colour from staying. For scars from deep wounds, ask a dermatologist.

notWorking.title: If it isn't healing well
steps: If after 2–3 days redness is spreading, there's pus, or you have a fever, see a doctor. You need antibiotics by mouth.
If you have diabetes or weak immunity, see a doctor early even for small wounds.

faq.q: Should a wound be left to dry or covered?
faq.a: **Covering it and keeping it moist** heals it faster and with less scarring. Even if a scab forms, don't pick it, and change a moist dressing only when fluid leaks out.

faq.q: When do I use iodine (povidone)?
faq.a: About **once**, after first washing a wound with soil in it. Repeating it every day damages new skin. For clean wounds, running water is the best disinfection.

faq.q: Do I need a tetanus shot?
faq.a: Get one if your last shot was more than **10 years** ago. For dirty wounds — soil, a rusty nail, an animal bite — get one if it's been more than **5 years**. If you don't know when you had it, getting one is the safe choice.

wound.clinic: The wound is cleaned and **stitched if it's gaping**. If there are signs of infection, an antibiotic; for an older wound, tetanus vaccination status is checked.
wound.pharm: **A clean wound doesn't necessarily need antibiotic ointment.** Washing it and covering it with a moist dressing is better. Use fusidic acid only if pus forms or redness spreads.

hangover.lead: Dehydration and a hangover the day after drinking **come together but are different things**. Water quenches thirst, but in the data so far **how bad a hangover is had nothing to do with how much water people drank**. So what the pharmacy can do is not 'cure the hangover' but **ease the symptoms — head, stomach, sleep — one at a time**. If you choose a headache medicine, **acetaminophen on top of alcohol strains the liver** and anti-inflammatories strain the stomach, so be careful with both — if needed, a small dose of ibuprofen after food, and only if you have no heartburn.
how: Drink lukewarm water or broth **a cup at a time**. As much as quenches your thirst is enough — forcing down more won't make the hangover pass faster.
If you vomited or had diarrhoea through the night, sip pharmacy oral rehydration solution a cup at a time. Then you really have lost salt and water.
If your headache is bad, take just one ibuprofen 200 mg tablet after food. Acetaminophen on top of alcohol strains the liver.
The surest thing is **sleep**. A hangover settles as time passes.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I drank a lot last night” and they'll suggest something other than acetaminophen.
Say **whether you've already taken anything containing acetaminophen** — combined with alcohol, it puts more strain on the liver.
selfcare: Sleep is the surest remedy. A light walk is good too.
Drink enough water to quench your thirst. Warm broth does the same job.
No 'hair of the dog'. It only makes the next hangover worse.
avoid: On a day you've drunk a lot, taking acetaminophen, acetaminophen combination painkillers or cold medicines several times strains the liver. If you drink more than 3 drinks every day, check with a pharmacist or doctor first.
Anti-inflammatories on an empty stomach damage the stomach.
Lots of coffee delays sleep. Sleep does the most for a hangover, so it actually works against you.

plan.title: A cup of water at a time — oral rehydration if you vomited or had diarrhoea
plan.why:
Thirst and dry mouth are relieved by water. But **water doesn't reduce the hangover itself** — how much water people drank once the hangover came had nothing to do with how bad it was.

If you vomited or had diarrhoea all night, it's a different story. Then you really have lost salt and water, so **oral rehydration solution** is right.

plan.title: If needed — a small dose of ibuprofen after food
plan.why: Acetaminophen on top of alcohol strains the liver, so avoid it (the package insert also says not to take it after drinking). Anti-inflammatories irritate the stomach — if you have heartburn, take neither.

plan.title: Heartburn — antacid or alginate
plan.why: Protects the stomach lining. Don't take painkillers at this point.

notWorking.title: When to go to hospital
steps: If you vomit for more than 24 hours, can't keep even water down, have black stools or vomit blood, or have severe pain in the pit of the stomach (pancreatitis), go to hospital.

faq.q: Do hangover drinks and pills work?
faq.a: **A survey of 82 hangover products on the market found that not one had peer-reviewed journal data confirming effect or safety in people.** More than 60 in 100 products contained vitamins above the daily recommended amount. A review that gathered every method claimed to prevent or treat hangovers also found none with convincing evidence.

faq.q: I heard pharmacy oral rehydration solution is good for hangovers?
faq.a: **There's no evidence it helps hangovers.** Where oral rehydration has proven itself is 'water and salt lost through diarrhoea and vomiting'. In hangovers, electrolytes, blood sugar and the hormones that signal dehydration had nothing to do with how bad the hangover was. But **if you vomited all night**, that's real dehydration, so oral rehydration is right.

faq.q: Not even one acetaminophen the day after drinking?
faq.a: The day after drinking, **it's better not to** — the package insert says people who have been drinking shouldn't take it. It's especially risky **if you drink daily, on an empty stomach, or when it doubles up with acetaminophen in cold medicine**. If you have no heartburn, a small dose of ibuprofen after food is an alternative.

faq.q: Does a hangover soup help?
faq.a: Warm broth going down settles the stomach and quenches thirst. But that doesn't mean it clears the hangover faster. And **no 'hair of the dog'** — it only makes the next hangover worse.

faq.q: So is drinking water before bed pointless?
faq.a: Not wasted. People who drank water while drinking and right after had a **slightly** milder hangover the next day. But the difference wasn't big, and water drunk after the hangover had already started didn't reduce it. **Drinking less alcohol** makes a far bigger difference than water.

hangover.clinic: People rarely see a doctor for a hangover, but **if vomiting stops you keeping fluids down, a drip** works fastest. If it keeps happening, the drinking itself needs dealing with.
hangover.pharm: **Time is what cures it** — water quenches thirst but doesn't reduce a hangover. For headache, **avoid acetaminophen** — it's a strain on a liver that's been drinking. For heartburn, an acid medicine or antacid. Be honest that hangover remedies have no evidence.

motion.lead: Motion-sickness medicine is **too late once symptoms start** — take it before you set off. For short trips, dimenhydrinate taken 30 minutes to 1 hour before; for boats and long journeys, a scopolamine patch put on 4 hours before. Both cause drowsiness, and drivers, children 7 and under, pregnancy, glaucoma and an enlarged prostate should avoid them.
how: Take it with water 30–60 minutes before you set off.
Sit in the front, look at distant points outside, and don't read or look at your phone. Let in fresh air often too.
pharmacy: Mention a child's age (in Korea the scopolamine patch for ages 8–15 needs a prescription), pregnancy, glaucoma or prostate problems, and whether you'll drive.
**Tell them the medicines you take.** Combined with cold medicine or sleep aids, drowsiness and dry mouth double.
selfcare: Eat lightly before setting off. Both an empty stomach and overeating make motion sickness worse.
Sit in the front and look at distant points outside. Don't read or look at your phone.
Ginger tea or wrist acupressure are worth a try (the evidence is weak).
avoid: Adding cold medicine or sleep aids to motion-sickness medicine doubles up the drowsy ingredient (antihistamine).
Don't rub your eyes with hands that touched the scopolamine patch. Your vision gets blurry.

plan.title: 1–4 hour trips — dimenhydrinate
plan.why: 1–2 tablets 30–60 minutes before setting off. Analysis pooling several studies: preventive effect confirmed, with drowsiness.

plan.title: Boats and long journeys — scopolamine patch
plan.why: Behind the ear 4 hours before setting off; lasts 3 days. Wash your hands after applying.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't helping much
steps: If motion sickness has already started, opening a window, lying down and closing your eyes help more than medicine.
If dizziness and vomiting keep happening even when you're not travelling, have your inner ear (balance organ) checked.

faq.q: Can I drive after taking motion-sickness medicine?
faq.a: No. Both dimenhydrinate and the scopolamine patch cause drowsiness and blurred vision. If you're driving, use the front seat, fresh air and looking into the distance instead of medicine.

faq.q: I put on a scopolamine patch and my vision is blurry.
faq.a: It's a common side effect, especially if you touched your eyes with the hand you used to apply it. It returns to normal within a day of removing it. With glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or age 65 and over, it's safer to avoid it from the start.

faq.q: What motion-sickness medicine can children use?
faq.a: The scopolamine patch is not allowed for children 7 and under; ages 8–15 use the children's version (prescription). Children's oral motion-sickness medicine is given by age and weight, 30 minutes before. Under 2, the right approach is no medicine — open the window and take frequent breaks.

motion.clinic: People rarely see a doctor for motion sickness itself. But **if you're dizzy regardless of travel**, the ear or brain needs looking at.
motion.pharm: The key is taking it **30 minutes to 1 hour before you travel**. Tablets for short trips, a patch for long ones. Avoid the patch if you have **glaucoma or an enlarged prostate**.

mouth.lead: Canker sores (aphthous ulcers) heal on their own in 1–2 weeks; ointments reduce the pain meanwhile. Choose between a mild steroid paste (triamcinolone) and a 'cauterising' policresulen solution, and when many spots are sore over a wide area, a **mouth rinse** is easier. Lip blisters (herpes) and white patches (candida) must not get steroids, so telling them apart matters.
mouth.planLabel: Mild vs fast · rinse if it's widespread
how: Dab the spot dry and place a small amount of medicine on it. After meals and before bed is best.
For a rinse, hold about 15 mL in your mouth, swish for 30 seconds and spit it out. Don't swallow, and avoiding water and food for 30 minutes afterwards keeps the medicine there longer.
Avoid spicy and hot food, and if it keeps coming back, check that you're not short of B vitamins or iron.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist which it is: “It's a blister on my lip” or “It's a sore inside my mouth.” Blisters (herpes) need a different medicine.
If several spots are sore and hard to dab, ask “A rinse, please” and you can get chlorhexidine.
If it hurts so much you can't eat, ask for a **benzydamine rinse**. You can buy it at the pharmacy, and it directly numbs the pain.
selfcare: Use a soft toothbrush, and try switching to a mild toothpaste without the foaming ingredient.
Getting enough sleep and lowering stress reduces repeat episodes.
avoid: Don't put steroid ointment on blisters (herpes) or white patches (candida). It makes them spread.
Don't spread undiluted policresulen over a wide area. Only a dab on the sore spot.
Don't swallow rinses. Using chlorhexidine for more than 2 weeks can stain teeth brown.

plan.title: Benzydamine rinse — directly reduces the pain
plan.why:
A benzydamine mouth rinse. It's not a disinfectant but a medicine that **directly calms pain and swelling**, so it's especially handy when many spots are sore and ointment is hard to apply. Use 15 mL each time, swish 2–3 times a day like rinsing after brushing, and spit. Don't keep using it for more than 7 days without a doctor's advice.

Chlorhexidine is a **disinfectant rinse that prevents infection**, so it doesn't control pain. For less pain, benzydamine is the one.

plan.title: Triamcinolone paste — when there are only a few sores
plan.why: A topical steroid calms inflammation and shortens how long it hurts. Before bed, dab dry and cover thinly. Don't use it if an infection such as fungus or herpes is suspected.

plan.title: If it hurts a lot — painkillers by mouth
plan.why: If eating and drinking are hard, add a painkiller. **An anti-inflammatory (ibuprofen)** also takes down the swelling; if your stomach is sensitive or you need to avoid anti-inflammatories, just dulling the pain with **acetaminophen** is fine. Doctors also choose between the two depending on the case.

plan.title: Policresulen — fast, but it really stings
plan.why: A medicine that **chemically cauterises** the sore so it heals faster. It works well, but **the sting when applied is so strong** that it's generally not recommended. If you use it, put it on a cotton swab and touch **only the sore, very narrowly**, just once. Spreading it widely damages healthy lining too.

notWorking.title: If it isn't healing well
steps: If it doesn't heal in more than 2 weeks, comes back more than once a month, or sores also appear on the eyes or genitals, see a doctor. They'll check for Behçet's disease, nutritional deficiency and autoimmune disease.

faq.q: Policresulen hurts so much — is that normal?
faq.a: It lightly burns the sore with acid, so a moment of pain is normal. Put a small amount on a cotton swab and touch only the sore spot — don't spread it. If you don't like the pain, switch to triamcinolone paste (a mild steroid).

faq.q: I keep getting mouth ulcers.
faq.a: Lack of sleep, stress, injuries inside the mouth (braces, rough food) and irritating toothpaste are common causes. Low vitamin B12, iron or folate can also be behind it, so if you get them **more than once a month**, have a blood test.

faq.q: Will taking vitamins cure it?
faq.a: Only if you're short of something. Taking high-dose vitamins for a long time without testing isn't recommended. Check sleep, toothpaste and mouth injuries first.

mouth.clinic: Doctors tend to prescribe **benzydamine mouthwash together with a topical steroid**. Policresulen works well but cauterises, so it hurts and isn't used much. For pain, an anti-inflammatory or acetaminophen is added; if it doesn't heal in 2 weeks or keeps coming back, the cause is looked for.
mouth.pharm: **Benzydamine mouthwash is the easiest start** — it reduces the pain directly. If there are only a few ulcers, use **a topical steroid paste such as triamcinolone** as well. Policresulen cauterises, so it hurts a lot.

nausea.lead:
Nausea has **many causes** — indigestion, gastroenteritis, motion sickness, a hangover, pregnancy, a medicine you've just started, and rarely even a problem with **the heart or brain**. So the right order is to look at **the cause first**, before medicine.

If you've vomited once or twice and **can still drink water, even a little at a time**, it usually settles in a day or two. The most important thing is **preventing dehydration**.

The pharmacy option is **domperidone (oral liquid and others)**. For ages 12 and up and 35 kg and over, use it briefly — **no more than 30 mg (3 bottles) a day, for under a week**. If you have heart disease or are over 60, talk to a doctor first.
nausea.planTitle: When you feel sick, do this
how: Take it **15–30 minutes before meals**.
Up to three times a day — **don't go past a week.**
Once your stomach settles, start with small amounts of plain food like **rice porridge, bananas or toast**.
pharmacy: Say **since when**, for example **“I feel sick and like I'm going to throw up — for a few hours now.”**
Be sure to mention **possible pregnancy, heart disease, and any antibiotics or antifungal tablets** you take.
selfcare: Drink **a little, often**, and when lying down **raise your upper body slightly.**
Avoid strong-smelling food and cooking smells, and **let fresh air in**.
If ginger tea suits you, it's fine to have.
avoid: **Don't gulp water right after vomiting.** It's easy to vomit again.
**Don't take domperidone more than 3 times a day or for longer than a week.**
If you're pregnant, **don't take** pharmacy anti-nausea medicine — talk to your obstetrician.

plan.title: Water a little and often — first of all
plan.why:
Drinking a lot at once brings it back up. Take **a sip or two every 5–10 minutes**. If you also have diarrhoea or haven't been able to drink for a while, **oral rehydration solution** is better than plain water.

If you're passing urine as usual, you're not dehydrated.

plan.title: Domperidone — before meals, 3 times a day, within a week
plan.why:
It helps the stomach push food onward and reduces nausea. **Don't go over 30 mg (3 bottles) a day** — heart side effects increased above this.

**Don't use it together with antifungal tablets for athlete's foot or thrush, or antibiotics such as clarithromycin.**

plan.title: For motion sickness, indigestion, hangover or gastroenteritis, those pages fit better
plan.why: If you feel queasy in a car, see **motion sickness**; bloated after overeating, **indigestion**; the day after drinking, **hangover**; with diarrhoea, **gastroenteritis**. There are medicines suited to each cause.

notWorking.title: If it continues after two days
steps: **See a doctor.** The cause needs to be found.
If you've started a new medicine, **bring the medicine packet.** Side effects are a common cause.
If it keeps recurring for weeks with weight loss, tests such as an **upper endoscopy** may be needed.

faq.q: Can I take medicine right after vomiting?
faq.a: Right after vomiting, medicine tends to come back up too. **Wait about 30 minutes; if a sip or two of water stays down**, take it then.

faq.q: Can I take domperidone liquid for a hangover?
faq.a: The package insert lists **nausea and vomiting**, so you can use it when you feel queasy. But **don't go over 3 times a day**, and don't take several bottles while still not sober.

faq.q: I heard domperidone is bad for the heart?
faq.a: In an analysis pooling observational studies, the risk of **ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death was about 1.7 times** higher while taking it, but this wasn't clear **at 30 mg a day or less**. So sticking to the set amount (3 bottles a day) and under a week matters, and it isn't used if you have heart disease or take antifungal tablets for athlete's foot or thrush, or antibiotics such as clarithromycin.

nausea.clinic: At the clinic, **the cause** (gastroenteritis, gastritis, pregnancy, medicine side effects, dizziness and so on) is sorted out first, and if vomiting stops you eating, **fluids and anti-sickness medicine are given by injection or drip**.
nausea.pharm: At the pharmacy you can buy **oral rehydration solution** (to prevent dehydration) and **domperidone liquid** (for nausea). Domperidone isn't used **during pregnancy, with heart disease, or with antifungals or some antibiotics**. **If you're over 60**, check with a doctor before taking it — the leaflet says so.

arthritis.lead: For long-standing joint pain, the surest treatment isn't medicine but **exercise and weight control**. What international osteoarthritis guidelines all put first is education, exercise and weight loss, and among medicines **anti-inflammatory gels come first**. Anti-inflammatory tablets work well but burden the stomach, kidneys and heart, so they're used briefly. Over 65, this difference matters especially.
arthritis.planLabel: The key point: step 1 isn't medicine
how: Spread **the topical medicine** thinly over the painful joint 3–4 times a day. Don't rub it in — let it soak in.
Only on very painful days, add ibuprofen after a meal. If you're 65 or older, keep famotidine alongside too.
Check that morning stiffness doesn't last more than 30 minutes. If it does, it may be a different arthritis (rheumatoid).
Give **30 minutes of walking a day and thigh-strengthening exercise** the same weight as medicine. This is the real treatment.
If the knee is swollen and hot, rest a few days with ice packs, and get moving again once it settles.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I have knee arthritis. An anti-inflammatory gel, please. And something to take on very painful days.”
Be sure to mention blood-pressure medicine, blood thinners, and any kidney or stomach problems. Whether anti-inflammatory tablets are OK depends on this.
selfcare: Try **front-thigh exercise** for just 10 minutes a day. Sitting on a chair, straighten your knee and hold for 5 seconds, 20 times, morning and evening. It builds the strength that supports the knee.
Losing even a little weight clearly eases the knees. Walking and exercise in water are gentle on the joints.
Use warm packs to loosen stiffness, and ice packs on days it swells.
Going down stairs puts several times more strain on the knee than going up. Always hold the handrail.
Avoid squatting, sitting cross-legged and kneeling as much as you can.
avoid: If you stop moving altogether because it hurts, the muscles waste and it hurts more. Rest only for the few days the pain is bad, then get moving again.
Don't take anti-inflammatory tablets every day for months. Especially over 65, the risk of stomach bleeding and kidney strain is high.
Don't take two anti-inflammatories at once.
Don't decide on injections or procedures 'good for joints' from adverts alone. The evidence is divided on many of them.

plan.title: Exercise and weight — the surest treatment
plan.why: Thigh-strengthening exercise and walking work as well as painkillers with no side effects. Losing 1 kg of body weight takes three to four times that much force off the knee.

plan.title: Acetaminophen — as a base
plan.why: It can ease pain a little, but large analyses show only a small effect in arthritis. Anti-inflammatory gels and exercise come first; add it if it still hurts.

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory patch — a 'profen' type
plan.why:
An anti-inflammatory you stick right on the painful joint. **It works about as well as tablets with far less burden on the stomach**, so doctors also prescribe it alongside and recommend it a lot. Choose one with 'profen' in the name, such as ketoprofen.

But **itching or burning of the skin happens more often than with gels.** Don't keep sticking it on the same spot — move it a little each time. With ketoprofen, the skin where it was becomes sensitive to sunlight, so keep that area covered for up to 2 weeks after removing it.

plan.title: Gel — for places like fingers where patches won't stay
plan.why: For fingers and wrists where patches are hard to stick, diclofenac gel is handy. It tends to cause fewer skin reactions than patches. Don't use it on top of a patch — they're the same family.

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory tablets — briefly, when it hurts
plan.why: Only briefly, for the few days with swelling and warmth. In older people they burden the stomach, kidneys and blood pressure, so they're not a medicine to take every day on and on.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues. Over 65, the risk of stomach bleeding from anti-inflammatories rises sharply — use them briefly.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't helping much
steps: First check that you're using enough of the topical medicine, regularly 3–4 times a day. A little here and there doesn't work.
Are you exercising too? Medicine alone has clear limits. Learning exercises from a physiotherapist helps a lot.
If pain keeps you awake at night or the distance you can walk drops noticeably, see a doctor. It's time to discuss injections or surgery.
If the knee suddenly swells, gets hot and you have a fever, it may be infection or gout. See a doctor that same day.

faq.q: Is glucosamine worth taking?
faq.a: Guidelines disagree. The international osteoarthritis society doesn't recommend it, while the European osteoporosis and osteoarthritis society recommends a particular formulation. A 2024 combined analysis comparing many treatments at once found that **on its own it fell short of a clinically meaningful drop in pain**, but showed a meaningful difference when used with omega-3 or ibuprofen. If you notice no difference after 3 months, there's no reason to keep going.

faq.q: Do cartilage injections regrow cartilage?
faq.a: No. What people call cartilage injections (hyaluronic acid) **help lubrication to reduce pain**; they can't bring worn cartilage back. The effect also varies a lot from person to person.

faq.q: Is it a problem if it hurts more going up or going down stairs?
faq.a:
**If it hurts more going down**, there's often a lot of strain at the front of the knee (the kneecap joint). The force on the knee is much greater going down.

Then avoid stairs and do **front-thigh exercise** first. Using the lift isn't 'getting weak' — it's saving the joint while it hurts. Once the pain settles, build up walking on flat ground first.

arthritis.clinic: Doctors use **an anti-inflammatory briefly when it hurts**, often together with **a profen-type anti-inflammatory patch**. If surrounding muscles are tight too, a muscle relaxant is added, and an acid medicine if the stomach is sensitive. If it's severe, joint injections or rehabilitation exercise follow.
arthritis.pharm: **Patches are the easiest tool at the pharmacy** — put an anti-inflammatory patch such as ketoprofen on the sore joint, and add an oral painkiller or anti-inflammatory for a few days when it hurts. For places like fingers where patches are hard to stick, use a gel.

bite.lead: Most bites settle in a few days. The most important thing is **not scratching** — the real problem is germs getting in through scratch wounds. **Ticks are different**, though. A tick attached to you after time in long grass, field work or clearing graves needs to be **removed right away and properly**, and for 2 weeks afterwards you must watch for fever. In Korea, ticks carry serious diseases (scrub typhus and severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome), and **the older you are, the more dangerous they are**. And **shortness of breath or a swelling face after a bee sting is an emergency**.
bite.planTitle: What to do after a bite
bite.planLabel: The goal is to stop the scratching
how: **If a tick is attached**, grip it with fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin as possible and pull **straight up without twisting**. Wash the spot with soap and water and disinfect it.
Wash the bite with soap and water and hold ice wrapped in a towel on it for 10 minutes.
Apply anti-itch cream only on the bite, 3–4 times a day for 3–4 days.
If you have many bites and itch all over, add an antihistamine tablet once a day.
**If a bee stinger is left in**, scrape it out sideways with a fingernail or a card. Squeezing it with tweezers pushes in more venom.
**Write down the date of the tick bite and watch for fever for 2 weeks.** If you get a fever, be sure to tell the doctor about the bite.
pharmacy: Just tell the pharmacist “Something for mosquito (insect) bites, please.” If you have many bites, add “and something to take by mouth too.”
**If a tick bit you, go to a doctor, not the pharmacy.** Especially right away if you have a fever.
If it's for a child, give their age. Each product has different age limits.
selfcare: **Don't scratch.** Keep nails short, and if it's hard to bear, repeat the ice packs.
If itching keeps you awake at night, an antihistamine before bed helps.
**For field work, grave clearing, grave visits or hiking, wear long sleeves and long trousers with cuffs tucked in**, and don't leave clothes on the grass or lie down on it.
When you get back, **shake out and wash your clothes right away, and check your whole body while bathing** — especially armpits, groin, behind the knees and in your hair.
Spraying repellent on clothes and exposed skin helps.
avoid: **Don't grab and rip or twist a tick off with your fingers.** Its mouthparts stay in the skin.
**Don't hold a flame to a tick or put alcohol or petroleum jelly on it.** The tick releases more saliva, raising the risk of passing on disease.
Don't put saliva on it or press a cross into it with your fingernail. Germs get in.
Don't squeeze a bee stinger with tweezers. The venom sac gets pressed and more venom goes in.
Don't take cold medicine together with an antihistamine tablet. The drowsy ingredient doubles up.
Don't pop blisters.

plan.title: If one is attached — pull it straight out with tweezers
plan.why: Grip it with fine-tipped tweezers **as close to the skin as possible (at the tick's head)**, and pull slowly **straight up** without twisting. Squeezing the body pushes more saliva into you. After removing it, wash with soap and water and disinfect.

plan.title: Cold pack for 10 minutes
plan.why: Ice wrapped in a towel noticeably reduces itching and swelling. It's often faster than medicine.

plan.title: Anti-itch cream
plan.why: Antihistamine, numbing and menthol ingredients calm the itch right away. Use only on the bites, for a few days.

plan.title: Antihistamine tablets — for many bites
plan.why: Helps when you itch all over or can't sleep at night. A non-drowsy one in the daytime; at night it doesn't matter.

plan.title: Antibiotic ointment — only if scratching made it infected
plan.why: Use it only when there's pus and redness is spreading. Putting it on just in case only builds resistance.

notWorking.title: If it isn't healing or you get a fever
steps: **A fever within 1–2 weeks of outdoor activity should raise suspicion of a tick-borne infection.** See a doctor that same day, and **be sure to say you were in grassy areas.** That one sentence speeds up the diagnosis.
A **black scab (eschar)** at the bite with fever may be scrub typhus. It responds well to antibiotics, but delay is dangerous.
If the bite keeps getting bigger after a day and redness is spreading, it may be a bacterial infection. See a doctor.
If the itching lasts more than a week, other skin conditions such as scabies need to be checked.
If you've ever had hives all over or shortness of breath after a bee sting, it's dangerous next time too. Discuss how to prepare with a doctor.

faq.q: The bite has swollen up to the size of my palm. Is that OK?
faq.a: A large swelling just around a mosquito bite isn't unusual in children and sensitive people. **If there's no fever and breathing is easy**, cold packs and medicine for a few days is fine. But if the redness keeps spreading and it hurts, that's infection — see a doctor.

faq.q: I heard holding a flame to a tick makes it drop off?
faq.a: **Don't.** A flame, alcohol or petroleum jelly startles the tick so it releases more saliva, actually raising the risk of passing on disease. **Gripping it close to the skin with tweezers and pulling straight up** is the right way.

faq.q: Is a tick bite always dangerous?
faq.a: Most pass without trouble. But in Korea ticks carry **scrub typhus** and **severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome**, and they're more dangerous the older you are. So two things matter: **write down the date of the bite and watch for fever for 2 weeks**, and if you get a fever, **say you were in grassy areas**.

bite.clinic: Topical medicine is usually enough. **If scratching makes it infected**, an antibiotic ointment or tablets; if it swells badly, a short course of steroids.
bite.pharm: **A topical anti-itch medicine comes first**, and if you've been bitten in several places, add an oral antihistamine. An ice pack reduces itching quite a bit.

burn.lead: With a burn, **the first 20 minutes change the outcome** — 20 minutes under running cool water (not ice water), **within 3 hours of the injury**. In data from 2,495 children, those who got this **clearly needed skin grafts less often.** This one step matters more than any ointment. Ice, alcohol, soybean paste, potato and toothpaste make the wound deeper.
burn.planTitle: When you get burned — do this
burn.planLabel: Red and stinging from boiling water, oil or an iron
how: To size a burn, **your palm (with fingers) is about 1% of your body**. Over 3 palms in adults, or over 1 in children, go to hospital.
Oil and steam burns are deeper than they look. For electrical or chemical burns, go to hospital even if the surface looks fine.
After it heals, **keep it out of the sun for at least 1 year** — otherwise dark pigment stays (up to 2 years for deeper burns).
pharmacy: “I burned myself with boiling water. There's a blister, and I didn't pop it. A burn dressing, please.”
“How big does it have to be before I should go to hospital?”
selfcare: Running cool water for 20 minutes — time it by the clock. It's longer than you think.
Leave blisters alone. If one bursts on its own, don't peel off the skin — just cover it.
If nothing leaks through, the dressing only needs changing every 2–3 days.
avoid: Putting it on ice or in ice water (makes the wound deeper)
Applying alcohol, soybean paste, soy sauce, potato, toothpaste or raw aloe leaves
Popping blisters or peeling off the skin
Putting cotton wool (not gauze) directly on it — it sticks to the wound

plan.title: 20 minutes under running cool water — right now
plan.why: Run the tap **gently for 20 minutes**. Ice or ice water tightens blood vessels and makes the wound deeper. Take off **rings, watches and tight clothing near the burn before it swells**. Keep the rest of the body warm so you don't get chilled (especially children and older people).

plan.title: Don't pop blisters — cover them
plan.why: The blister skin is the best dressing there is. A **moist dressing (hydrocolloid, foam)** hurts less and leaves less scarring. If you don't have one, you can loosely cover it with clean cling film and go to hospital.

plan.title: Painkillers if it hurts
plan.why: Burns hurt a lot. Don't put up with it — take **acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen**. Taking it 30 minutes before a dressing change makes it much easier.

plan.title: If you're worried about infection — antibiotic ointment
plan.why: If the skin has come off, apply thinly and cover. But **large or deep burns need a hospital, not an ointment**. Yellow oozing scabs with redness spreading around them mean infection.

plan.title: What happens in hospital
plan.why: The dressing is chosen by depth and size, and dead skin is removed if needed. Tetanus vaccination is checked, and deep burns are assessed up to skin grafting. Burns on the **face, hands, feet, joints or genitals** need specialist care even if small.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Superficial burns heal in 1–2 weeks. **If it hasn't healed after more than 2 weeks**, it's a deep burn — see a doctor.
If the pain suddenly gets worse, or the fluid turns yellow and smells, that's infection — see a doctor right away.

faq.q: Should I use burn cream (silver sulfadiazine)?
faq.a: For shallow burns, an analysis (2013 combined analysis) found it actually slows healing. It's a **prescription** medicine for deep burns or when infection risk is high. For shallow burns, 20 minutes of cool water + a burn dressing is enough.

faq.q: My blister burst.
faq.a: Rinse under running water, don't peel off the skin — leave it and cover it. Use a **non-stick dressing**, not cotton wool, and if the fluid turns yellow and smells, that's infection — see a doctor.

faq.q: How big before I go to hospital?
faq.a: **Bigger than your palm**, on the face, hands, feet, joints or genitals, electrical or chemical burns, or large blisters or skin that is white and numb — see a doctor. For babies, people 65 and over, and people with diabetes, go even for smaller ones.

burn.clinic: **Depth and area** decide the dressing, and dead skin is removed if needed. Tetanus vaccination is checked.
burn.pharm: **20 minutes under cool running water** comes first (not ice). Don't burst blisters; cover them with a moist dressing. If it hurts, don't hold back on painkillers.

conjunctivitis.lead: Pink eye (conjunctivitis), with red eyes and discharge, comes in **viral, bacterial and allergic** kinds, and each is handled differently. Clear, watery discharge that starts in one eye and spreads is viral — antibiotics don't help, and handwashing is the treatment. Lots of thick yellow discharge is bacterial, but an analysis pooling several studies shows **more than half get better on their own in 4–9 days without treatment**, and antibiotics raise that chance only a little.
conjunctivitis.planTitle: Eye infections — sort out the type first
conjunctivitis.planLabel: The kind of discharge is the fork in the road
how: **Wash your hands often** and don't touch your eyes. Use your own towel and pillowcase and change them daily.
Wipe away discharge with clean gauze dampened in lukewarm water, **from the inner corner outwards**. Throw each piece of gauze away after one use.
**Cold compresses** a few times a day reduce swelling and burning.
Rinse often with artificial tears. Throw single-use vials away after one use.
If you use several eye drops, wait at least 5 minutes between them.
Take a break from contact lenses and eye make-up until it has fully cleared.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist what the discharge is like: “It's clear, like tears” / “It's yellow and sticky” / “It's terribly itchy” — that one phrase decides the medicine.
Be sure to say whether you wear contact lenses. Redness in a lens wearer can be a corneal infection, so the rules are different.
selfcare: **Handwashing is half the treatment.** Epidemic eye infections in particular spread through hands.
Keep towels, pillowcases and toiletries separate from your family's, and boil or change them often.
Use cold compresses 3–4 times a day. They reduce swelling and the gritty feeling.
Epidemic eye infection is **contagious for 1–2 weeks** after symptoms start. Avoid crowded places and swimming pools.
Don't rub your eyes. It's the commonest way to spread it to the other eye.
avoid: Don't wear an eye patch. Tears pool and germs grow more easily.
Don't share eye drops someone else has used.
Don't use steroid eye drops on your own. They raise eye pressure, and with a corneal infection they make things much worse.
Don't wear contact lenses during treatment.
Don't wash your eyes with salt water or home remedies.

plan.title: Handwashing, separate towels — most important
plan.why: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis in particular is extremely contagious. Washing your hands often and keeping towels and pillows separate both treats you and protects your family.

plan.title: Artificial tears, cold compresses
plan.why: They ease the gritty, burning feeling. Preservative-free single-use vials irritate less. For viral infections, this is essentially the main treatment.

plan.title: If itching is the main symptom — antihistamine (tablet or allergy eye drops)
plan.why: If both eyes are very itchy and runny nose and sneezing come along, it's allergic. An antihistamine by mouth helps. If only the eyes itch, **allergy eye drops (ketotifen, cromolyn)** work right in the eye.

plan.title: Antibiotic eye drops — when there's a lot of yellow discharge
plan.why: If there's lots of yellow discharge and the eye is swollen or painful, it may be **bacterial conjunctivitis**, so **see a doctor** — you may need antibiotic eye drops or ointment. It often gets better without them, but they speed recovery by a few days.

notWorking.title: If it isn't healing well
steps: A viral eye infection can last **1–2 weeks**. It's not unusual for it not to clear in a few days.
If it's unchanged after a week or getting worse, see an eye doctor.
**If the eye hurts, your vision drops, or light is very glaring**, it has gone beyond conjunctivitis (keratitis, uveitis). Go to an eye doctor right away.
Redness and pain in a contact-lens wearer can be a corneal infection and is close to an emergency.
If itching is the main symptom and it comes back every season, it's allergic conjunctivitis. A prescription eye drop from an eye doctor makes it much easier.

faq.q: Do I really need antibiotic eye drops?
faq.a: Even when bacterial, **56 in 100 people got better on their own within 4–9 days on a dummy treatment**, and 68 with antibiotics (2023 combined analysis) — so for every 100 people using them, 12 more get better sooner. They work, but not by much. They matter when you need to get back to school or work quickly or symptoms are bad. If the discharge is clear, it's viral and they don't help at all.

faq.q: How contagious are eye infections?
faq.a: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is extremely contagious and can spread for **1–2 weeks after symptoms start**. Handwashing, separate towels and avoiding crowded places are needed.

faq.q: How many days until an eye infection clears?
faq.a:
**A viral eye infection usually takes 1–2 weeks**, and the first 3–5 days are the worst. Starting in one eye and moving to the other is also a common course.

**It stays contagious longer than you'd think** — keep using a separate towel and wash your hands often until the discharge dries up. For children, it's best to ask at the visit when they can go back to nursery or school.

conjunctivitis.clinic: The medicine depends on **whether it's bacterial, viral or allergic**. Bacterial: antibiotic eye drops; allergic: antihistamine eye drops.
conjunctivitis.pharm: All you can do is soothe it with **artificial tears and cold compresses**. If itching is the main symptom, an oral antihistamine helps. **Don't put just any medicine in your eyes.**

dizziness.lead:
With dizziness, **sorting out the cause comes before medicine**. Most of it comes from the ear (loose ear crystals, vestibular neuritis) and isn't a big worry, but **the problem is that dizziness from the brain can look exactly the same from the outside**.

When **136 people in an emergency room who just said they were 'dizzy' and had a normal neurological exam** had a brain MRI, **about 4 in 100 (3.7%) had a cerebellar stroke**. That was true even without 'obvious signs' like slurred speech or weakness on one side.

So **don't get through new dizziness on pharmacy medicine — see a doctor.** If it's loose ear crystals, a positioning manoeuvre fixes it on the spot; if it's the brain, time is everything.
dizziness.planLabel: Finding the cause comes before medicine
how: First check for **danger signs**. Slurred speech, weakness on one side, or seeing double — call 119 right away.
While the room is spinning, **lie still** somewhere safe with your eyes open, looking at one point. Closing your eyes makes it worse for some people.
If you feel like vomiting, take one dose of motion-sickness medicine — **don't go past 3 days.**
When getting up, sit on the edge of the bed for 1 minute, then stand slowly. Especially if you take blood-pressure medicine.
Once it settles, don't just lie down — **move around a little at a time.** The brain needs movement to relearn balance.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I'm dizzy and feel like I'm going to vomit,” and mention any blood-pressure medicine, sleeping pills or prostate medicine you take. Medicines are often the cause of dizziness.
If you're 65 or older, be sure to say so. Motion-sickness medicine raises the risk of falling.
selfcare: Get up **slowly**. Making a habit of sitting for 1 minute before standing reduces falls from dizziness.
Clear door thresholds and cables in the house, and leave a small light on at night. Falling while dizzy is the bigger problem.
Drink enough water. Dehydration is a common cause.
If your ears feel blocked and ringing comes with it, write that down. It helps the diagnosis a lot.
After it settles, gradually walk more. Not moving slows recovery.
avoid: Don't take motion-sickness medicine for more than a week. It hinders recovery, and in older people it causes falls, constipation and urine retention.
Don't stay lying down for days because you're dizzy.
Don't stop blood-pressure or other medicines on your own. Adjust them with your doctor.
Don't drive or climb ladders or stairs while dizzy.
Alcohol definitely makes dizziness worse.

plan.title: ① Call 119 right away — if there's even one of these
plan.why:
Slurred speech · weakness in an arm or leg on one side · seeing double · numbness on one side of the face · **unable to stand or walk on your own** · with the worst headache of your life.

**'Unable to walk on your own' is especially important.** People who are dizzy from the ear may stagger, but they can walk with support. Not being able to walk at all, or falling to one side, points to the cerebellum.

plan.title: ② Only a few seconds when lying down or turning over → possibly loose ear crystals
plan.why:
The most common dizziness. It **stops within 10 seconds to 1 minute**, and you're fine while still, but it comes back only when you change position.

**The treatment is a positioning manoeuvre (Epley), not medicine.** An ear, nose and throat doctor or neurologist does it on the spot, and it usually gets better in one or two tries.

**But don't decide for yourself that 'it's ear crystals'.** Dizziness from the brain can also seem to change with position.

plan.title: ③ Anaemia, thyroid, irregular heartbeat — one blood test sorts them out
plan.why:
There's dizziness that is **neither ear nor brain**. Rather than a 'spinning' feeling, it often comes as **lightheadedness, a floating feeling, or vision going dark**.

**Anaemia** — along with dizziness, you **get breathless easily, feel weak, and your face and inner eyelids are pale**. For women, clues are heavy or long periods; for everyone, **black or bloody stools** (there may be hidden stomach or bowel bleeding). If you've taken acid reducers for a long time or had stomach surgery, **low vitamin B12 or iron** is also common.

**Thyroid** — when underactive you feel sluggish, puffy and cold; when overactive you get palpitations and lose weight.

**Irregular heartbeat** — dizziness **comes on suddenly and stops suddenly**, with palpitations or 'briefly feeling faint'.

All three are sorted out with **one blood test and one heart tracing (ECG)**. If dizziness keeps coming back and the ears look normal, be sure to check this side.

plan.title: If you feel faint when standing up — the answer isn't more medicine
plan.why:
Feeling faint when you get up from sitting, especially in the morning or after the toilet, is **blood pressure dropping for a moment**. It's a common cause of falls in older people, and **medicines are often the cause** — blood-pressure medicine, water pills, prostate medicine (tamsulosin) and antidepressants are typical.

**What to do**
· **Sit on the edge of the bed for 30 seconds** before getting up
· Drink enough water — dehydration is the most common trigger
· Avoid hot baths, heavy drinking and standing for long
· Squeeze and relax your calf muscles a few times before getting up

**Don't stop medicines on your own.** Instead, tell the doctor “I feel faint when I stand up” and show your list of medicines — they can move the time you take them or switch to another medicine.

plan.title: It may be the medicines you take
plan.why:
Dizziness is **one of the most common medicine side effects**. Especially for older people on several medicines, the right order is to look at current medicines before adding a new one.

Common ones — blood-pressure medicine, water pills, prostate medicine, sleep aids, 1st-generation antihistamines (cold and motion-sickness medicine), antidepressants. Especially **if dry mouth and constipation come with it**, anticholinergic effects are likely piling up.

If you add your medicines to **My medicine box** in this app, it works out overlapping ingredients and a burden score.

plan.title: Motion-sickness medicine — 'just a few days' when you feel like vomiting
plan.why:
Helps when nausea and vomiting are bad (dimenhydrinate). But **using it for three days or more stops the brain relearning balance**, so recovery is slower.

**Older people should be especially careful** — drowsiness, dry mouth, urine retention and falls come with it. And this medicine **covers up the cause.** Don't put off seeing a doctor because it settles.

plan.title: What happens in the clinic
plan.why:
Medicine comes only after the cause is sorted out. Three are often used for dizziness in the clinic.

· **Motion-sickness medicine (dimenhydrinate)** — the first few days when you feel like vomiting. Short for older people because of drowsiness and falls.
· **Ginkgo leaf extract** — also sold at pharmacies. In dizziness trials it was no different from betahistine, but there are reviews finding **betahistine itself no different from a dummy pill**, so it's hard to say it 'definitely works'.
· **Betahistine** — a prescription medicine long used for Ménière's disease, but re-pooling several analyses found no clear benefit over a dummy pill.

**The weak medicine isn't the flaw — the flaw is reaching for medicine without looking for the cause.** For ear crystals it's a positioning manoeuvre, for anaemia iron, and for irregular heartbeat the heart side.

notWorking.title: If the dizziness continues
steps: If it spins for a few seconds **only when lying down or turning over**, it's most likely loose ear crystals. An exam by an ear, nose and throat doctor or neurologist and a positioning manoeuvre on the spot usually fix it in one or two goes. It's not something to get through on medicine.
If your ears feel blocked with ringing and it recurs for tens of minutes to hours at a time, it may be Ménière's disease. You need to see a doctor.
Please review the medicines you take. Blood-pressure medicine, sleeping pills, prostate medicine and water pills are common causes.
If walking becomes noticeably unsteady along with dizziness, or your face goes numb, the brain needs to be checked.
Dizziness from anaemia, thyroid problems or irregular heartbeat is also common. A blood test and heart tracing (ECG) can check.

faq.q: Why isn't medicine used for loose ear crystals?
faq.a: The cause is tiny stones (ear crystals) in the inner ear that have come loose and roll around, so **a positioning manoeuvre that puts the stones back (the Epley manoeuvre)** is the treatment. In studies it also worked better than rehabilitation at 1 week. Medicine only reduces nausea and can't fix the cause.

faq.q: Could my dizziness be from anaemia?
faq.a: Anaemia tends to come as **lightheadedness and weakness rather than spinning**. If you get breathless climbing stairs and look pale, have a blood test.

faq.q: I'm dizzy — do I really need a brain MRI?
faq.a:
**Most people don't.** But deciding 'not needed' is what the exam is for — the jerking of the eyes, how the eyes react when the head is turned quickly, and whether you can walk on your own. Looking at these three often sorts it out more accurately than imaging.

However, **in the early phase even an MRI can miss a small stroke**, so if the exam points to the brain, you're watched even with a normal scan. So don't be reassured just by 'they did a scan and said it's fine' — listen to the doctor's explanation too.

dizziness.clinic: **Dizziness is diagnosed by looking at the eyes and walking.** Which way the eyes flicker, whether the eyes keep up when the head is turned quickly, whether you can walk unaided — these three sort out **whether it's the ear or the brain**. If needed, a repositioning manoeuvre (Epley) is done on the spot, and if the brain is suspected, imaging is done too. **Blood tests for anaemia and thyroid, and an ECG for heart rhythm problems** are also done at this point.
dizziness.pharm: All the pharmacy can offer is **a motion sickness medicine (dimenhydrinate)**, and it's **a medicine that settles nausea for a few days**, not one that fixes the cause. Using it beyond three days actually slows recovery. **Don't cover up dizziness of unknown cause with medicine.**

eczema.lead: Managing eczema and atopic dermatitis stands on **three legs** — moisturising (at least twice a day, within 3 minutes of bathing), avoiding irritants (hot water, soap, wool, sweat), and calming inflammation (steroid ointment, **short and generous**). Applying steroids sparingly out of fear actually makes it last longer — one fingertip length covers 2 palms' area, 1–2 times a day; once it clears, stop and just moisturise.
eczema.planTitle: Itchy eczema and atopic skin — do this
eczema.planLabel: Dry, red and itchy on inner arms, neck or hands
how: Face, skin folds and children: a mild strength (hydrocortisone); body, hands and feet: one step up. If the same spot still needs it after more than 1 week, see a doctor — there are prescription strengths and **non-steroid ointments (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus)**.
Antihistamines have weak evidence for **directly** reducing eczema itch. Use them only to help sleep when scratching keeps you up at night.
pharmacy: “My inner-arm eczema is itchy — a mild steroid ointment and a moisturiser, please. Can I use it for a few days, and is there something to take if it itches at night?”
Be sure to say if it's for **the face, armpits or nappy area** — the steroid strength used is different.
selfcare: Oozing, yellow crusts or sudden worsening → bacterial infection (impetigo), needing antibiotic ointment or antibiotics by mouth (prescription). Small blisters **in clusters** that hurt → herpes — see a doctor now.
Food and house-dust-mite tests are done by a doctor **when there's a suspicion**. Cutting out foods without testing harms children's nutrition.
avoid: Hot water, long baths, scrubbing with exfoliating towels
Soap and scented cleansers
Applying steroids sparingly out of fear — or the opposite, strong strengths on the face for long
Steroids alone on infected skin
Wool and tight clothing, scratching (keep nails short)

plan.title: Moisturiser — at least twice a day, within 3 minutes of bathing
plan.why: The backbone of eczema care. It comes **before and lasts longer** than anti-inflammatory medicine. Apply a low-irritant one generously. If it stings, switch from one with urea to **a gentle moisturiser**.

plan.title: Steroid cream — short and generous on red, itchy patches
plan.why: **Applying a little makes it last longer.** One fingertip length is for two palms' area. Cut down once the redness settles. On the face and skin folds, a mild one for a short time.

plan.title: When scratching stops you sleeping — antihistamines
plan.why: Know this first — **the itch itself isn't well controlled by antihistamines.** Eczema itch isn't caused by histamine alone, and adding an antihistamine to creams brought no clear benefit (analysis pooling several studies). So they're used not as an eczema treatment but **to protect sleep** — more nights without scratching give the skin time to heal. Cetirizine is a little drowsy for a 2nd-generation one, so once in the evening is right; use it for a few days and stop.

plan.title: Dexpanthenol
plan.why: A gentle repair ointment for dry, cracked spots without oozing, and for children. **It can't replace steroids** — it doesn't work on red, flared-up inflammation. Its place is after inflammation settles, or alongside moisturiser in spots like the face where steroids are hard to use for long.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Pharmacy steroid ointment (hydrocortisone) is **within 1 week per the package insert**. If it's unchanged after 1 week or you need it longer, a doctor sets the strength and duration. For babies under 2, talk to a doctor before applying. Keep moisturising.

First check the amount and frequency of moisturiser (usually too little) → steroids **generously for 1–2 weeks** → if that still fails or it keeps recurring, a dermatologist (prescription strengths, non-steroids, tests).

faq.q: I'm scared of steroid cream side effects.
faq.a: With pharmacy creams, sticking to **under 1 week** and a mild strength keeps the risk of skin thinning low. Applying it thinly for a long time out of fear is actually worse. Once it clears, stop and just keep moisturising.

faq.q: Which moisturiser should I buy?
faq.a: It's **amount and frequency**, more than the type. A fragrance-free cream or ointment, within 3 minutes of bathing, generously at least twice a day. Applying it thinly to save it doesn't work. An analysis pooling 77 trials (6,603 people) found **no evidence that any one moisturiser is better.** Instead, using a moisturiser reduced flare-ups (risk of a flare cut by more than half) and, over the trial period, people **used an average of 9.3 g less steroid cream**. But these two results each came from just two small trials, so the quality of evidence is low. A moisturiser works best not as a 'replacement' for steroids but **alongside** them.

faq.q: Can I just take an antihistamine when it itches?
faq.a: For atopic itch the effect is small (2019 combined analysis). Only something like cetirizine when scratching keeps you from sleeping at night. The real medicine for itch is moisturising and ointment that calms the inflammation.

eczema.clinic: **Moisturising is the foundation, and steroid ointment puts out the flare.** Strength and duration are matched to the condition; if it's severe, other types of ointment or tablets follow.
eczema.pharm: **Applying moisturiser at least twice a day, within 3 minutes after bathing,** is half the job. On red, itchy patches, hydrocortisone **for a short course, in the appropriate amount**. Applying too little can prolong the flare.

gastroenteritis.lead: The treatment for sudden gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhoea is **not medicine but water and electrolytes**. Anti-diarrhoeals and antibiotics are mostly unnecessary and often do harm. What international guidelines consistently put first is **oral rehydration solution**. Older people and babies can become dangerously dehydrated within a single day, so be sure to watch how much they drink and whether they're passing urine.
how: Drink **oral rehydration solution**, a cup (about 200 mL) each time you have diarrhoea or vomit. If you're vomiting, start with **a spoonful every 5 minutes** and slowly increase.
Don't starve. If your stomach can take it, start with soft food like **porridge, white rice, bananas or boiled potato**. The old way of fasting for a day slows recovery.
Avoid milk, fatty food, alcohol and coffee for a few days.
If you use diosmectite, keep it 2 hours apart from other medicines.
Rather than whether the diarrhoea stops, watch **whether you're passing urine well**. That's the traffic light for dehydration.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I think it's gastroenteritis. No fever or blood (or: there is). Oral rehydration solution, please.”
Say first whether there's fever or bloody stool. Whether an anti-diarrhoeal is OK depends on this.
If it's for an older person or a baby, give their age. The dehydration thresholds are different.
selfcare: **Water a little and often.** Gulping it down brings it straight back up. Chilled goes down much more easily.
Wash your hands with soap often. Norovirus isn't killed well by hand sanitiser. 30 seconds under running water.
Wipe the toilet and door handles with diluted bleach. It's the surest way to stop it spreading to family.
Don't prepare food for others until you've recovered. Be careful for two days after symptoms stop.
Probiotics have evidence for preventing diarrhoea caused by antibiotics. Whether they speed recovery from ordinary gastroenteritis was unclear in recent analyses.
avoid: Don't take anti-diarrhoeals for diarrhoea with fever or blood. The germs get trapped in the body and it gets worse.
Don't give anti-diarrhoeals to babies and young children.
Don't take antibiotics for gastroenteritis on your own. It's mostly viral, so they don't help and cause more diarrhoea.
Don't take anti-inflammatory painkillers (ibuprofen and the like) while dehydrated. They damage the kidneys.
Don't drink only sports drinks. They're high in sugar and low in sodium and can increase diarrhoea. If you use them, dilute about half with water.
Don't starve. Long fasting slows the recovery of the gut lining.

plan.title: Drink often — this is the treatment
plan.why:
Vomiting and diarrhoea drain water and salt fast. Drinking a lot at once brings it back up — **a sip or two, often.**

**First choice is pharmacy 'oral rehydration solution'.** Salt and glucose have to be there **together** for water to be absorbed from the gut. It's what international guidelines consistently put first, and the World Health Organization formula shortened diarrhoea by about a quarter of a day compared with the old formula.

**If you can't get it**, dilute a sports drink about half with water. Plain sports drinks have a lot of sugar and can increase diarrhoea, and plain water alone dilutes your salt.

plan.title: If you vomit, step down one level
plan.why:
**If you vomit after rice, step down to porridge; if you vomit after porridge, step down to water** — one level at a time.

Forcing food down while vomiting can make you **choke and get it into the lungs** (aspiration pneumonia). Older people especially need to be careful.

If you hold one level down for a couple of hours, step back up: water → porridge → rice. The trick is **a little, often**, not a lot at once.

plan.title: Diosmectite — a gentle helper
plan.why: Coats the gut lining and shortens diarrhoea a little. Unlike anti-diarrhoeals it doesn't trap germs in the body, so it's relatively safe. Keep it 2 hours apart from other medicines. **It's for adults only** — the current package insert says not to use it in children.

plan.title: Loperamide — only when conditions fit
plan.why:
For watery diarrhoea with no fever and no blood, an anti-diarrhoeal (loperamide) shortens diarrhoea a little. But **if there's fever, or blood or mucus in the stool**, germs can stay in the gut, so it isn't used. That's why doctors don't give anti-diarrhoeals alone for long either.

For watery diarrhoea with no fever and no blood, use it briefly **only when you have a real reason it must stop**.

plan.title: If it cramps — trimebutine
plan.why: Twisting belly pain is the gut cramping. Trimebutine relaxes that cramp. In Korea **you can buy it at the pharmacy.**

plan.title: Ondansetron — when even water won't stay down
plan.why: If vomiting stops you keeping even water down, dehydration comes quickly. In the clinic, **ondansetron** stops the vomiting so you can drink oral rehydration solution. If you still can't drink, **getting a drip** is the answer.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: **If no urine for more than half a day**, or you feel faint standing up, that's dehydration. Don't hold out at home — get fluids by drip.
If you're vomiting so much you can't keep water down, **go to the emergency room that same day** — you need fluids and medicine to stop the vomiting.
If it's unchanged after two days, or you have diarrhoea more than six times a day, see a doctor.
