Blood in the stool or a fever over 38 degrees may mean a bacterial cause. See a doctor that same day.
For older people, babies and those with weak immunity, set the bar much lower. If something seems wrong for even half a day, go to hospital.

faq.q: Shouldn't I take something to stop the diarrhoea first?
faq.a: Diarrhoea is **the body's way of flushing out something bad**. Brief use by an adult for watery diarrhoea with no fever and no blood is fine, but **with fever or bloody stool, never.** It traps the germs in the gut and makes things much worse. The heart of treatment is always water and electrolytes.

faq.q: Do I have to eat only porridge?
faq.a: No. If your stomach can take it, eating **close to your normal diet** speeds recovery. Just avoid milk, fatty and spicy food for a few days, and start with soft food like porridge, white rice and bananas.

faq.q: How do I stop it spreading to my family?
faq.a: **Washing hands with soap under running water for 30 seconds** is the surest. Norovirus isn't killed well by alcohol hand sanitiser. Wipe the toilet and door handles with diluted bleach, and don't prepare food for others for two days after symptoms stop.

gastroenteritis.clinic: You need to stop vomiting before you can keep fluids down, so **an anti-sickness medicine** is used, **an antibiotic that stays inside the gut** for bacteria, and a medicine to relax spasms for tummy pain. If you're dizzy and your mouth is dry, a drip is the fastest fix.
gastroenteritis.pharm: **Taking a sip or two of water often** is the treatment. If you're vomiting, step down one stage at a time: from rice to porridge, from porridge to water. For medicine, use **one that binds toxins in the gut**, and acetaminophen for fever and pain. Antidiarrhoeals only briefly, and only when there's no fever or bloody stool.

hemorrhoid.lead: Blood in the toilet with a sore, itchy bottom most likely means haemorrhoids. Medicine works in three directions. **Ointments ease the pain right now, and flavonoid tablets reduce bleeding.** And **softening the stool removes the cause.** In an analysis pooling several studies, the tablets clearly reduced bleeding and itching, but their effect on pain wasn't certain. So for pain, sitz baths and ointments are the answer.
how: Take a **sitz bath** 2–3 times a day, especially after a bowel movement and before bed. Sit in warm water at about 40 degrees for 5–10 minutes. Don't add soap or disinfectant.
After the sitz bath, pat dry gently and apply **ointment or a suppository**. For 1 week at most.
Take **haemorrhoid tablets** after meals as the label says. Many products use a higher amount for the first few days, then less.
**Soften your stools.** Adjust a laxative such as magnesium hydroxide until stools are soft, and eat more vegetables and drink more water.
If it hurts a lot, use acetaminophen. Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers (ibuprofen, naproxen) while there's bleeding.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I have haemorrhoids and there's blood (or: it hurts). Something to apply and something to take, please. I'd also like to soften my stools.”
Say whether you're pregnant, have kidney problems, or take a blood thinner.
selfcare: **Don't sit on the toilet for more than 3 minutes.** Take your phone in and before you know it, 10 minutes have passed. This habit makes haemorrhoids worse.
Increase fibre with vegetables, fruit and whole grains, and drink 1.5–2 L of water a day.
When you feel the urge, go right away. Holding it makes stools harder.
Don't rub hard with toilet paper — rinse with water and pat dry gently.
If you sit for long periods, get up and walk briefly every 30 minutes.
avoid: Don't push hard for a long time. That's the moment haemorrhoids get pushed out.
Don't use haemorrhoid ointment containing a steroid for more than 1 week. The skin around the anus gets thinner.
Don't wipe often with wet wipes. Alcohol and fragrance damage the skin around the anus.
Don't assume all bleeding is haemorrhoids. Especially new bleeding after age 50 needs checking.
Don't sit in hot water for long. Lukewarm for 5–10 minutes is enough.

plan.title: Haemorrhoid ointment or suppository — for pain now
plan.why: The numbing ingredient eases pain and itching right away. Don't use products with a steroid for more than 1 week.

plan.title: Haemorrhoid tablets (diosmin) — when there's bleeding
plan.why: In an analysis pooling several studies, bleeding and itching clearly decreased. The effect on pain wasn't clear.

plan.title: Soften the stools — this is the real treatment
plan.why: Hard stools keep pushing haemorrhoids out. Softening them with a magnesium laxative sharply reduces recurrence. If your kidneys are poor, no magnesium.

plan.title: When it hurts a lot — acetaminophen
plan.why: For the few days when haemorrhoids are swollen and even sitting is hard. **Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers (ibuprofen, naproxen) here** — they burden the stomach and slightly interfere with stopping bleeding, which is worse while there's blood. Take it after meals, and cut down as soon as the pain settles.

plan.title: Warm sitz bath — as important as medicine
plan.why: Sitting in warm water for 5–10 minutes relaxes the anal muscles and reduces pain. It's a method that also reduced pain after haemorrhoid surgery.

notWorking.title: If treatment isn't helping much
steps: Check that you're doing sitz baths and stool softening together. It's an illness that medicine alone doesn't cure well.
If bleeding continues after 1–2 weeks, see a doctor. A simple procedure such as rubber band ligation often helps a lot.
A hard, very painful lump sticking out may be a thrombosed haemorrhoid. Treatment **within a few days** brings much more relief.
New bleeding after age 50, thinner stools, weight loss or anaemia — always have a bowel examination.

faq.q: Is it better to add salt or disinfectant to a sitz bath?
faq.a: No. **Plain water is enough.** There's no evidence salt water is better, and disinfectant or soap actually irritates the skin around the anus.

faq.q: Do I have to have surgery?
faq.a: Mostly not. Stages 1–2 are managed with lifestyle and medicine; stages 3–4 or repeated bleeding are reliably treated with a procedure or surgery. These days there are many methods, like rubber band ligation, that don't need a hospital stay.

faq.q: Is sitting on the toilet for a long time really bad?
faq.a:
Yes — it's **the easiest cause to fix**. The sitting position itself makes blood pool in the veins around the anus.

Don't go past **3 minutes**. Many people get better just by not taking their phone in. If nothing comes, it's better to get up and go back when you feel the urge.

hemorrhoid.clinic: **Softening the stool is the real treatment**, with ointments and tablets prescribed alongside. If a lump won't go back in, a procedure is considered.
hemorrhoid.pharm: **Soothe the current pain with ointment or suppositories**, and if there's blood, add an oral haemorrhoid medicine (diosmin). And **softening the stool** is the real treatment.

sprain.lead: The best evidence is for **moving early**, as far as it doesn't hurt. For the first 2–3 days soothe the pain with ice, and avoid heat, alcohol and massage.
sprain.planTitle: Sprained ankle and bruises — do this
how: **Moving early comes first** — from the first week, within a pain-free range, do ankle circles and 'write letters' with your foot, and if you can walk, walk a little at a time. In mild to moderate sprains, those who exercised in the first week got ankle function back sooner (a trial that split 101 people into groups). The longer it's immobilised, the slower the recovery.

Ice for the first 2–3 days — wrapped in a towel, 15–20 minutes at a time, 4–5 times a day. When resting, keep your foot above heart level; a bandage only as tight as doesn't make your toes tingle. (The evidence for rest, ice, compression and elevation one by one is weak, so they can't replace moving.)
Apply anti-inflammatory gel thinly over the swollen area 3–4 times a day. Don't put it on broken skin.
Warm compresses only after 2–3 days, once the swelling has gone down.
pharmacy: “I've twisted my ankle. An anti-inflammatory gel, please. And just one tablet medicine for if it hurts at night.”
If you take a blood thinner (warfarin, aspirin), say so — bruising can spread widely.
selfcare: To stop the ankle twisting again, wear an ankle brace for 2–4 weeks, and once it's healed, strengthen your balance muscles by standing on one leg (30 seconds, 3 times a day). It reduces repeat sprains.
A bruise changes from purple → green → yellow over 2–3 weeks and fades. That's normal.
avoid: Warm compresses, massage or alcohol in the first 2–3 days (they worsen swelling)
Forcing yourself to walk through bad pain — only as much as doesn't hurt

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory gel or patch
plan.why: For sprains and bruises, anti-inflammatory gels work about as well as tablets (2015 analysis pooling 61 trials) without burdening the stomach, kidneys or heart. 3–4 times a day on the swollen area, thinly, without rubbing.

plan.title: If it hurts, a painkiller by mouth — acetaminophen
plan.why: If it throbs at night so you can't sleep, add acetaminophen 500 mg. No burden on stomach or kidneys, and it doesn't double up with the gel.

plan.title: If swelling is bad — anti-inflammatory tablets for 3 days
plan.why: When swelling and warmth are bad, ibuprofen after meals for 3 days only. It's the same family as the anti-inflammatory gel, so using both adds to the burden — pick one.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: If swelling and pain are unchanged after 3–5 days, get an X-ray.
If you can't put weight on it, or pressing on the bone (behind the ankle bones, the inner top of the foot, the base of the little toe on the outer edge) hurts, it may be a fracture — see a doctor.

faq.q: Which is better, a pain-relief patch or tablets?
faq.a: For sprains and bruises, **anti-inflammatory gels and patches** work about as well as tablets, without burdening the stomach, kidneys or heart (2015 analysis pooling 61 trials). If you're 65 or older, or take stomach or blood-pressure medicine, start with the topical one especially.

faq.q: Do I really need an X-ray?
faq.a: The Ottawa ankle rules decide — get one **if pressing behind the ankle bones hurts, or you couldn't take 4 steps right after the injury and at the clinic**. If none apply, the chance of a fracture is under 1–2 in 100.

faq.q: When can I start moving it?
faq.a: Once the swelling goes down after 2–3 days, start ankle circles and writing letters with your foot **within a pain-free range**. The longer it's immobilised, the slower the recovery. Put only as much weight on it as doesn't hurt.

sprain.clinic: First doctors check **that no bone is broken**. If it's fine, swelling is controlled, then a brace and rehabilitation follow.
sprain.pharm: For the first 2–3 days, ease the pain with ice while **moving early, as far as it doesn't hurt** — that matters more than medicine. If swelling is bad, an oral anti-inflammatory for a few days, and a topical anti-inflammatory on the sore spot.

uti.lead: If you need to pee often, it stings when you go, and you still feel full afterwards, it's likely cystitis. **This isn't something the pharmacy can fix — it needs a prescription antibiotic.** Holding out for days on painkillers can let it climb to the kidneys and become pyelonephritis. One more thing — cystitis pain is cramping pain from **the bladder squeezing**, so painkillers alone don't control it well. Above all, **with fever and pain in your back or side, go to hospital that same day**.
uti.planLabel: The key is seeing a doctor quickly
how: **See a doctor the same day if you can.** Simple cystitis gets better in a day or two with a short course of antibiotics.
Until you get to the doctor, if it hurts, take acetaminophen every 4–6 hours.

If it's a squeezing pain, adding an **antispasmodic (trimebutine and others)** makes it much more bearable. It works differently from acetaminophen, so they can be used together. Using trimebutine for this is clinical experience outside its approved use.
Drink more water than usual and don't hold in your urine.
If you were given antibiotics, **take them to the end of the prescribed days even if you feel better**.
A warm water bottle on your lower belly eases the ache.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I need to pee often and it stings” and they'll advise you to see a doctor. It's not an illness pharmacy medicine cures.
Be sure to say whether you have a fever or pain in your side, and whether you could be pregnant. The rules change completely.
If you say **“It's a squeezing pain when I pee”**, the pharmacist will choose an antispasmodic for you too. But pharmacy medicine alone won't cure it, so do see a doctor.
If you have an enlarged prostate or glaucoma, ask for **trimebutine instead of hyoscine butylbromide**. Otherwise your urine could become completely blocked.
selfcare: Drink 1.5–2 L of water a day and **don't hold in your urine.**
A warm water bottle on your lower belly really does ease the cramping.
After peeing, wipe from front to back.
Avoid tight underwear and sitting for long periods; wear cotton underwear.
After menopause it comes back often. If it keeps recurring, you can discuss prevention with a gynaecologist or urologist.
Washing often with vaginal washes actually removes good bacteria and increases recurrences.
avoid: Don't hold out for days on painkillers alone. If it reaches the kidneys, you may need to be admitted.
Don't take leftover antibiotics from before. If the germ and the medicine don't match, you only build resistance.
Don't hold in your urine.
Don't take anti-inflammatory painkillers while dehydrated. It doubles the strain on the kidneys.
Cutting back on coffee, alcohol and spicy food for a few days reduces irritation.

plan.title: See a doctor and get an antibiotic prescription
plan.why: Simple cystitis usually gets better in a day or two with a short course of antibiotics. Putting it off lets it climb to the kidneys.

plan.title: Fosfomycin — done in a single sachet
plan.why: An option for simple cystitis taken just once. Simple to take, with less burden of resistance. With fever or side pain, this alone isn't enough. If the squeezing pain is bad, you can be prescribed an **antispasmodic such as tiropramide** as well — just say “It's a squeezing pain when I pee.”

plan.title: Acetaminophen — until you get to the doctor
plan.why: Takes the edge off the stinging and pain. Anti-inflammatories can strain the kidneys, so for cystitis acetaminophen is the safe choice.

plan.title: If it squeezes — add an antispasmodic
plan.why: Cystitis pain comes from the bladder muscle contracting on its own. So adding an **antispasmodic, which works differently from painkillers**, makes it much more bearable. Pharmacies use **trimebutine**, and hospitals sometimes use tiropramide. Hyoscine butylbromide is in the same family, but avoid it with an enlarged prostate or glaucoma. Note that trimebutine's approved use is for the digestive system, so using it for bladder pain is **clinical experience outside its approved use** (not a regimen confirmed in large trials).

plan.title: Plenty of water — as important as medicine
plan.why: Peeing often to flush out germs helps recovery. Don't hold in your urine.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't working
steps: If it's **unchanged two days after starting antibiotics**, the germ and the medicine may not match. A urine culture checks this.
**Fever with pain in your back or side** is pyelonephritis. Cystitis medicine isn't enough — you need to see a doctor that same day.

In adult women, symptomatic urinary infection twice or more in 6 months, or three or more times in 1 year, counts as recurrent and is checked by a doctor. Preventive treatment can be discussed. Men, pregnant women, and people with urinary tract abnormalities or weak immunity need separate assessment.
Cystitis is uncommon in men. Whether there's also a prostate problem needs to be checked.
If blood keeps showing in your urine, other causes need to be checked.

faq.q: I heard cranberry is good?
faq.a: It depends on who. In an analysis pooling several studies, **recurrences fell by a quarter in women with frequent recurrences and by half in children**, but **there was no difference in older people living in care homes.** No effect was confirmed in pregnant women either. And it doesn't cure cystitis you already have — that's the antibiotic's job.

faq.q: An older relative's urine test found bacteria, but there are no symptoms.
faq.a: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms (asymptomatic bacteriuria) is **common in older people and usually not treated.** Many studies conclude that antibiotics only increase resistance with no benefit. Pregnancy and some procedures are exceptions.

faq.q: Painkillers don't help much. Why?
faq.a:
Cystitis pain is **squeezing, cramping pain**, so ordinary painkillers alone don't control it well. Adding an **antispasmodic**, which works differently, makes it much easier — pharmacies use trimebutine, hospitals use tiropramide.

But **antispasmodics don't kill the germs either.** If you only dull the pain and put off seeing a doctor, it can climb to the kidneys. Think of it as something to take alongside seeing a doctor.

(Using antispasmodics for bladder cramps isn't a regimen confirmed in large trials; it's based on **how they work and clinical experience**.)

uti.clinic: There's **a single-sachet antibiotic treatment** (fosfomycin), so it usually clears in a day. If there's squeezing pain, an antispasmodic is added. A urine test confirms it.
uti.pharm: **Pharmacy medicines won't cure it.** Cystitis is a bacterial infection, so it needs antibiotics. Until you see a doctor, all you can do is take a painkiller and drink plenty of water.

athletes-foot.lead: If the skin between your toes is soggy and itchy, or the sole is peeling white, it's athlete's foot. Creams work well — in an analysis pooling several studies, **allylamines such as terbinafine had a third fewer failures than azoles**. But **fungal nail infection, where the nail is thick and yellow, won't clear with cream.** For nails, a medicated nail lacquer for 6–12 months, or tablets (prescription) if several nails are affected, is more reliable.
athletes-foot.planTitle: Athlete's foot — it depends on where
athletes-foot.planLabel: Skin or nail is the fork in the road
how: Wash your feet, **dry them completely**, and apply the cream thinly to the affected area and 2 cm around it.
Terbinafine 1–2 times a day for 1–2 weeks; clotrimazole 2–3 times a day for 2–4 weeks.
**Keep applying for a few days to 1–2 weeks after the symptoms are gone.** Stopping at that point almost always means it comes back.
For nail fungus, file down the nail surface, then apply nail lacquer 1–2 times a week, steadily for months.
Change socks daily, and alternate two pairs of shoes so each dries for a day.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “It's athlete's foot between my toes. Terbinafine cream, please.” For a nail: “It's a fungal nail — do you have a nail lacquer?”
If you have diabetes, be sure to say so. Foot care rules are different.
selfcare: After washing, **dry completely**, even between the toes. Pat with a towel, then leave them in the air for a bit.
Change cotton socks daily, or twice a day if you sweat a lot.
Wear slippers at public baths and pools. Use a separate foot towel from your family.
Use your own nail clippers too. It's a common route for spreading through the whole family.
Alternate shoes every other day so the inside dries out.
avoid: Don't put steroid-containing ointment on athlete's foot. The itch eases briefly, but the fungus spreads wider.
Don't soak your feet in vinegar, garlic or bleach. It only causes burns and dermatitis.
Don't stop as soon as the symptoms disappear. That's the biggest cause of it coming back.
Don't keep putting only cream on a fungal nail. It just wastes time.
If you have diabetes, don't cut or file your nails yourself. A wound can turn into a serious problem.

plan.title: Terbinafine cream — first choice for athlete's foot
plan.why: 1–2 weeks is enough, with the fewest failures. Keep applying a few days after symptoms go to reduce recurrence. **Naftifine** is in the same allylamine family and can be used at the same level.

plan.title: Clotrimazole — groin and skin folds
plan.why: It also covers candida, so it's better for groin fungal rash and skin folds. It takes a bit longer, 2–4 weeks.

plan.title: Nail lacquer — fungal nails (amorolfine, ciclopirox)
plan.why: Cream can't get through the nail. 1–2 times a week: 6 months for fingernails, 9–12 months for toenails. If several are badly affected, tablets are much more reliable. **Ciclopirox nail lacquer** has the same role — for the first month, every other day; the application schedule differs.

plan.title: Drying — as important as medicine
plan.why: Fungus grows where it's damp. Washing, drying well and changing socks daily greatly reduces recurrence.

notWorking.title: If the cream isn't helping much
steps: Check that you completed the full course. Terbinafine 1–2 weeks and clotrimazole 2–4 weeks are the standard.
Are you applying it **2 cm wider** than the affected area? Fungus left at the edges often brings it back.
If it's unchanged after 4 weeks, it may not be athlete's foot. Eczema, psoriasis and contact dermatitis often look like it. A dermatologist can scrape it and check under a microscope straight away.
If several nails are damaged, or they're thick and crumbling, discuss tablets (prescription). Liver tests are needed, so it's started at a clinic.
If the foot is red, swollen, painful and you have a fever, it's a bacterial infection (cellulitis). See a doctor that same day.

faq.q: Why does it itch more after applying antifungal cream?
faq.a: It may be irritation from the medicine itself, or temporary irritation as the fungus dies. If it improves within a few days, keep using it; **if redness spreads and blisters appear**, it may be contact dermatitis — stop and talk to a pharmacist.

faq.q: How do I avoid spreading it to my family?
faq.a: Use separate foot towels, slippers and nail clippers, and clean the floor often. Athlete's foot spreads through **flakes of skin**.

faq.q: Why am I the only one in the family with athlete's foot?
faq.a:
**Not everyone exposed to the fungus gets it.** How long the feet stay damp, how well shoes breathe, how tight the spaces between toes are, and conditions like diabetes differ from person to person.

Still, **the family should be careful together** — use separate bath mats and slippers, and don't share towels. A fungal nail keeps reviving athlete's foot.

athletes-foot.clinic: **A topical antifungal** is the basis; for nail fungus or widespread infection, **tablets** are taken for a few months (while checking liver tests).
athletes-foot.pharm: **Terbinafine cream** is the first choice for athlete's foot. Keep applying it **1–2 weeks more** after symptoms go to reduce relapses. Nails are hard to treat with topical medicine alone.

cramp.lead: Night-time leg cramps that wake you with a knotted calf are common after 60. To be honest, **there's no medicine that prevents the cramps themselves** — the only proven one is quinine, and it's too risky to use. In an analysis pooling several studies, magnesium had no meaningful effect on night cramps in older people. Instead, **calf stretching before bed** cut cramps by 1.2 a day in a comparison trial. However, **for people with frequent cramps that keep hurting after the knot releases**, doctors sometimes use an anti-inflammatory or muscle relaxant briefly.
cramp.planTitle: When you get a cramp, in order
cramp.planLabel: There's something more reliable than medicine
how: At the moment of the cramp, **straighten your knee and pull your toes towards you**, and hold for 30 seconds. Standing and stretching the calf as if pushing a wall also works.
Once it settles, apply warmth and massage gently.

If you use medicine, **an anti-inflammatory for 3–5 days** only. Pharmacy muscle-relaxant combinations, per the package insert, aren't taken with anti-inflammatories — choose one of the two. If you feel you need both, talk to a pharmacist (they're sometimes used together when needed). Over 65, muscle relaxants aren't recommended because of the risk of falls. Neither is a medicine to keep taking for long.
Prevention is stretching **right before bed** every day. Stand one step from a wall with your hands on it, keep the back leg straight, and hold 30 seconds, three times on each side.
Drink enough water during the day, and if you take a water pill, ask your doctor about the timing.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I often get calf cramps at night,” and mention the medicines you take (especially water pills and cholesterol medicine). Medicines can be the cause.
Be sure to say **whether you take water pills or cholesterol medicine**. Cramps caused by medicine aren't fixed by supplements.
selfcare: **Calf stretches right before bed, 30 seconds three times.** This one thing is the most reliable method found so far.
Cover yourself loosely so the bedding doesn't press your toes down. Toes pointed downwards bring on cramps.
Drink enough water during the day, and more on days you sweat a lot.
Warming your calves with warm water before sleep helps.
They often come on nights after standing a long time or sudden heavy exercise. Be sure to stretch on those days.
avoid: Never take quinine. It was used in the past, but it's no longer recommended because of blood side effects.
Taking lots of magnesium won't make it better. It only makes diarrhoea worse.
Don't forcefully knead or hit the cramped muscle. It can damage the muscle.
Cramps come more easily on nights you've been drinking. Try cutting back on late drinking.

plan.title: Pull your toes towards you
plan.why: Stretching the calf at the moment of the cramp is the fastest fix. Straighten your knee, grab your toes and pull them towards you, and hold 30 seconds.

plan.title: Calf and hamstring stretches before bed
plan.why: In a trial that split 80 people aged 55 and over into two groups, cramps fell by 1.2 a day after 6 weeks and pain eased too. Doing it right before bed every day is the key.

plan.title: Magnesium — lower your expectations
plan.why: In an analysis pooling several studies, it had no clinically meaningful effect on night cramps in older people (difference of −0.18 cramps a week). But side effects are minor, so some people try it for about a month. Diarrhoea is common.

plan.title: If cramps are frequent and it stays knotted and sore afterwards — an anti-inflammatory or muscle relaxant for a few days only
plan.why: One feature of night cramps is **pain that lingers after the cramp releases**. In the clinic, such people get an **anti-inflammatory** (pain of the knotted muscle) or a muscle relaxant (repeated cramps) for just a few days — this is the reviewing doctor's clinical experience, not proven in well-designed trials (a 2016 review of night cramps in older people also found quinine to be the only drug proven to reduce cramps). So it's 'worth a try', not 'sure to work'. Pharmacy muscle relaxants (chlorzoxazone combinations) cause drowsiness and dizziness, so if you're 65 or older take them in the evening and be careful getting up at night. **Over 65, muscle relaxants aren't recommended because of the risk of falls.** Pharmacy muscle-relaxant combinations, per the package insert, aren't taken with anti-inflammatories — choose one of the two. If you feel you need both, talk to a pharmacist (they're sometimes used together when needed).

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues.

plan.title: Adding — acetaminophen
plan.why: What doctors add when an anti-inflammatory alone isn't enough. In theory taking them at the same time isn't recommended (package insert), but they're sometimes used together and work better than either alone — keep each medicine's interval and daily total separately.

notWorking.title: If it keeps happening
steps: Stretch **every day right before bed** for 6 weeks. It takes a few weeks to work.
Review your medicines. Water pills, some blood-pressure medicines, cholesterol medicines (statins) and asthma medicines can cause cramps.
If your calf hurts when walking and eases with rest, it may be a leg blood vessel problem. You need to see a doctor.
If only one calf is swollen, painful and hot, it may be **a blood clot**. Go to hospital that same day.
If numbness and dulled feeling in hands and feet come with it, nerve, diabetes and thyroid tests are needed.

faq.q: I see a lot of magnesium adverts — doesn't it work?
faq.a: Results are mixed for leg cramps in pregnancy, but **for night cramps in older people, an analysis pooling several studies found no meaningful difference from a dummy pill.** It's a classic example of a big gap between adverts and the actual evidence. If you want to try it, use it for a month and stop if there's no difference.

faq.q: Could cramps be a sign of a serious illness?
faq.a: Mostly not. But if **only one leg is swollen and painful**, it hurts when walking and eases with rest, or numbness or weakness comes with it, blood vessel or nerve problems need checking.

faq.q: Does stretching before bed really help?
faq.a:
**Calf stretching is worth trying.** Hands on a wall, heel flat on the floor, lean forward until you feel the calf pull, **30 seconds 3 times**, before bed.

The effect isn't huge, but **it has no side effects and costs nothing.** That's why it's worth trying before medicine or supplements. Not tucking the bedding tight over your toes helps too.

cramp.clinic: Most need no treatment, but **if it happens every night**, the cause is looked for — medicines, electrolytes, blood vessels and nerves.
cramp.pharm: **Calf stretches before bed** work more surely than medicine. Keep expectations low for magnesium — an analysis pooling several studies found no effect.

dandruff.lead:
Dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis are partly driven by **a yeast (Malassezia)** that feeds on scalp oil. So an **antifungal shampoo** tends to work better than just switching to another ordinary shampoo (the evidence isn't high quality, but it points the same way).

In an analysis pooling 51 trials with 9,052 people, after 4 weeks of **ketoconazole 2% shampoo**, **52 in 100 were clear**, versus 31 with a dummy treatment. It worked about as well as steroids, with **fewer side effects.**

But it's **a condition you 'control' rather than cure**. Using it now and then even after it improves means fewer flare-ups.
dandruff.planTitle: Dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis — here's what to do
dandruff.planLabel: Antifungal shampoo for 4 weeks, then now and then
how: Wet your hair, work up **plenty of lather**, and rub your scalp with your fingertips (don't scratch with your nails).
**Leave it on 3–5 minutes**, then rinse well.
On the other days, use your usual shampoo.
pharmacy: Just say **“My scalp itches and white flakes fall off.”**
Say if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, or if it's for a child.
selfcare: Wash your hair **in the evening and dry it completely** before bed.
It flares up more easily when **sleep and stress** get worse.
**Don't scratch your scalp with your nails** — broken skin makes the shampoo sting and gets infected.
avoid: Don't use medicated shampoo on **a scalp with sores or oozing**.
**Don't leave it on long or use it every day.** It only dries out your scalp.
Don't use adult medicated shampoo on a baby's yellow scalp crusts (infant seborrhoeic dermatitis) — talk to a paediatrician.

plan.title: Ketoconazole shampoo — twice a week, leave on 3–5 minutes, rinse
plan.why:
Rub the lather into your scalp and **leave it 3–5 minutes** before rinsing. Rinsing straight away gives the medicine no time to work. Try it for **2–4 weeks**.

If it doesn't suit your scalp, switching to **ciclopirox shampoo** (2–3 times a week) worked about as well.

plan.title: Once every 1–2 weeks — fewer flare-ups
plan.why: Seborrhoeic dermatitis comes back easily with **stress, lack of sleep and the season (winter)**. Using the antifungal shampoo **once every 1–2 weeks** after it improves means fewer flare-ups.

plan.title: If the sides of the nose, eyebrows or behind the ears go red and flaky
plan.why: The same condition appears on **oily areas of the face**. Some people briefly put shampoo lather on the face, but **keep it out of the eyes**, and for the face it's better to get **a cream from a dermatologist**.

notWorking.title: If it's unchanged after 4 weeks
steps: See **a dermatologist**. It may be **psoriasis** or another skin condition.
If the itching is bad, a doctor may add a **steroid lotion** for a short time.
If it suddenly got worse, look back at **stress, sleep and new hair products**.

faq.q: Can I use dandruff shampoo every day?
faq.a: For treatment, **twice a week** is enough. Using it daily won't clear it faster and only **dries out the scalp**. Use your usual shampoo on the other days.

faq.q: Does washing my hair often cause more dandruff?
faq.a: No. Seborrhoeic dermatitis is caused by **oil and yeast**, so **not washing tends to make it worse**. Just avoid hot water and scratching hard.

dandruff.clinic: At a skin clinic, if itching and redness are bad, **a steroid lotion** is added briefly, and patches on the face are treated with **a cream**. Psoriasis is ruled out too.
dandruff.pharm: At the pharmacy you can buy **ketoconazole shampoo** or **ciclopirox shampoo**.

dryeye.lead: Artificial tears are a 'moisturiser' that tops up the tear film. Bottled products with preservative: up to 4 times a day; if you need them more often, use preservative-free single-use vials. 'Red-eye' drops (decongestants) cause rebound redness if used for more than 3 days.
dryeye.planLabel: Choose the product by how often you need it
how: Put in one drop, close your eyes and wait 1 minute.
Use a single-use vial right after opening, then throw it away.
After 20 minutes of screen time, look at something far away for 20 seconds, and blink often.
pharmacy: Say whether you wear contact lenses. There are separate lens-safe products.
If there's redness, pain or worse vision, see an eye doctor instead of using artificial tears.
selfcare: Cover your eyes with a warm towel for 5–10 minutes, and keep your eyelids clean.
Keep the room humid, and don't let fan or air-conditioner air blow straight into your eyes.
avoid: Don't use redness-relief drops often. Later your eyes get even redder.
Throw single-use artificial tears away after one use.

plan.title: Artificial tears (carboxymethylcellulose)
plan.why: Bottled if up to 4 times a day; preservative-free single-use if more often.

plan.title: If it's severe — hyaluronic acid and prescription eye drops (see a doctor)
plan.why: Dry eye tests, treatment of the eyelid oil glands, prescription eye drops.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: If there's no change after 2 weeks, or it hurts or your vision drops, see an eye doctor.

faq.q: How many times a day can I use artificial tears?
faq.a: Bottled products with preservative **up to 4 times a day**; if you need them more often, use preservative-free single-use vials. Over contact lenses, use only ones labelled for lenses.

faq.q: Is hyaluronic acid better?
faq.a: In an analysis pooling several studies (43 trials), there was no clear winner among artificial tear products. Choose the one that feels **comfortable**. Preservative-free and how often matter more than the ingredient.

faq.q: Do warm compresses really work?
faq.a: Yes. Blocked eyelid oil glands are a common cause of dryness, so a warm towel for 5–10 minutes + cleaning the eyelids is **step 1** in international dry eye guidelines. Do it every day along with artificial tears.

dryeye.clinic: Doctors have you use **preservative-free artificial tears** often, and if it's severe, prescription eye drops that reduce inflammation. If eyelid inflammation is the cause, that's treated first.
dryeye.pharm: **Artificial tears** are the basis. If you'll use them more than four times a day, choose **preservative-free single-use** ones. Warm compresses on the eyes help too.

gout.lead:
**First check — is this an attack like one you were diagnosed with as gout?** If it's a red, hot, painful joint for the first time, or it comes with fever, it may be a bacterial infection (septic arthritis), so **see a doctor that same day** first. If it's the same pattern as attacks you were diagnosed with, do the following.

If a single joint **swells up red overnight and hurts even when the bedsheet touches it**, it may be a gout attack. It's inflammation from uric acid crystals building up in the joint.

**It's not only the big toe.** In a study of 93 people with gout, the big toe was most common at 77 in 100. But **the ankle was 46, the knee 22 and the fingers 20** (several joints overlap in one person). Many people come in thinking a suddenly swollen ankle is 'just a sprain'.

**Attacks are stopped by putting out the inflammation; recurrences are prevented by lowering uric acid.** Don't mix the two — don't newly start a uric-acid-lowering drug during an attack, and if you already take one, don't stop it during an attack.
gout.planTitle: Putting out an attack, in order
gout.planLabel: The sooner, the better it works — within 24 hours
how: If it's an attack like one you were diagnosed with, take an anti-inflammatory painkiller at a generous dose **right away** when the pain starts, after food. Once it settles after a day or two, lower the dose. If it's a first attack or you have a fever, **seeing a doctor that same day** comes before medicine.
Raise the painful joint, and hold an ice pack wrapped in a towel on it for 15–20 minutes at a time.
Drink more water than usual. It helps uric acid leave in the urine.
If you were already taking a uric acid medicine like allopurinol, **keep taking it as usual even during the attack**.
After the attack has fully settled, get your uric acid checked at a clinic and discuss preventive medicine.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I was diagnosed with gout before and I think it's another attack. A generous dose of anti-inflammatory, please. And an acid reducer to ease heartburn too.”
Be sure to say if you have kidney problems, have had a stomach ulcer, or take a blood thinner. An anti-inflammatory may not be suitable.
selfcare: During an attack, rest with the painful foot raised above heart level. Keep socks and bedding from touching it.
Drink plenty of water — about 2 L a day.
Beer and soju, organ meats, oily fish and drinks high in fructose are typical triggers. Avoid them especially for a few days after an attack.
Losing weight gradually reduces how often attacks happen. But crash dieting actually triggers attacks.
Low-fat milk and yoghurt are known to help lower uric acid.
avoid: Don't take aspirin for the pain. It blocks uric acid leaving the body and can make the attack worse.
Don't **newly** start a uric-acid-lowering drug during an attack. It can make the attack worse.
On the other hand, don't stop a uric-acid-lowering drug you were already taking during an attack.
Don't massage the painful joint or apply heat. The inflammation gets worse.
Don't fast or suddenly exercise very hard. Rapid shifts in uric acid bring on attacks.

plan.title: For an attack like the ones you were diagnosed with — an anti-inflammatory at a full dose, right away
plan.why: Guidelines strongly recommend it for sudden attacks. Holding out before taking it makes it last much longer. Start right away at a generous dose when pain begins, and lower it once it settles.

plan.title: Famotidine — when taking an anti-inflammatory for several days
plan.why: A gout attack needs several days of anti-inflammatory, so stomach strain builds up. **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues.

plan.title: Adding — acetaminophen
plan.why: What doctors add when an anti-inflammatory alone isn't enough. In theory taking them at the same time isn't recommended (package insert), but they're sometimes used together and work better than either alone — keep each medicine's interval and daily total separately.

plan.title: Steroid tablets — when anti-inflammatories can't be used
plan.why:
**They work as well as anti-inflammatories and, used briefly, are actually safer** — that's the conclusion of an analysis pooling 26 trials (moderate certainty). So for **people who can't take anti-inflammatories because of a weak stomach or kidneys**, and for older people, it's a route doctors often choose.

But **there's no evidence to rank one as best** — anti-inflammatories, low-dose colchicine and steroids sit side by side. They can't be bought at a pharmacy, so **you need to see a doctor**.

plan.title: Colchicine — within 24 hours of an attack
plan.why: Used for people who can't take anti-inflammatories (kidney or stomach problems) or when they aren't enough. Low dose is the rule, and diarrhoea is common.

plan.title: Allopurinol — after the attack settles
plan.why: Lowering uric acid below 6 mg/dL is the real treatment. It's started if you have two or more attacks a year or have lumps (tophi). In Korea, a genetic test (HLA-B*5801) to check the risk of a severe drug rash from allopurinol is sometimes done first, so ask at your visit.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't helping much
steps: Check that you started on time with a full enough dose. With gout, holding out and taking a little at a time makes it work much less well.
If swelling and pain are unchanged after 2–3 days, see a doctor. Switching to a steroid injection or colchicine brings it under control much faster.
If you have two or more attacks a year, or feel lumps on your toes or ear rims, it's time to start treatment to lower uric acid.
If the joint is red and hot **with fever**, it may be a bacterial infection rather than gout. See a doctor that same day.

faq.q: Can it be gout if it's not my big toe?
faq.a: Yes, it can. In a study of 93 people with gout, **the ankle was 46 in 100, the knee 22 and the fingers 20**. In particular, **many people come in thinking a suddenly swollen ankle is 'just a sprain'**. If it swelled up red overnight with no memory of injury, gout is suspected.

faq.q: I heard steroids are used — is that OK?
faq.a: **Used briefly they're fine, and they work as well as anti-inflammatories.** In a review pooling 26 trials, steroid tablets worked the same as anti-inflammatories and were actually safer. 'Steroids are scary' applies to **long-term use**. But **using them together with anti-inflammatories raises the risk of stomach ulcers**, so for older people doctors pick just one of the two, or switch to another medicine instead of a steroid.

faq.q: My uric acid is normal, but they say it's gout?
faq.a: During an attack, uric acid moves into the joint, so **the blood level can actually come out normal**. That's why gout isn't diagnosed from the level alone — measuring again after it settles is more accurate.

faq.q: Do I have to give up meat completely?
faq.a: No. Diet alone lowers uric acid only a little (usually about 1 mg/dL). **Cutting back on alcohol, organ meats and fructose drinks** is the key; the rest is more realistically managed with medicine.

faq.q: I started gout medicine and had an attack instead.
faq.a:
**It's common at the start, and it can also mean the medicine is working.** As uric acid drops quickly, crystals that had built up in the joint shift.

**Never stop it on your own.** If you stop and restart, it happens all over again. Doctors know this, so for the first 3–6 months they give **attack-preventing medicine alongside**. If you had an attack, just tell them.

gout.clinic:
For an attack, one of **an anti-inflammatory, low-dose colchicine or an oral steroid** that suits your health is started within 24 hours. If it's severe, two are sometimes used together.

Once it settles, **a medicine that lowers uric acid** is taken steadily to prevent attacks coming back.
gout.pharm:
If it's an attack of already-diagnosed gout, taking **an anti-inflammatory at an adequate dose straight away** is what you can do from the pharmacy. If it's a first attack or you have a fever, it's a same-day doctor's visit, not the pharmacy. Avoid aspirin, which actually raises uric acid, and take an acid medicine alongside if your stomach burns.

If you can't take anti-inflammatories because of your stomach or kidneys, **don't hold out with pharmacy medicines — see a doctor** — an oral steroid takes their place.

shingles.lead: If blisters come up in a band on one side of the body only, and the spot burns and hurts, it's shingles. **This isn't an illness to get through at the pharmacy.** Antiviral medicine has to be started **within 72 hours of the rash appearing** to shorten healing time and pain. Nerve pain that lasts months after shingles (post-herpetic neuralgia) affects about 20 in 100 people, and it's not certain whether antivirals prevent this nerve pain itself — if pain remains, don't put up with it; see a doctor.
how: **Go to a doctor today.** This is the first and most important thing.
Until you get there, if it hurts, take acetaminophen every 4–6 hours.
Don't pop the blisters — cover them loosely with clean gauze.
Wash with lukewarm water and don't rub. A cool compress eases the burning.
The prescribed antiviral **is taken many times a day.** Keep to the times and finish the whole course.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I think it's shingles” and they'll send you straight to a doctor. It's not an illness the pharmacy can solve.
If you've already been prescribed medicine, be sure to say if your kidneys are weak. The dose changes.
selfcare: Until the blisters crust over, **avoid contact with babies who haven't had chickenpox, pregnant women and people on cancer treatment.** They can catch chickenpox from it.
Rest well and eat well. Being run down slows recovery.
Wear loose, soft clothing so it doesn't rub.
If the pain is bad, don't put up with it — be sure to mention it at your visit.
Over 50, it can be prevented with a vaccine. People who have already had it are also eligible.
avoid: Don't pop or squeeze the blisters.
Don't use folk remedies like moxibustion or apply alcohol or vinegar. Burns and infection pile on.
Don't put it off for days to 'wait and see'. After 72 hours, the benefit of the medicine drops a lot.
Don't put steroid ointment on it on your own.

plan.title: Go to a doctor today
plan.why: Starting antiviral medicine within 72 hours of the rash is the key. Don't put it off, even at the weekend.

plan.title: Antiviral medicine
plan.why: It stops the virus multiplying, shortening the time the rash takes to heal and reducing pain. Usually taken for 7 days.

plan.title: Acetaminophen — until you get to the doctor
plan.why: Helps take the edge off the pain. Shingles pain tends to be strong, so prescription painkillers are often needed.

plan.title: Leave the blisters alone and cover them
plan.why: Popping them leaves scars and lets bacteria in. They're contagious until they crust over, so cover them loosely.

notWorking.title: If it still hurts after starting treatment
steps: Pain remaining after the rash heals isn't unusual. It's post-herpetic neuralgia, affecting about 20 in 100 people.
**Don't put up with it — see a doctor.** It needs nerve-pain medicines (such as gabapentin or pregabalin) or a lidocaine patch or cream, not ordinary painkillers.
Blisters around the eye, on the tip of the nose or the ear carry a risk of sight or hearing complications. You need an eye or ear, nose and throat doctor.
If the blisters go yellow with pus and you have a fever, a bacterial infection has set in. See a doctor again.

faq.q: There's only pain and no blisters yet?
faq.a: It's hard to tell if it's shingles from pain alone. Even without blisters, **if the pain is bad, the face or around the eye hurts, or your immunity is weak**, don't wait — see a doctor. The 72 hours for timing treatment is counted not from the pain but **from when the skin rash first appears** — **if red spots came first, don't wait for them to turn into blisters.** See a doctor as soon as the rash appears.

faq.q: Is it too late after 72 hours?
faq.a: Sometimes it isn't. Even after 72 hours, **if new blisters keep appearing, it involves the eye or ear, or your immunity is weak**, antiviral treatment may be needed. **People with severe pain or a widespread rash** should also see a doctor. **If ear blisters or severe ear pain come with facial weakness, hearing loss or dizziness**, see a doctor today.

faq.q: Is it contagious?
faq.a: Shingles itself isn't passed on, but **people who've never had chickenpox can catch chickenpox from it.** It spreads by direct contact with the blisters, so keep them covered until they crust over.

faq.q: Once I've had it, can I get it again?
faq.a: Yes, you can. That's why **people who've had it are also eligible for the vaccine.** It's usually given 6 months to 1 year after recovery.

faq.q: Is the shingles vaccine worth having?
faq.a:
**You get it even if you've had shingles.** Shingles can come back even after one episode, and the vaccine reduces that chance and **the risk of lasting nerve pain**.

The timing is usually **a few months after you've fully recovered**, and for people with weakened immunity only certain types can be used. Tell your doctor 'when you had it' and the medicines you take, and they'll decide.

shingles.clinic: **Starting an antiviral within 72 hours** is what matters. The sooner, the shorter the blister healing and early pain. Painkillers are given too if it hurts.
shingles.pharm: **Pharmacy medicines won't solve it.** While you hold out with painkillers, time slips away. If blisters appear in a band on one side, **come to a clinic right away**.

stye.lead: If the edge of your eyelid is swollen and sore, it's a stye. The first treatment isn't medicine but **warm compresses 3–4 times a day**, and most get better on their own in 1–2 weeks. Eye ointment is a helper when pus forms or the eyelid edge is red and swollen. **Don't squeeze it** — the inflammation spreads into the eyelid.
how: Cover the eye with **a warm towel (about 40 degrees) for 5–10 minutes, 3–4 times a day**. Re-warm the towel when it cools.
After the warm compress, gently wipe the base of the eyelashes with a clean cotton bud or finger.
For eye ointment, gently pull down the lower lid, put a rice-grain amount inside, then close your eye and roll it. 2–4 times a day, for no more than 1 week.
During treatment, take a break from contact lenses and eye make-up.
Eye ointment blurs your vision briefly. Don't drive straight away.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I've got a stye. Eye ointment, please.”
Say whether you wear contact lenses, and whether the eye hurts or your vision has dropped. If your vision has changed, it's a job for an eye doctor, not medicine.
selfcare: **Wash your hands often and don't touch your eyes.** You can pass it to the other eye or to family.
Use your own towel and pillowcase and change them often.
Take a break from eye make-up until treatment is over, and throw away old products.
If you get styes often, a daily eyelid hygiene habit (warm compress and cleaning once a day) reduces repeats.
They come more often when you're short of sleep and tired. Resting is part of the treatment.
avoid: **Don't squeeze it.** The inflammation can spread into the eyelid and around the eye.
Don't pop it with a needle.
Don't use steroid eye drops on your own. Eye pressure can rise.
Don't wear contact lenses during treatment.
Don't use eye drops someone else has used.

plan.title: Warm compresses 3–4 times a day
plan.why: 5–10 minutes each with a warm towel. The blocked oil gland opens and it drains on its own. It's what guidelines put as first-line treatment.

plan.title: Wipe the eyelids
plan.why: Gently wiping the base of the lashes opens the oil gland openings. It works best after a warm compress.

plan.title: Antibiotic eye ointment — as a helper
plan.why: When pus forms or the eyelid edge is red and swollen. Use for no more than 1 week.

plan.title: Acetaminophen if it hurts
plan.why: Helps when it's swollen and throbbing.

notWorking.title: If it isn't healing well
steps: Check that you're doing warm compresses properly, **3–4 times a day, 5–10 minutes each**. A quick dab isn't enough.
If a painless lump remains after 1–2 weeks, it's a chalazion. An eye doctor can remove it simply or dissolve it with an injection.
If swelling spreads beyond the eyelid onto the face or you have a fever, it's an infection around the eye socket. **See a doctor that same day**.
If the eyeball itself hurts, your vision drops or you see double, it's an emergency.
If it keeps coming back in the same spot, rarely it can be something else, so an eye doctor needs to check.

faq.q: Are styes contagious?
faq.a: A stye itself doesn't spread easily, but **touching it and then rubbing the other eye can cause one on the other side.** Use a separate towel and wash your hands often.

faq.q: A painless lump is left.
faq.a: It's a chalazion. The inflammation has settled and only a lump of oil is left, so antibiotics don't clear it well. Keep up warm compresses for a few more weeks, and if it's unchanged, **an eye doctor can remove it in 5 minutes**.

faq.q: Do I really need antibiotic eye drops for a stye?
faq.a:
**For most, warm compresses come first.** Press a warm damp cloth on it **3–4 times a day, 10 minutes each**, and massage lightly. Once the blocked oil gland opens, it often settles on its own.

**Don't squeeze it.** Around the eyelid, inflammation spreads inward easily. If the whole eyelid is swollen and painful or you have a fever, tablets are needed, so see a doctor.

stye.clinic: **Warm compresses** are the basis; if pus forms or redness spreads, an antibiotic eye ointment is added. If a lump remains, a simple procedure drains it.
stye.pharm: **Warm compresses 3–4 times a day** matter more than medicine. Use an antibiotic eye ointment as a helper only if pus forms or redness spreads, and **never squeeze it with your fingers.**

wart.lead:
Warts are caused by **a virus** getting into the skin. So they **spread**, and scratching or picking spreads them further. Children's warts **often go away on their own.**

In an analysis pooling 85 trials with 8,815 people, pharmacy **salicylic acid** cleared warts **1.56 times as often** as a dummy treatment, and worked better **on hands than on feet**. There was no clear difference between clinic **freezing treatment** and salicylic acid.

**They're easy to confuse with corns** — if pinching from the sides hurts, and paring it shows **tiny black dots**, it's more likely a wart.
wart.planLabel: Salicylic acid for a few weeks → freezing if that fails
how: **If you have diabetes**, talk to a doctor before using salicylic acid — the package insert says not to use it. Feeling in the feet is dulled and small wounds heal poorly.
**Soaking in warm water for 5 minutes** before applying helps the medicine soak in.
**Don't share** the tool you use to rub off dead skin, or use it elsewhere on your body.
pharmacy: Say **where** it is, for example **“I have a bumpy wart on my finger.”** Pharmacy medicine isn't used on the face or genitals.
Say first whether you have diabetes.
selfcare: **Don't pick or bite them** — they spread to other fingers and around the mouth.
Wear **slippers** at swimming pools and public baths (plantar warts).
Use **separate towels and bath mats** from your family.
avoid: Don't use salicylic acid on **warts on the face or genitals, warts with hair growing from them, or moles you were born with**.
Using it **without advice if you have diabetes or poor circulation**.
**Don't cut them out with a knife or nail clippers.** Bleeding spreads them and they get infected.

plan.title: Corn or wart?
plan.why: **If pressing down on it hurts, it's a corn**; **if pinching from the sides hurts and you see tiny black dots**, it's more likely a wart. Plantar warts get pressed when walking and can look **like corns**. If unsure, see a dermatologist.

plan.title: Salicylic acid plaster — only on the wart, for a few weeks
plan.why:
Softens the hard skin so it peels away bit by bit. Change it every 2–5 days and **gently rub off the softened skin**. **Hand warts respond better than foot warts.**

It turns surrounding healthy skin white and soggy, so **cut it to the size of the wart**.

plan.title: If it's unchanged after a few weeks — freezing treatment
plan.why: A dermatologist does **freezing treatment** every 2–3 weeks. It stings and can blister. **Combined with** salicylic acid it cleared warts a little more often than salicylic acid alone.

notWorking.title: If it's unchanged after a few weeks
steps: Get **freezing treatment at a dermatologist**.
If you keep getting several, your **immunity** may be low — mention it to your doctor.
For children's warts, **watching and waiting if it's not urgent** is also an option — they often go away on their own.

faq.q: I heard covering it with clear tape makes it go away?
faq.a: In an analysis pooling several studies, **clear tape was no different from a dummy treatment.** It does no harm, but don't rely on it alone and wait.

faq.q: Are warts contagious?
faq.a: Yes, **they're caused by a virus, so they spread.** Picking or scratching spreads them to other fingers and around the mouth, and towels and bathroom floors can spread them to family.

wart.clinic: At a skin clinic, **cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen** is done a few times, 2–3 weeks apart. If it doesn't go for a long time, other medicines are sometimes used.
wart.pharm: At the pharmacy you can buy **salicylic acid plasters** (products whose leaflet lists warts). Don't use them on **warts on the face or genitals, or hairy warts**, and **if you have diabetes, check with a doctor first** (the leaflet says not to use them).

bph.lead: Very common in men after their 50s. As the prostate grows it presses on the urine passage, so **the stream gets weaker, you have to wait for it to start, it feels like there's some left after you finish, and you wake several times at night**. Pharmacy medicine won't solve it — you need **prescription medicine**. And the single most important thing with this condition is **being careful with cold medicine**. Every year people come to the emergency room with urine completely blocked after one sachet of combination cold medicine.
bph.planTitle: Enlarged prostate — here's what to do
how: Taking the medicine at the same time **after dinner** usually means less dizziness during the day.
Don't rush in the toilet; after you finish, wait a moment and **go once more** to ease the feeling that some is left.
Drink less from 2–3 hours before bed, and avoid alcohol and caffeine in the evening.
**Leave a small light on** for trips to the toilet at night. Falling is actually the most common way people get hurt with this condition.
You can tell within 1–2 weeks whether it works. If there's no change, the medicine is switched or added to at the next visit.
pharmacy: **When buying cold medicine, runny-nose medicine, sleep aids or motion-sickness medicine, always say “I take prostate medicine.”** That one sentence prevents a trip to the emergency room.
Supplements sold at pharmacies such as saw palmetto were no different from dummy pills in large studies. They can't replace prescription medicine.
If you can't pass urine and your lower belly is tight, it's **the emergency room**, not the pharmacy.
selfcare: Studies suggest regular exercise such as walking reduces symptoms.
Sitting for long periods and staying in the cold for long make symptoms worse.
Constipation presses on the bladder and makes it more uncomfortable.
Don't hold urine for long. Holding it can lead to a sudden blockage.
avoid: **Don't buy cold medicine on your own.** You may not be able to pass urine at all.
Don't drink little water all day. Drink enough in the day and cut back only in the evening.
Don't stop the medicine yourself. The symptoms come straight back.
Don't try to solve waking at night with sleeping pills. The risk of falling goes up a lot.
Don't replace prescription medicine with supplements such as saw palmetto.

plan.title: See a urologist — rule out other causes first
plan.why: The same symptoms come from cystitis, diabetes, prostate cancer and medicine side effects. Checking once with a urine test and a prostate blood test is the safe way.

plan.title: Tamsulosin — widens the urine passage
plan.why: It doesn't shrink the prostate; it relaxes the muscle to widen the passage. You feel it working within days. Remember just two things: **dizziness when standing up** in the first few days, and **telling the surgeon before cataract surgery**.

plan.title: Evening water, caffeine and alcohol
plan.why: Cut back on water 2–3 hours before bed; caffeine and alcohol directly increase how often you wake at night. Drink enough during the day.

plan.title: Be careful with cold medicine and sleep aids — urine can get blocked
plan.why: Pseudoephedrine in combination cold medicines and old runny-nose medicines (1st-generation antihistamines) narrow the urine passage further. Always say at the pharmacy **“I take prostate medicine”** and they'll choose a safe one.

notWorking.title: If medicine isn't helping
steps: If there's no change after 1–2 months, a medicine that actually shrinks the prostate (finasteride, dutasteride) can be added or switched to. These take 6 months to work.
If medicine doesn't work or your urine has been blocked before, procedures or surgery (transurethral resection, holmium laser, etc.) are considered.
If you wake especially often only at night, the cause may be heart failure, sleep apnoea or the timing of a water pill rather than the prostate.
If there's blood in your urine or you're losing weight, other causes need checking.

faq.q: Why is cold medicine so dangerous?
faq.a: **Pseudoephedrine** in combination cold medicine tightens not only the blood vessels in the nose but **also the muscle at the bladder outlet.** Old runny-nose medicines (1st-generation antihistamines) weaken the bladder's squeeze. With the passage already narrow, adding just one of these can cause **acute urinary retention**, where no urine comes out at all. A catheter has to be put in at the emergency room. There are safe alternatives such as plain acetaminophen, so always tell the pharmacist.

faq.q: I heard saw palmetto is good?
faq.a: In several large clinical trials it was **not clearly different from a dummy pill.** It isn't very harmful, but it can't replace prescription medicine. Spending that money and time on one doctor's visit is the surer choice.

faq.q: Does an enlarged prostate turn into cancer?
faq.a: **No.** An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer are different conditions, and enlargement doesn't turn into cancer. The symptoms can be similar, so a doctor just checks both together.

bph.clinic: **A medicine that widens the urine passage** (tamsulosin) comes first, and if the prostate is large, a medicine to shrink it is added. If you can't pass urine at all, it's an emergency.
bph.pharm: **Pharmacy medicines won't solve it.** Health supplements such as saw palmetto were no different from placebo in large trials. Cold medicines (antihistamines, decongestants) make urine flow worse, so be careful.

coldsore.lead: Aciclovir cream earns its keep when applied at **the first sign, before blisters appear** (tingling, itching, burning) — once blisters have formed, the effect is small. About every 4 hours, 5 times a day, for 5 days. If you get them often, buy it in advance and apply as soon as you feel the sign.
coldsore.planLabel: The edge of the lip tingles, then blisters form
how: The virus (herpes simplex type 1) stays in the body and comes back with tiredness, sunlight, periods or colds. If it recurs 6 or more times a year, there's the option of suppressing it with **antiviral tablets (prescription)**.

It's contagious while blisters are present — avoid kissing and sharing cups or towels, wash your hands after applying, and don't rub your eyes (corneal infection). Be especially careful around newborns, people with eczema and people with weak immunity.
pharmacy: “My lip has started tingling — aciclovir cream, please. How many times a day and for how many days? Can I buy it in advance if I get them often?”
Say **how many hours since the tingling started**. The sooner, the better it works.
selfcare: Don't apply steroid ointment — the virus spreads more. If sunlight is the trigger, use lip sun protection.
While blisters are present, don't rub your eyes with a hand that touched your lips — spreading it to the eye is serious.
Use a moisturising lip balm often so your lips don't crack. But throw away the lip balm you used while you had blisters once it heals.
They often come up on days you're tired or had a lot of sun — on those days, put on a sun-protection lip balm in advance.
avoid: Popping blisters or picking scabs
Steroid ointment
Kissing or sharing cups or lip balm while blisters are present
Touching your eyes or contact lenses with the hand you applied it with

plan.title: Aciclovir cream — right at the first tingle
plan.why: **The cream can be bought at pharmacies (over the counter).** Applied at the first tingling or itching, it makes blisters smaller. Once blisters have formed, the effect is small. Every 4 hours, 5 times a day, for 5 days (if it's unchanged after 5 days, you can use it 5 more days). **Per the package insert it isn't used while breastfeeding or in children** — talk to a doctor. (Aciclovir tablets need a prescription and are prescribed when it recurs often or is severe.)

plan.title: When it hurts — acetaminophen
plan.why: With cold sores, **the stinging, throbbing pain** is often harder than the blisters. Acetaminophen doesn't overlap with aciclovir cream and is gentle on the stomach, so they go well together. If the inside of your mouth is sore too and food hurts, try taking it 30 minutes before meals.

plan.title: Patches — not a cure, but for covering up
plan.why:
Hydrocolloid patches for cold sores. **They don't make it heal faster** — in two comparison trials, healing time was the same as with aciclovir cream (351 people: 7.6 vs 7.0 days · 180 people: 9.7 vs 9.8 days).

Their value lies elsewhere. **They're less noticeable, and you touch it less, so it spreads less from fiddling.** Think of them not as a replacement for cream but as something to add over the cream when you need to meet people. Use them after the blister has burst.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: It heals on its own in 7–10 days. If it doesn't heal in more than 2 weeks, or recurs 6 or more times a year, see a doctor.
Check you applied it at the first sign → after blisters, use patches and pain relief for comfort → if over 2 weeks or frequent recurrences, see a doctor (antiviral tablets).

faq.q: How much faster does it heal with the cream?
faq.a:
**Not even a day faster.** Pooling 25 trials with 8,453 people, using antivirals (tablets and creams together) shortened healing time by **0.74 days** (1.09 days for typical blisters, 0.38 days for pain). Cream alone is likely to do even less. Honestly, it's not a big difference.

Still, **applying it right at the first sign (tingling, itching)** is worth it — once blisters form, even that effect shrinks. If you get them often, **tablets** work better than cream (valaciclovir did better than aciclovir). If it recurs 6 or more times a year, talk to a doctor.

faq.q: What if I don't have aciclovir cream at home?
faq.a: If blisters have already formed, the cream's effect is small anyway. Moisturise with petroleum jelly, take acetaminophen if it hurts, and use a cold sore patch if you want to cover it. It heals on its own in 7–10 days.

faq.q: Can I pass it on to others?
faq.a: Yes. It spreads most easily **when there are blisters or oozing**. Avoid kissing babies, pregnant women and people with weak immunity, and sharing cups, spoons or lip balm, until it crusts over.

faq.q: Why does it keep coming back?
faq.a: The virus hides in a nerve and wakes up with tiredness, sunlight, periods or colds. Lip **sun-protection balm** prevented recurrences under laboratory UV light but wasn't confirmed in real sunlight (2015 combined analysis) — it does no harm, so it's worth trying. If it recurs 6 or more times a year, discuss **antiviral tablets**. Cream has no preventive effect.

coldsore.clinic: If it comes back often or is severe, **an oral antiviral** is used. It's more reliable than cream.
coldsore.pharm: **Aciclovir cream is sold at pharmacies.** The key is applying it at the first tingle — once blisters form, it does less. **Sores “inside” the mouth aren't this condition but mouth ulcers**, which need completely different medicine.

frozen-shoulder.lead:
There are two main reasons a shoulder won't lift — **frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis)** and **rotator cuff problems**. They're treated differently, so telling them apart comes first.

**The biggest difference you can see at home is 'when someone else lifts it for you'.** With frozen shoulder, **it won't go up even when someone else lifts it**; with a rotator cuff problem, **it goes up if you relax and let them** (it just won't go up under your own power).

Either way, **movement matters more than medicine**, and pain relief is there to help you do that movement. **Anti-inflammatory gels or patches** are especially good for older people — they work just on that spot without burdening the whole body.
frozen-shoulder.planLabel: Medicine is a tool to help you exercise
how:
**① Ask someone to lift your arm.** Relax completely and let them.
· If it **still won't go up and catches** → frozen shoulder
· If it **glides up** (painful, but it goes up) → rotator cuff

**② Keep your elbow against your side and rotate just the forearm outwards.**
With frozen shoulder this movement is **much worse than the other side**. With rotator cuff problems it's relatively OK.
**Pendulum exercise**: bend forward, let the sore arm hang down and swing it slowly in circles. 1–2 minutes at a time, several times a day.
**Wall climb**: face a wall and walk your fingers up it bit by bit to raise the arm. Just one finger-joint higher than yesterday.
**Towel stretch**: hold a towel diagonally behind your back and gently pull the sore arm up with the good arm.
**A warm compress for 10 minutes** before stretching makes it stretch much more easily.
During the painful phase, use acetaminophen before bed and **patches or anti-inflammatory gel**, and prop a pillow under the sore arm when sleeping.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “My shoulder won't lift and it hurts at night. **Patches and a painkiller for the night**, please.”
If you also say **whether it goes up when someone else lifts it**, it's easier for the pharmacist to guess which it is.
Say if you have diabetes. With diabetes, frozen shoulder is much more common and lasts longer.
selfcare: **A little every day, within a pain-free range.** Little and often beats one hard stretching session.
Loosen up with a warm compress first and stretching is much easier.
Not using the arm at all because it hurts makes it stiffer. Keep up everyday movements like dressing and combing your hair.
Tucking a pillow between the sore arm and your side when sleeping reduces night pain.
With diabetes, blood sugar control affects how fast you recover.
avoid: Avoid forceful pulling or having someone bend it hard for you. The inflammation gets worse.
Don't immobilise the arm for weeks because it hurts. Stiffening is the nature of this condition.
Don't take anti-inflammatory tablets for months on end.
If you do nothing because 'it gets better with time', it can recover stiff. You do need to exercise.
Avoid lifting heavy things and suddenly swinging the arm backwards.

plan.title: Work out which it is, then move every day
plan.why: For frozen shoulder, **gradually stretching the stiff joint capsule** is the only treatment going in the right direction. For rotator cuff problems, the focus is **building strength while avoiding the painful angle**, a different direction. So tell them apart first, then do it within a pain-free range, split into several sessions every day.

plan.title: Patches and anti-inflammatory gel — start here
plan.why:
They work **only on the sore spot**, without burdening the whole body. There's almost no strain on the stomach, kidneys or heart, so they're **especially good for older people.**

Shoulder recovery is long, so it's easy to end up on anti-inflammatory tablets for a long time — patches take their place. **Don't keep sticking them on the same spot**, move them around a little, and **don't put an electric blanket or heat pack over them.**

plan.title: Acetaminophen — when it hurts at night
plan.why: Losing sleep to night pain is the hardest part of this condition. Taking it before bed helps.

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory tablets — only for the bad few days
plan.why: Briefly, during the most painful phase. If you have stomach, heart or kidney problems, talk to a pharmacist or doctor before taking them. For stomach protection, follow the 'Stomach protection' box below.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues.

plan.title: Steroid injection — in the painful phase
plan.why: In the phase of severe pain, an injection into the joint can help. Exercising after the injection keeps the benefit going.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: This condition **naturally takes a long time.** It goes through a freezing phase, a frozen phase and a thawing phase, and can take 1–2 years. Not being better in a few weeks doesn't mean something's wrong.
Check that you stretch **every day**. Studies of manual therapy and exercise therapy are low quality, so the best method can't be pinned down, but they all need consistency.
If the phase of night pain keeping you awake goes on, ask a clinic about a steroid injection into the joint. It can help in the painful phase.
If there's no improvement for more than 6 months and daily life is hard, there are also options such as hydrodilatation or arthroscopy.
If your arm **goes up when someone else lifts it**, it may be a rotator cuff problem rather than frozen shoulder. The treatment is different, so it needs checking.

faq.q: How can I tell frozen shoulder from a rotator cuff problem?
faq.a:
The biggest difference is **'when someone else lifts it for you'**. Relax completely and let them: if it **still won't go up, it's frozen shoulder**; if it **glides up, it's the rotator cuff**.

Also, with frozen shoulder, **keeping the elbow at your side and rotating outwards** is much worse than on the other side.

**If your arm is weak so you drop things, or you can't hold the arm up**, a tendon may be torn, so see a doctor.

A definite distinction needs an examination plus ultrasound or MRI — what you can check at home only tells you **which to suspect first**.

faq.q: Can I use pain-relief patches?
faq.a:
Yes — **they're what we recommend first.** The anti-inflammatory goes only into the sore spot, so there's **almost no strain on the stomach, kidneys or heart.** Shoulder problems last a long time, so it's easy to end up on anti-inflammatory tablets for months — patches take their place.

**Don't keep sticking them on the same spot**, move them a little each time, and **don't put an electric blanket or hot pack over them** — blisters can form.

faq.q: I heard frozen shoulder gets better on its own?
faq.a: It usually improves, but **it takes 1–2 years, and if you do nothing it can set stiff.** Stretching is needed to keep your range of movement. 'It gets better if you wait' and 'you don't need to do anything' are different things.

faq.q: How is it different from a rotator cuff tear?
faq.a: There's a simple hint. **When someone else lifts your arm** — with frozen shoulder it still won't go up well, while with rotator cuff problems it tends to go up with help. A precise distinction needs an examination and imaging.

faq.q: Will an injection make it heal faster?
faq.a:
**It helps get you through the painful phase.** Steroid injections especially shorten the early phase of 'pain so bad at night I can't sleep'.

But **an injection alone won't free up a stiff shoulder.** Stretching **steadily** while the pain is lower is what ultimately brings back the joint's range of movement. Think of the injection as 'something that makes exercise possible'.

frozen-shoulder.clinic: **In the painful phase, the pain is controlled**; in the stiff phase, **movement exercises** are the treatment. In the very painful phase, injections help.
frozen-shoulder.pharm: Start with **a topical anti-inflammatory**, and add a painkiller if pain keeps you awake at night. But more than medicine, **moving the arm a little every day** is the real treatment for frozen shoulder.

incontinence.lead: There's nothing to be embarrassed about, and **it's not true that it can't be fixed because of age.** But there's no pharmacy medicine for urinary leakage. Instead, the most effective first treatment isn't medicine but **pelvic floor exercises**. In an analysis pooling several studies, **56 in 100 people with stress incontinence (leaking when coughing or sneezing) were cured** (versus 6 in 100 who didn't exercise). Start by working out which kind of leaking it is.
incontinence.planTitle: Urinary leakage — here's what to do
how: **First work out which kind it is.** A spurt when coughing, sneezing or laughing is stress incontinence; leaking on the way to the toilet because of sudden urgency is urge incontinence; both is mixed.
**Kegel exercises**: squeeze as if holding in urine for 3–5 seconds, then relax completely for 5 seconds. 8–12 times is one set; 3 sets a day. Don't hold your breath.
Doing them at **set times**, like on the bus or watching TV, helps you not forget. You'll feel the effect from 6–12 weeks.
Try keeping **a bladder diary** for just 3 days. Writing down when and how much you leak helps a doctor find the cause much faster.
Pads aren't embarrassing — they're **a tool so you can keep going out**. But don't rely on them alone; get treatment too.
