pharmacy: Pharmacies have no medicine that cures leakage. **If you say “I'm leaking urine,” they'll advise you to see a doctor.**
Incontinence pads, unlike period pads, are made to hold urine. You can buy them at pharmacies or supermarkets.
If you already take a bladder medicine, be sure to say so when buying cold medicine or sleep aids. Anticholinergic ingredients double up.
**If you're a man who's leaking or can't pass urine well**, don't try to fix it with pharmacy medicine — see a urologist.
selfcare: Losing even a little weight reduces leaks. That's how much less pressure is on the bladder.
Constipation makes leakage worse. Increase water and fibre.
Stopping smoking reduces coughing, which improves stress incontinence.
Caffeine (coffee, green tea, cola) and alcohol directly irritate the bladder. Cut back for just 2 weeks and see the difference.
Light the way to the toilet at night and clear things you could trip on. **Falling** is more dangerous than the leaking itself.
avoid: Don't drink less water on purpose. Concentrated urine irritates the bladder more and increases cystitis and constipation.
Don't just put up with it because 'that's what happens with age'. It's a treatable condition.
If you take a water pill, don't stop it on your own — ask at your visit whether you can change the **time** you take it.
Going to the toilet 'just in case' all the time trains the bladder to be smaller. It's the opposite of bladder training.
Don't take someone else's bladder medicine. If the cause is the opposite, urine can be blocked completely.

plan.title: Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises — 3 times a day, 8–12 squeezes
plan.why: Squeeze the muscle you use to hold in urine, hold 3–5 seconds and relax completely, 8–12 times, 3 times a day. Keep it up for **at least 3 months**. In an analysis pooling several trials, stress incontinence was cured in 56 in 100 versus 6. If your belly, buttocks or thighs tense up, you're doing it wrong.

plan.title: Bladder training and lifestyle changes
plan.why: When you feel the urge, hold on, starting with 5 minutes and building up, to retrain the bladder. Cut back on caffeine, alcohol and fizzy drinks, and moderate water in the evening but **drink enough during the day**. Drinking less makes urine concentrated and irritates the bladder more.

plan.title: If it's the urgent kind — mirabegron / solifenacin
plan.why: For **urge incontinence**, leaking on the way to the toilet because you can't hold on, prescription medicine helps. Older people should first ask about **mirabegron**, which has no anticholinergic burden; with solifenacin-type drugs, check for dry mouth, constipation and memory effects. These medicines don't work for stress incontinence, the spurt when you cough.

plan.title: Check these first — infection, prostate, medicine side effects
plan.why: Cystitis can look like incontinence, and in men an enlarged prostate is often the cause. Water pills, sleeping pills and some blood-pressure medicines are also common causes. Take all your medicines with you and see a doctor at least once.

notWorking.title: If exercise isn't helping
steps: If there's no change after doing it properly for **3 months**, your technique may be off. A urologist or gynaecologist can check you're squeezing correctly with biofeedback.
If urge incontinence is bad, prescription medicine (mirabegron, solifenacin) is added. Give it 2–4 weeks before judging.
If medicine doesn't work either, there are options such as botulinum toxin injections into the bladder, sacral nerve stimulation, and for stress incontinence, mid-urethral sling surgery.
Leakage that starts suddenly is often due to infection, constipation or a newly started medicine. Once the cause is found, it improves quickly.

faq.q: How do I know I'm doing Kegels right?
faq.a: Try stopping your urine midstream **just once**. The muscle you use then is the right one (don't make a habit of this). If your belly, buttocks or thighs tense, or you hold your breath, you're doing it wrong. If you're not sure, a clinic can check with a biofeedback machine.

faq.q: Can't I just take medicine first?
faq.a: Those medicines don't work for **stress** incontinence, leaking when coughing or sneezing. Even for **urge** incontinence, they work better combined with exercise and bladder training. And for older people, side effects (dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, falls) can outweigh the benefit, so the order matters.

faq.q: I heard bladder medicine causes dementia.
faq.a: **Not all bladder medicines do.** The concern is **anticholinergics** such as solifenacin. In a study following 3,434 people aged 65 and over for an average of more than 7 years, those who had used more than 3 years' worth in total over the previous 10 years had 1.54 times the risk of dementia. If you plan to use one long-term, ask at your visit about **mirabegron**, which has no anticholinergic burden.

incontinence.clinic: **The medicine is completely different depending on how it leaks** — if it leaks with sudden urgency, a medicine that calms the bladder; if it leaks when you cough, exercises and other treatments.
incontinence.pharm: **There's no suitable medicine at the pharmacy.** Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) work as well as medicine for leaking when you cough. Don't just get by with pads — see a doctor.

nosebleed.lead: Most nosebleeds come from thin blood vessels at the front of the inside of the nose, and **they stop if you just press properly.** The first-aid step in the American Academy of Otolaryngology guideline is **pressing firmly on the soft part of the nose (the lower third) for at least 5 minutes**. Two things many people get wrong — **tilting the head back** and **pressing the bridge (the hard bony part)**. Neither stops bleeding.
nosebleed.planLabel: Where you press and how you sit is everything
how: Sit and **lean your head slightly forward**. Don't tilt it back.
**Pinch the soft lower part of the nose with your thumb and index finger and press firmly for at least 5 minutes, without letting go**. Timing it by the clock helps.
Breathe through your mouth, and spit out blood that collects in your mouth instead of swallowing it.
Put ice wrapped in a towel on the bridge of your nose.
If it's still bleeding after 5 minutes, press **for another 5–10 minutes**. Most stop at this point.
For a few hours after it stops, don't blow or pick your nose, and don't lift heavy things or bend over.
Once it stops, **put a thin layer of ointment inside your nose before bed**. It stops the scab drying out and breaking open again.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist “I get nosebleeds often,” and be sure to say **whether you take a blood thinner (aspirin, warfarin, etc.)**. It changes what to do.
Just say **“An ointment to put inside my nose, please.”** You'll get mupirocin or fusidic acid ointment. Petroleum jelly is fine too.
If it keeps happening because your nose is dry, using a saline spray as well helps.
selfcare: They happen more when it's dry in winter or with heating. **Use a humidifier and spray saline often.**

Putting **a rice-grain amount of ointment (petroleum jelly, mupirocin, fusidic acid) inside the nostrils** before bed greatly reduces repeats. The trick is to apply it to the **inner wall**, not the outside of the nose.
Don't pick your nose. It's the commonest cause of nosebleeds in children.
Blow your nose gently, one side at a time.
For people with high blood pressure, keeping it controlled also helps prevent nosebleeds.
avoid: Don't tilt your head back. Blood runs down your throat and you may vomit.
Don't press the hard bridge of the nose. It won't stop the bleeding.
Don't let go before 5 minutes to check. The clot that's just forming comes off again.
Don't push tissue deep into your nose. It reopens when you pull it out, and any left behind causes inflammation.
For a few hours after it stops, don't blow your nose or take a hot bath.
Don't stop a blood thinner on your own because of nosebleeds. Always talk to your doctor.
Don't push ointment deep into the nose. 1 cm inside the entrance is enough.
Don't put ointment in the nose of a baby under one.

plan.title: Lean your head slightly forward
plan.why: Tilting back makes blood run down your throat so you swallow it, and you can't tell how much is coming. You may feel sick and vomit.

plan.title: Press the soft part of the nose firmly for at least 5 minutes
plan.why: Pinch the **soft lower part** of the nose with thumb and index finger. Pressing the hard bridge is useless. Don't let go midway to check.

plan.title: Cold compress on the outside of the nose
plan.why: It narrows the blood vessels and helps stop the bleeding. Put ice wrapped in a towel on the bridge of your nose.

plan.title: Keep the inside of the nose moist — a thin layer of ointment
plan.why: Dryness is the commonest cause. Before bed, **use a cotton bud to put a rice-grain amount just inside the nostril entrance (on the middle wall)** to reduce repeats. Petroleum jelly works, and if picking has made it sore, **an antibacterial ointment such as fusidic acid** is better.

notWorking.title: If it won't stop
steps: If it **doesn't stop after pressing properly for 20 minutes (two or three rounds of 5–10 minutes)**, go to hospital. Packing or cauterising (sealing the vessel) stops it simply.
People on blood thinners need to press longer, and should go to hospital sooner if it won't stop. **Don't stop the medicine on your own.**
If it keeps coming from one side only, the vessel there has weakened, and cauterising often solves it.
If it recurs on both sides or runs in the family, causes such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia are checked.
If you also bleed from the gums or bruise easily, a blood test is needed.

faq.q: But I was taught to tilt my head back?
faq.a: That's the old way, and **it's wrong.** It doesn't stop the bleeding — the blood just runs down your throat. Swallowing it makes you feel sick and may cause vomiting, and you can't tell how much you're losing. **Leaning forward and pressing the soft part of the nose** is the current standard.

faq.q: My child keeps getting nosebleeds.
faq.a: Children's nosebleeds are mostly caused by **nose-picking and dryness**. Keep their nails short, put petroleum jelly just inside the nostrils before bed, and humidify the room. If they're still frequent, an ear, nose and throat doctor can gently cauterise the vessel, and that usually ends it.

faq.q: Does ointment really make them happen less?
faq.a:
**It's not proven to 'definitely work'.** In an analysis pooling several studies of recurrent nosebleeds in children (5 comparison trials, 468 children), neither antibacterial cream nor petroleum jelly was clearly different from no treatment.

But **it does no harm**, and it directly prevents **dryness and scabs**, the commonest cause of nosebleeds. That's why doctors recommend it, and many people with recurring winter nosebleeds do find it helps. Feel free to try it, but **if it keeps bleeding from one side only**, don't rely on ointment — see a doctor.

nosebleed.clinic: It usually comes from blood vessels at the front of the nose. If it won't stop, **packing or cauterising the vessel** is done, and if it keeps happening, the cause is looked for.
nosebleed.pharm: **Dryness is the commonest cause.** Putting a rice-grain-sized dab of ointment inside the nostrils before bed reduces repeats. When it bleeds, **lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for at least 5 minutes** — don't tilt your head back.

osteoporosis.lead: Osteoporosis **doesn't hurt.** That's why it's a condition people only find out about after a bone breaks. A hip fracture in particular changes the rest of an older person's life a great deal. But contrary to common belief, **calcium and vitamin D supplements alone didn't reduce fractures** — that's the result of an analysis pooling 33 comparison trials with 51,145 community-dwelling people aged 50 and over. What actually reduces fractures is **prescription treatment** and **not falling**.
osteoporosis.planLabel: Test → treatment → not falling, in that order
how: **Pick a fixed day for bisphosphonates.** Mark it on the calendar or set an alarm so you don't forget.
As soon as you get up, before eating or drinking anything, swallow it with **a full glass (200 mL) of plain water**. Not coffee, milk or juice.
After taking it, **sit or stand for 30 minutes.** Don't lie down, and don't take other medicines or food during those 30 minutes.
Keep calcium, iron and antacids **at least 2 hours** apart from this medicine.
If a dull ache in the thigh or groin goes on for weeks, see a doctor.
pharmacy: Osteoporosis medicine can't be bought at a pharmacy. Saying **“I'd like a bone density test”** at a clinic is the starting point.
Pharmacies sell vitamin D and calcium, but **they don't replace treatment.**
If you also take a multivitamin, ask them to add up the international units on the labels to make sure vitamin D doesn't double up.
selfcare: Get calcium from milk, yoghurt, tofu, small dried anchovies and green vegetables. Food comes before supplements.
Get sun on your arms and legs 3 times a week, about 15–20 minutes each time.
Sit-to-stand, heel raises and light resistance-band exercise, 10 minutes a day. Bones get stronger when they bear load.
Stop smoking, and keep alcohol to no more than 2 drinks a day.
Walk round your home and remove **things you could trip on**: rugs, cables, door thresholds, dark hallways.
avoid: Don't put off testing and treatment because it doesn't hurt. Osteoporosis gives no signal until a bone breaks.
Taking bisphosphonates with coffee or milk, or lying down straight after, means **they don't work and can ulcerate the oesophagus.**
Don't stop treatment on your own. Whether to continue or take a break after 3–5 years is decided with your doctor.
Don't take many calcium supplement tablets a day. Fractures don't fall, and constipation and kidney stones can increase.
Don't habitually take medicines that make falls more likely (sleep aids, 1st-generation antihistamines).

plan.title: Start with a bone density test — you need a baseline
plan.why: Have one if you're **a woman 65 or older**, a man at risk, have lost 3 cm or more in height, have broken a bone in a minor fall, or have taken steroids for a long time. It takes 10–15 minutes and doesn't hurt. Writing down the result (T-score) lets you compare next time.

plan.title: If treatment is needed — bisphosphonates
plan.why: A medicine that actually reduces fractures. But **on an empty stomach in the morning with a glass of plain water, and no lying down for 30 minutes** — if you can't keep to this, it barely works. And **always mention that you take it before dental procedures.**

plan.title: If you're on treatment, take vitamin D with it
plan.why: If you're on treatment, vitamin D isn't optional — it's a partner. On the other hand, people with healthy bones taking it for prevention didn't have fewer fractures. A single blood test shows whether you're deficient.

plan.title: Not falling — as important as medicine
plan.why: Most fractures in older people happen at home. Non-slip mats in the bathroom, a small light at night, tidying thresholds, cables and rugs. And at your visit, review **medicines that cause dizziness** (sleep aids, anticholinergics, blood-pressure medicines).

plan.title: Food, strength exercise, stopping smoking
plan.why: For calcium, **food** comes before supplements (milk, yoghurt, tofu, small dried anchovies, green vegetables). Walking alone isn't enough — **light strength exercise like sit-to-stand** is needed too. Smoking directly weakens bones.

notWorking.title: If a bone broke despite treatment
steps: First check you were taking the medicine correctly. **Empty stomach in the morning, plain water, 30 minutes** — if even one of the three is off, it's barely absorbed.
If you're short of vitamin D, the treatment doesn't work properly. A blood test checks.
The medicine can be changed, or switched to an injection (every 6 months or yearly).
Other conditions that cause osteoporosis (parathyroid, thyroid, multiple myeloma, etc.) may need checking.
If you keep losing height and your back is curving, your spine may be quietly collapsing. Get an X-ray.

faq.q: I've been taking calcium faithfully — was it useless?
faq.a: Calcium from food **does count.** What wasn't shown to work is **taking supplements separately for prevention**. In an analysis of 51,145 community-dwelling people aged 50 and over, calcium and vitamin D supplements didn't reduce any fractures, including hip fractures. It's different for people in care homes, people with a confirmed deficiency, and people also on osteoporosis treatment.

faq.q: Can't I just get a 'bone injection'?
faq.a: Osteoporosis injections **do exist and work well** (an injection under the skin every 6 months, or into a vein once a year). They're a good alternative if tablets are a hassle or upset your stomach. But they're completely different from steroid injections sold as 'bone shots' — steroids actually weaken bones. Always check with your doctor.

faq.q: Is a stooped back osteoporosis too?
faq.a: It can be. When vertebrae quietly collapse (compression fractures), you lose height and your back curves. It often passes without you even feeling pain. **If you've lost 3 cm or more in height**, have a bone density test and a spine X-ray.

osteoporosis.clinic: **A bone density test decides whether to treat.** If needed, a medicine that stops bone loss is used, along with calcium and vitamin D.
osteoporosis.pharm: **Calcium and vitamin D are available at the pharmacy.** But they alone don't treat osteoporosis. **Not falling** matters as much as medicine.

plantar.lead: Plantar fasciitis is heel pain that's **worst with the first steps in the morning** and eases as you walk. It's an **overuse** injury where the band under the foot is strained and swollen a little every day, so medicine only helps — **calf and sole stretching** (pulling your toes back before getting up, wall push 30 seconds × 3, 2–3 times a day) is the real treatment, with evidence behind it. Rolling a frozen water bottle under the foot helps too.
plantar.planTitle: Plantar fasciitis and heel pain — do this
plantar.planLabel: A sharp heel pain with the first steps in the morning
how: Keep anti-inflammatory tablets brief; anti-inflammatory gels have fewer side effects. With ketoprofen patches, keep the area out of sunlight **for up to 2 weeks after removing**.

Shoes are half of it — **off-the-shelf insoles and heel cups** with heel cushioning and arch support (cheap ones are enough; evidence shows little difference from custom ones), and avoid bare feet, slippers and flat shoes with no heel. A **night splint** that holds the ankle up overnight also helps.
pharmacy: “My heel hurts with the first steps in the morning. Do you have an anti-inflammatory gel and heel insoles? How many days can I take tablets?”
Say **whether the first steps in the morning hurt most** — it's the best clue to plantar fasciitis.
selfcare: Look at your weight and **any sudden increase in exercise**. It usually improves within 6–12 months, but **slowly** — repeating injections out of impatience can tear the fascia.

Prescription options — steroid injection (short-lived effect and tear risk), shockwave therapy, physiotherapy. If they don't work, other causes (trapped nerve, stress fracture, ankylosing spondylitis) are tested for.
avoid: Bare feet or slippers on hard floors
Running through the pain
Anti-inflammatory tablets for a long time
Cutting heel calluses with a blade (especially with diabetes)
Repeated steroid injections

plan.title: On the sore heel — anti-inflammatory gel (patches at night)
plan.why: The plantar fascia is shallow under the skin, so topical anti-inflammatories reach it. Unlike tablets there's almost no strain on stomach or kidneys, so they suit this condition that takes weeks. Patches fall off the sole when you walk, so it's more practical to use **gel during the day** 3–4 times and **a patch at night**. With ketoprofen patches, keep the area **out of sunlight for up to 2 weeks after removing** — sunlight can make just that spot red, swollen or blistered (photosensitivity). Patches: **1–2 a day** as the package insert says (it varies by product — check the pack); not for under-15s.

plan.title: Another patch option — topical flurbiprofen
plan.why: A **stick-on anti-inflammatory** you can switch to if ketoprofen patches don't suit you or you're worried about photosensitivity. Keep the patched area out of sunlight.

plan.title: If it hurts a lot — add an anti-inflammatory tablet
plan.why: Using **a tablet together with** the topical one helps (doctors give both too). Naproxen lasts a long time per dose: as the package insert says, **2 capsules (500 mg) first, then 1 capsule every 6–8 hours**, no more than 5 capsules (1,250 mg) a day. Take it with food to reduce heartburn. This condition takes weeks to heal, so **don't drag out tablets** — within a few days move over to topical medicine and stretching.

plan.title: Menthol, camphor, methyl salicylate (patches, ointments)
plan.why: Not anti-inflammatories — these patches **cover pain with a cooling or warming feeling**. The evidence is weak — an analysis pooling several studies (17 trials) concluded there's no evidence that salicylate patches and ointments are useful for acute injury or chronic pain. Think of them as **something to try instead** if anti-inflammatory patches don't suit your skin or you're worried about photosensitivity, and don't stick with them if they don't work. Not for broken skin.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues. The heel takes weeks to heal, so if it looks like you'll need anti-inflammatory tablets for long, it's safer to get them prescribed.

plan.title: Adding — acetaminophen
plan.why: What doctors add when an anti-inflammatory alone isn't enough. In theory taking them at the same time isn't recommended (package insert), but they're sometimes used together and work better than either alone — keep each medicine's interval and daily total separately.

plan.title: If the calf and sole are knotted — muscle relaxant ingredient
plan.why: If the calf and sole feel stiff and tight, a muscle-relaxing ingredient can be added for a few days. **It can make you drowsy, so be careful driving.** Rarely it can damage the liver, so **if fever, rash, dark urine or yellowing (jaundice)** appear, stop at once and see a doctor. Not for people with liver disease or who are breastfeeding. In the clinic, an anti-inflammatory, acetaminophen and a muscle relaxant are often given with stomach protection. Pharmacy muscle-relaxant combinations contain a painkiller (ethenzamide), so per the package insert they aren't taken with anti-inflammatory tablets — choose one of the two. If you feel you need both, talk to a pharmacist (they're sometimes used together when needed).

plan.title: What happens in the clinic
plan.why: Guidelines use stretching, shoes, insoles, a night splint and painkillers (acetaminophen, anti-inflammatories) for 6–12 weeks, and if they don't work, consider a steroid injection (explaining the short-lived effect and tear risk) or shockwave therapy. 80–95 in 100 people get better within a year, so surgery is only considered when every treatment has failed for over a year.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Patches and stretching for 2–3 weeks. If it's unchanged after 6–12 weeks, see an orthopaedic or rehabilitation doctor.
Check you stretched **every day** and start with shoes → insoles and a night splint → see a doctor after 6–12 weeks (injection, shockwave, physiotherapy, tests for other causes).

faq.q: Do insoles help?
faq.a: Yes. Even off-the-shelf insoles help about as much as custom ones in the short term. Choose ones with heel cushioning and arch support, and wear them at home too.

faq.q: Do I need an injection?
faq.a: A steroid injection makes it comfortable for a few weeks, but repeated injections can thin the heel's fat pad and tear the fascia. It's a decision for the clinic when stretching and insoles haven't worked after 6–12 weeks.

faq.q: Why are the first steps in the morning the worst?
faq.a: Overnight the foot droops and the fascia shortens, then the first step suddenly stretches it. **Pull your toes back while still in bed** before getting up, and if it's bad, a night splint reduces morning pain.

plantar.clinic: **Stretching, footwear and insoles** for 6–12 weeks; if that doesn't work, injections or shockwave therapy are considered.
plantar.pharm: **Calf and sole stretches are the real treatment**. Medicine only helps. Off-the-shelf heel cushion insoles are good enough, and use a topical anti-inflammatory on the sore spot.

tendon.lead: Tendon pain is caused by **repetitive movements**, so **cutting back on that movement** comes before medicine. Wrist and elbow braces spread the force on the tendon.
tendon.planTitle: Wrist and elbow tendinitis, tennis elbow — do this
tendon.planLabel: Gripping or twisting makes the outer elbow or thumb side of the wrist ache
how: Tennis elbow mostly heals on its own within 6 months to a year. Steroid injections reduce pain quickly, but **the effect may not last** (tennis elbow studies), so it's better to try exercise and a brace first and discuss it with a doctor.
The thumb side of the wrist (De Quervain's) typically hurts when you tuck your thumb into your fist and bend the wrist towards the little finger — carrying a baby and smartphones are common causes.
pharmacy: “I think it's elbow tendinitis — an anti-inflammatory gel and a brace, please. Should I take tablets too?”
Saying **which hand you use and whether you use it repetitively for work or sport** helps choose the brace.
selfcare: Cutting back for 2 weeks on the painful movements (gripping heavy things, twisting, holding a mouse for long) is half the treatment.
Wear the elbow strap two finger-widths below the elbow, only while working or lifting.
Once the pain eases, do slow wrist-lowering exercises (eccentric exercise) 15 times, 3 times a day — rehabilitation with evidence behind it.
avoid: Repeating painful movements (gripping heavy things, twisting)
Doubling up two anti-inflammatory painkillers
Repeated steroid injections

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory gel or patch
plan.why: In knee arthritis data, anti-inflammatory gels worked about as well as tablets with less strain on the stomach and kidneys. Direct evidence for tendon pain is still limited, but they're safer than tablets, so worth trying first. Thinly on the sore tendon 3–4 times a day, for up to 2 weeks.

plan.title: If it hurts, a painkiller by mouth — acetaminophen
plan.why: Acetaminophen 500 mg when it throbs at night and you can't sleep. No burden on stomach or kidneys, and it doesn't double up with the gel.

plan.title: If it's swollen and warm — anti-inflammatory tablets for a few days
plan.why: Only for the few days it's swollen and warm, after food. It's the same family as the gel, so overlapping for long adds to the burden.

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory patch
plan.why: Ketoprofen patches: **1–2 a day** as the package insert says (it varies by product — check the pack), and keep the area out of sunlight **for up to 2 weeks** after removing it (photosensitivity). **Not for under-15s.** If it's unchanged after 1 week, stop and talk to a pharmacist or doctor.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues. Pharmacy famotidine eases heartburn; it hasn't been shown to prevent stomach bleeding from anti-inflammatories.

plan.title: What happens in the clinic
plan.why: Orthopaedic clinics use anti-inflammatory gels and tablets (briefly) plus **eccentric exercise, braces and physiotherapy** as the basics. Steroid injections **reduce pain quickly but the effect may not last** (tennis elbow studies), so it's decided after discussion. For De Quervain's tenosynovitis, a thumb splint and injection have evidence.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Medicine in 1–2-week blocks. If it's unchanged after more than 6 weeks or your hand goes numb, see an orthopaedic doctor.
First review cutting back the movement and the brace → how often you apply the gel → if it still fails, see a doctor (physiotherapy, splint, injection).

faq.q: Can I take anti-inflammatories for a long time?
faq.a: Tendon pain is more about **the tendon wearing** than inflammation, so anti-inflammatories only ease the early pain. Don't take them daily for more than 2 weeks — move on to cutting back the movement, a brace and gels. Anti-inflammatory gels and patches don't burden the stomach, so they're worth trying first, but know one thing — the 39 trials with 10,631 people pooled are **almost all 'knee arthritis' data**. It's not evidence from applying them to tendons directly.

faq.q: Will an injection make it heal faster?
faq.a: Steroid injections **reduce pain quickly for the first few weeks.** But in tennis elbow studies the effect didn't last and some found more recurrence a year later, so decide after hearing the pros and cons from your doctor. Repeated injections can weaken the tendon.

faq.q: How do I use a brace?
faq.a: Wear the tennis elbow strap about **two finger-widths** below the elbow, only when working or lifting. Take it off at night. For the thumb side of the wrist (De Quervain's), you can buy **a wrist brace that wraps the thumb (thumb splint)** at pharmacies and medical supply stores. **If the pain continues, get a proper splint fitted at the clinic.**

tendon.clinic: **Topical or oral anti-inflammatories together with a brace and exercise** are the basis. If it's severe, an injection is used; pain eases quickly but it may not last, so it's decided together.
tendon.pharm: **A topical anti-inflammatory comes first**, and add acetaminophen if it hurts at night. Wrist braces are at the pharmacy too. **Cutting down the movements that caused it** matters as much as medicine.

acne.lead: Benzoyl peroxide can cause redness and peeling for the first 2–4 weeks — start with 2.5–5%, once at bedtime, with a moisturiser, and increase if you can tolerate it. It **bleaches** white towels and pillowcases and makes skin sun-sensitive, so use sunscreen in the daytime. You need to use it **8 weeks** before judging.
acne.planLabel: Red spots and small bumps keep appearing on the forehead and chin
how: Don't squeeze — it leaves scars and dark marks. Wash twice a day with a gentle cleanser without scrubbing, and choose **non-comedogenic** cosmetics. Scrubs and alcohol toners actually irritate.

If it's unchanged after 8–12 weeks of pharmacy medicine, or red lumps, cysts or scars start appearing, see a dermatologist — the medicines used there work much better and prevent scarring — which medicine is for the doctor to decide. Don't **habitually** put steroid or antibiotic ointment on acne.
pharmacy: “Low-strength benzoyl peroxide for acne, please. How should I start so it stings less? Should I use a moisturiser too?”

**If you're pregnant or planning a pregnancy**, be sure to say so. The acne tablet (isotretinoin) is **a medicine that must never be used in pregnancy** — it causes severe birth defects. That's why you need contraception **from one month before, during, and for one month after stopping**, and **two methods together** are used to reduce failures (the Korean drug agency's pregnancy prevention programme). During the same period **you can't donate blood either.** Topical retinoids are also avoided in pregnancy.
selfcare: In women, acne around the chin and mouth that worsens before periods may respond well to hormonal treatment — discuss it with a doctor.
Change pillowcases and towels often. Hair oil on the forehead makes it worse.
Don't squeeze — squeezing leaves marks and makes it last longer. Only when one is very swollen is it better to have it drained at a dermatologist.
Choose cosmetics and sunscreen labelled 'non-comedogenic (doesn't clog pores)'. Don't wash with water only — use a gentle cleanser twice a day.
avoid: Squeezing or touching with your hands
Using steroid or antibiotic ointment on acne all the time
Corn-removal salicylic acid on the face
Applying benzoyl peroxide and a retinoid at the same time
Hard scrubs and washing too often

plan.title: Benzoyl peroxide — the basic pharmacy acne treatment
plan.why: Of the acne medicines you can buy at a pharmacy, it has the strongest evidence. It works on both blocked pores (comedones) and red, pus-filled spots, and unlike antibiotics, **bacteria don't become resistant to it.** Starting with a strong one stings and peels so people give up within days, so **start low, once a day at night**, thinly. It bleaches clothes, towels and pillowcases white, so keep a white towel just for this.

plan.title: Salicylic acid — only low-strength acne products (2% or less)
plan.why: For mild small bumps and blackheads. **Never put corn-removal liquid on your face** — it's the same ingredient but a completely different strength.

plan.title: Moist dressings (acne patches)
plan.why: Something to cover a spot that's burst from squeezing. **It's not a medicine that cures acne** — its value is that you touch it less, which reduces spreading and scarring from fiddling. Stick it on an oozing spot and remove it once the fluid dries. On small bumps that haven't come to a head yet, it does little.

plan.title: What happens in the clinic
plan.why: Dermatology guidelines use benzoyl peroxide **together with** a topical retinoid (adapalene) for mild acne; for moderate acne, add an antibiotic tablet (doxycycline) as briefly as possible (usually within 3–4 months); and for severe acne or scarring, isotretinoin. For women, a combined oral contraceptive (drospirenone combination) is another option. Antibiotics alone are avoided because of resistance.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Judge after 8–12 weeks. If lumps or scars appear before then, see a dermatologist.
First check the strength, frequency and moisturising (many people stop because it stings) → 8 weeks → dermatologist (the doctor chooses the medicine).

faq.q: Shouldn't I squeeze spots?
faq.a: Squeezing drives the inflammation deeper and leaves scars and dark marks. Even ones with white pus — leave them alone and apply medicine. If really needed, a dermatologist drains them with sterilised tools.

faq.q: Does washing more often help?
faq.a: No. Twice a day with a gentle cleanser is enough. Washing or rubbing more dries the skin and makes it produce more oil. A light moisturiser after washing actually helps.

faq.q: Benzoyl peroxide is making my face peel.
faq.a: It's a common adjustment reaction in the first 2–4 weeks. Cut back to every other day, and use a low strength (2.5%) with a moisturiser. If it swells or oozes, it's an allergy — stop and see a dermatologist.

acne.clinic: **A topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide together**, and for moderate acne, an oral antibiotic added for as short a time as possible (usually within 3–4 months). If scarring starts, isotretinoin is considered.
acne.pharm: **Benzoyl peroxide** has the best evidence of pharmacy acne medicines. Start with a low strength once at night. Put a patch on spots that have been squeezed open.

anxiety.lead:
Let me be honest first. **There's no pharmacy medicine that works well for anxiety.**

Some people use drowsy antihistamines to take the edge off, but they **don't treat anxiety itself.** The same goes for traditional herbal calming remedies.

So this screen isn't here to recommend a medicine — it shows **what you can do now** and **when to see a doctor**.
anxiety.planLabel: There are things to try before medicine
how: When you're anxious, the body reacts first — a pounding heart, shaky hands, breathlessness. **Calm the body first and the mind follows.** Breathing out slowly is the quickest way.

Taking the edge off with drowsy medicines (first-generation antihistamines) doesn't treat anxiety. You feel foggy the next day, and older people are more likely to fall — don't lean on pharmacy medicines.
pharmacy: “I've been tense lately and can't sleep. Could you check whether any of the medicines I take can make anxiety or palpitations worse?”
Mention **whether the pounding heart starts suddenly and stops suddenly**. If so, the heart needs checking first.
selfcare: **Try cutting down on caffeine.** Two cups of coffee can keep you on edge all day.
Soothing anxiety with alcohol makes you more anxious the next day — the body coming off alcohol itself creates anxiety.
For recurring anxiety, **cognitive behavioural therapy** works as well as medicine, and in the long run more reliably.
avoid: Calming down with alcohol
Caffeine
Taking sleep aids every night
Taking someone else's tranquillisers

plan.title: Right now — breathe out slowly
plan.why:
When you're anxious, breathing gets shallow and fast. **Making the out-breath longer than the in-breath** calms the body first. Breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six, for just a few minutes.

Turning your attention to **what's here right now** — the feel of your feet on the floor, the texture of something in your hand — also helps.

plan.title: We don't recommend managing anxiety with pharmacy medicines
plan.why:
Some people try to take the edge off with drowsy cold or allergy medicines (first-generation antihistamines), but **they don't treat anxiety**, you feel foggy the next day, and older people can get **dizziness, falls and trouble passing urine**. So this screen doesn't recommend pharmacy medicines.

Try slow breathing and less caffeine first, and if anxiety keeps coming back, discuss it with a doctor — talking therapy and prescription medicines work well.

plan.title: Traditional herbal calming remedies — not as much as hoped
plan.why: In Korea, a traditional herbal remedy called Woohwang Cheongsimwon is licensed for palpitations and nervousness and is popular before stressful moments, but **we couldn't find proper clinical trials comparing it with placebo.** If it made you feel calmer, there's no reason to deny that, but it isn't enough as the answer to recurring anxiety.

plan.title: Things that work more surely than medicine
plan.why:
**Caffeine** makes anxiety much worse — try cutting down on coffee and energy drinks. **Alcohol** eases things briefly but brings the anxiety back the next day.

Regular walking and sleep are as powerful as medicine. If anxiety keeps returning, **cognitive behavioural therapy** comes closest to a real solution.

plan.title: What happens at the clinic
plan.why:
**If panic attacks keep happening**, the first treatment is talking therapy (cognitive behavioural therapy) and an antidepressant.
**Propranolol** — dampens body symptoms like shaking and a pounding heart before a presentation or exam. Evidence for using it for panic disorder itself is lacking. It can slow the pulse or cause dizziness, and isn't used with asthma or a slow pulse.
Tranquillisers such as alprazolam — calm anxiety within 30 minutes, but long use leads to worse outcomes, so they're used only briefly.

For **long-lasting anxiety**, an antidepressant is the root medicine and takes a few weeks to work. If sleep is the problem, a prescription antihistamine such as hydroxyzine is sometimes used.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Have you tried cutting caffeine and alcohol and doing the breathing? Many people feel different from this alone.
**If attacks keep coming back**, it may be panic disorder. At the clinic, body symptoms (propranolol) and anxiety (tranquillisers) are handled separately.
If anxiety continues **for more than a month**, the path is an antidepressant and talking therapy — the route closest to a real solution.

faq.q: Is there really no anxiety medicine at the pharmacy?
faq.a: Yes, essentially none. Drowsy antihistamines only take the edge off briefly, so we don't recommend them. Medicines that treat anxiety (tranquillisers, antidepressants) all need a prescription.

faq.q: What about Woohwang Cheongsimwon?
faq.a: It's licensed in Korea for nervousness, but **clinical evidence that it beats placebo hasn't been confirmed.** It isn't enough as the answer to recurring anxiety.

faq.q: Are tranquillisers addictive?
faq.a: It's true that, as well as they work, **the body gets used to them easily**. So at the clinic they're used briefly, only as prescribed. That's no reason to avoid them out of fear — agree the length of use with your doctor.

anxiety.clinic: If panic attacks keep happening, **talking therapy (cognitive behavioural therapy) and an antidepressant** come first. Tranquillisers (such as alprazolam) lead to worse outcomes with long use, so they're used only briefly, and **propranolol** is used for body symptoms like shaking and a pounding heart before a presentation or exam.
anxiety.pharm: **There's no medicine we can recommend.** Taking the edge off with drowsy antihistamines isn't treating anxiety, and older people are more likely to fall. Try slow breathing first, and see a doctor if it keeps coming back.

corn.lead:
Corns form **where shoes or the way you walk keep pressing on one spot**. So **removing the pressure comes first**, and pharmacy **corn plasters (salicylic acid)** come after.

In a trial that randomised 202 people, with plasters **34 in 100 corns had gone completely** at three months, compared with 21 with scalpel paring.

But **if you have diabetes or poor circulation in your feet, talk to a doctor before using corn plasters** (the leaflet says not to use them) — wounds on the feet heal poorly.
corn.planLabel: Remove the pressure, then the medicine
how: **If you have diabetes**, talk to a doctor before using salicylic acid — the leaflet says not to use it. Feeling in the feet is dulled and small wounds heal poorly.
Put plasters **only on the hard spot**. If the skin around turns white and soggy, take a few days off.
When the skin is soft after a bath, **rub gently with a foot file or pumice**. **Don't cut it out with a knife or nail clippers.**
pharmacy: First mention **whether you have diabetes or circulation problems**. They'll then suggest another way instead of plasters.
Just say: **“One spot on the sole of my foot stabs every time I walk.”**
selfcare: After a bath, apply **moisturiser** so hard skin doesn't thicken.
Choose socks **whose seams don't touch your toes**, and keep feet dry.
On days of long standing or walking, **cushioned insoles** help.
avoid: **Using salicylic acid plasters or liquid without advice when you have diabetes or peripheral vascular disease.** A small wound can become a large ulcer.
**Don't cut it out yourself with a knife, razor blade or nail clippers.** It's the commonest route to infection.
Talk to a pharmacist before using it on a child.

plan.title: Corn or wart?
plan.why: **If it hurts when pressed from above, it's likely a corn**; **if it hurts when pinched from the sides and you see tiny black dots, it's likely a wart**. Warts **spread**, so they're handled differently — if unsure, have a skin clinic look.

plan.title: Shoes first — roomy at the front with low heels
plan.why: Narrow toe boxes, high heels and thin soles keep pressing one spot. Switch to **shoes roomy enough to wiggle your toes**, and put a **ring-shaped pad** on the sore spot to take the pressure off.

plan.title: Salicylic acid plaster — only on the hard spot
plan.why:
It softens hard skin so it peels away. In the trial it was used **with a foot specialist overseeing**, and compared with scalpel paring, **more corns went and there was less pain.** Whether it delays recurrence wasn't clear in a study that re-analysed the same data.

Apply it **only to the corn** — touching the healthy skin around makes it soggy. Wash and dry the foot before applying, change it every few days, and **gently rub off the softened skin**.

plan.title: Corns between the toes heal faster
plan.why: Following the same trial for a year, the time until **half had healed was 6 months between or on top of the toes, and 15 months on the sole**. Corns on the sole take a long time, so don't be impatient.

plan.title: For thick hard skin on heels and soles — urea cream
plan.why: For **broad thickened hard skin or cracked heels**, rather than a single stabbing corn, urea cream softens the hard skin. Use it once or twice a day after washing and drying. If cracks bleed or sting, switch to a mild moisturiser. If you have diabetes, don't pare hard skin on your feet yourself.

notWorking.title: Still the same after a few weeks
steps: **Have the core pared away at a skin or orthopaedic clinic.** It takes a few minutes and hurts less from that day.
If it keeps coming back in the same spot, it's due to **foot shape or the way you walk**. Ask about custom insoles.
It may have been **a wart**, not a corn. Have a skin clinic check.

faq.q: After a corn plaster, the skin went white and soggy.
faq.a: The salicylic acid has softened the skin. **If the healthy skin around has turned white too, take a few days off**, and next time cut the plaster to touch only the corn. **If it becomes painful and red**, stop and talk to a pharmacist.

faq.q: I have diabetes — what should I do about a corn?
faq.a: **Talk to a doctor before using any medicine** — having it pared at a clinic is safest. With diabetes, feeling in the feet is dulled so wounds go unnoticed, and small wounds heal poorly. The leaflet also says not to use it if you have diabetes. **Look at your feet every day.**

faq.q: Do I have to pull it out by the root so it doesn't come back?
faq.a: A corn doesn't have a root like a plant — **it's a hard core that forms where skin is pressed**. **Unless you remove the cause of the pressure**, it comes back even after paring.

corn.clinic: At a skin or orthopaedic clinic, **the hard core is pared away**, and if it keeps coming back, **foot shape, walking and footwear** are looked at. Insoles are sometimes recommended.
corn.pharm: At the pharmacy you can buy **salicylic acid corn plasters and liquid**. They soften hard skin so it peels away. **If you have diabetes, talk to a doctor before using them** (the leaflet says not to use them).

deworm.lead:
In the past, whole families in Korea took worming tablets every spring and autumn, but **parasite infections there have fallen a lot.** If you have no symptoms, there's no need to take them every year.

**When you should take them is clear** — when a child **scratches their bottom at night and sleeps badly** (pinworm), and when you often eat raw freshwater fish or often handle garden soil.

For pinworm, **one more dose 7 days later** and **the whole family together** — leaving out these two is the commonest reason it comes back.
deworm.planLabel: One tablet does it, but keep to “two things”
how: From age 2, take **1 tablet (400 mg)** with water. No need to fast.
**For pinworm, take 1 more tablet 7 days later.**
**The whole family takes it on the same day.**
On the day you take it, **wash underwear, pyjamas and bedding in hot water**.
For a few days, **wash hands and under the nails well** when you get up in the morning.
pharmacy: Just say: **“Worming tablets, please — for ○ people.”**
**Be sure to mention if you're pregnant or planning a pregnancy** — it isn't used in pregnancy.
**For babies under 2**, a doctor decides, not the pharmacy.
Tell them if you have liver problems or take medicine for your liver.
selfcare: Handwashing matters as much as the tablet — especially **after getting up in the morning** and after the toilet.
Keep nails short. Eggs stay under the nails.
So a child doesn't scratch their bottom, put them in cotton underwear at night and change it in the morning.
Don't eat freshwater fish raw — liver flukes aren't cleared by worming tablets.
Always wash after handling garden soil.
avoid: Don't take it during pregnancy. If you could become pregnant, take it **within ten days of your period starting** (or after a negative pregnancy test), and use contraception for three days after the last dose.
Don't give it to children under 2.
There's no need to take it every year out of habit if you have no symptoms and no reason.
Don't think “one tablet and done” — with pinworm, day 7 is what really counts.
If you have liver problems, don't take repeated doses on your own.

plan.title: Albendazole 1 tablet — available at the pharmacy
plan.why:
From age 2 (24 months), both adults and children take **1 tablet (400 mg)**. For roundworm, hookworm and whipworm, **one dose does it**.

If it's hard to swallow, you can chew it or take it with water. No need to fast or use laxatives.

plan.title: For pinworm — one more dose 7 days later
plan.why:
With pinworm, **the medicine doesn't work well on the eggs.** Even if the first dose kills the adult worms, leftover eggs hatch about a week later.

You need **1 more tablet 7 days later** to finish it. Missing this is the commonest reason people say “I took the tablet but it's itchy again”.

plan.title: The whole family on the same day
plan.why:
Pinworm eggs spread via **hands, underwear and bedding**. If one person has it, others living with them are usually infected too.

If only one person takes it, **it soon comes back.** If it was picked up at nursery or school, it's even more important that the whole household takes it together.

plan.title: Underwear and bedding in hot water — as important as the tablet
plan.why:
Even if the medicine kills the worms, it's no use if **eggs left on bedding and underwear** get back into the mouth.

On the day you take it, **wash underwear, pyjamas and bedding in hot water**, and for a few days **wash right under the nails when you get up in the morning.** Keeping nails short helps too.

notWorking.title: Took the tablet but it's itchy again
steps: Check **whether you took the second dose 7 days later** — this is the commonest reason.
Check **whether the whole family took it together**. If only one person does, it comes back.
See whether bedding and underwear were washed in hot water.
If it still continues, a doctor looks for **other causes** — an itchy bottom can also come from piles, eczema or fungal infection.

faq.q: Do I have to take it every spring and autumn?
faq.a: **No.** It was done in the past when infection was common, but it's much rarer now. Take it **when there's a reason** — a child scratching their bottom at night, often eating raw freshwater fish, or often handling soil.

faq.q: Why take it again 7 days later?
faq.a: With pinworm, **the medicine doesn't work well on the eggs.** Leftover eggs hatch about a week later, so you need one more dose then to finish it.

faq.q: I ate raw fish — will a worming tablet do?
faq.a: **Liver flukes caught from raw freshwater fish aren't cleared by this medicine.** A different medicine (praziquantel) is needed, on prescription. If you often have tummy pain or indigestion, get tested by a doctor.

faq.q: Can I take it during pregnancy?
faq.a:
**Don't buy it yourself — let a doctor decide.** But it's worth knowing this: in an analysis of treatment in pregnancy (23 studies), **albendazole didn't increase miscarriage or premature birth, and there were no serious adverse reactions caused by the medicine.** Cure rates were 90 in 100 for roundworm and hookworm, and 50 in 100 for whipworm (mebendazole was 70 in 100 or lower for all three).

So it isn't “a medicine you must never take in pregnancy”, but a doctor first decides **whether it's really needed**. That's especially so in early pregnancy (the first 3 months).

deworm.clinic: At the clinic, doctors first check **whether it's really worms**. Not every itchy bottom is pinworm — piles, eczema and fungal infection are far more common. If needed, a tape test confirms it.
deworm.pharm: Worming tablets are sold at pharmacies without a prescription. **For pinworm, the key is the whole family taking it together, and once more 7 days later** — because leftover eggs hatch again.

drymouth.lead: The **most common cause of dry mouth isn't an illness but medicine**. Cold medicine, sleep aids, motion-sickness medicine, bladder medicine and older antidepressants dry up saliva. Several together make it worse. So **the first thing to look at is your medicine box**, and then chewing and moisturising.
drymouth.planTitle: When your mouth is dry — do this
drymouth.planLabel: Mouth parched, waking at night looking for water
how: A dry mouth **dulls taste, loosens dentures, and makes your tongue stick when you talk**. Don't write it off as age — it's a symptom with a cause.
Drink water often, but **a little at a time**. Drinking a lot at once just sends you to the toilet at night.
Alcohol, smoking and caffeine dry it out more. Mouth breathing and a blocked nose are causes too.
pharmacy: “My mouth is very dry. Could you check whether any of my medicines cause it? I've brought my medicine bags.”
“Xylitol gum and a mouth moisturising gel, please — one to put on before bed.”
selfcare: Keep sugar-free gum in your pocket. If it's sweets, they must be **sugar-free**.
Moisturising gel before bed + water by the bed + a humidifier. You'll wake up less often before dawn.
Brush with fluoride toothpaste twice a day, and before bed **spit but don't rinse** (so the fluoride stays).
avoid: Keeping sugary sweets or drinks in your mouth
Wetting your mouth with alcohol because it's dry
Mouthwashes **containing alcohol** (they dry it more)
Leaving it because 'it's just age' — tooth decay and gum disease come quickly

plan.title: Look at your medicines first — that's most often where the cause is
plan.why: The **most common cause of dry mouth in older people is medicine**, usually because of **anticholinergic effects**. The more medicines you take, the worse it gets. If you've added your medicines to My medicine box, your [[symptom:drymouth|anticholinergic score]] appears below. If the score is high, ask a pharmacist or doctor whether any medicine could be switched — it doesn't mean stop them.

plan.title: Chew to get saliva flowing
plan.why: If your salivary glands still work, **chewing comes before any medicine**. Sugar-free xylitol gum or sweets for 5–10 minutes whenever your mouth is dry. Sugary sweets do the opposite and cause tooth decay.

plan.title: Top it up — especially before bed
plan.why: Spread artificial saliva or mouth moisturising gel thinly inside your mouth and on your tongue. If you breathe through your mouth at night, it's driest before dawn, so **once before bed** is worth it. One containing xylitol also helps prevent tooth decay.

plan.title: Preventing tooth decay is the real goal
plan.why: When saliva drops, **tooth decay and gum disease come quickly**. Fluoride toothpaste twice a day, floss and interdental brushes, and dental check-ups more often than usual. Dry mouth isn't just discomfort — it's **about losing teeth**.

plan.title: There are also medicines that stimulate the salivary glands
plan.why: When saliva really won't flow, as in Sjögren's syndrome or after radiotherapy, prescription medicines such as **pilocarpine** are used. But side effects include heavy sweating, nausea and needing to pass urine more often, and with asthma it can tighten breathing, so it's used carefully in older people. First see **whether a medicine can be switched**.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: First check whether a medicine can be switched. Gum and moisturising gel work straight away, so there's no need to wait. **If it stays dry 2–4 weeks after switching a medicine, see a doctor** (to find the cause).

If your eyes are dry and gritty too along with a dry mouth, it may be **Sjögren's syndrome** — a rheumatologist checks with a blood test. But it's **a rare condition**. Pooling studies from many countries, it affects about 6 in 10,000 people, and in Korea about 2 in 100,000 are newly diagnosed each year. More than 90 in 100 patients are women, with an average age of about 56. Dry mouth is mostly due to medicines, age or not drinking enough, so check for this cause **when the eyes are dry too and it lasts a long time**.

faq.q: Will drinking lots of water fix it?
faq.a: **A little, often** is better than a lot at once. If it's dry at night, keep water by the bed; during the day, sugar-free gum or ice chips. Coffee and alcohol dry it out more.

faq.q: Which of my medicines dry my mouth?
faq.a: Cold medicine, sleep aids, motion-sickness medicine, bladder medicine, older antidepressants and some blood-pressure medicines (water pills) are common. If you add your medicines to this app's **anticholinergic calculator**, it shows the overlaps. Whether to stop or switch is for your prescribing doctor.

faq.q: Is there a prescription medicine?
faq.a: If your salivary glands still work, there's a medicine that makes saliva flow (pilocarpine). It's used for Sjögren's syndrome and after radiotherapy, and has side effects like sweating and frequent urination, so a doctor decides.

drymouth.clinic: **The medicines you take are the commonest cause.** Doctors check for any that can be changed, and if saliva really isn't being produced, a medicine that stimulates the salivary glands is used.
drymouth.pharm: **Sugar-free xylitol gum** comes before any medicine. The chewing gets saliva flowing. Putting a mouth moisturising gel on before bed makes the early morning more comfortable.

earwax.lead: When one ear suddenly feels blocked and muffled, **earwax blockage** is the most common cause. Earwax normally works its way out by itself, but **digging with cotton buds pushes it further in** and blocks the ear. What you can buy at the pharmacy is **ear drops that soften earwax**; if it's hardened, **having it removed at an ear, nose and throat clinic** is quickest and safest.
earwax.planLabel: Don't dig — soften it and let it come out
how: **Don't put cotton buds or ear picks inside your ear.** Sticking to this alone prevents most blockages.
For the drops, **lie on your side with the blocked ear up**, put them in, and stay still for **5 minutes**.
Try them once or twice a day for **5 days**.
If it's still muffled after 5 days, go to an ear, nose and throat clinic — removal with instruments is the surest way.
After removal, leave the ear alone and wipe only the opening with a dry towel.
pharmacy: Just ask: **“Something to soften earwax, please.”** You'll get olive oil drops or a hydrogen peroxide type.
**Be sure to mention if you have a hole in your eardrum or have had ear surgery.** Then you shouldn't use ear drops either.
Ear pain or pus isn't earwax but an infection — see a doctor, not the pharmacy.
selfcare: Ears **clean themselves.** Doing nothing is the best care.
After a shower, wipe **only the opening of the ear** with a dry towel.
Wearing earphones for long blocks the way out for earwax — take them out now and then.
Ear candling **doesn't work and risks burns**. Don't use it.
avoid: Don't put cotton buds, ear picks or hairpins inside your ear. They push the wax deeper and injure the eardrum.
If you have a hole in your eardrum or have had ear surgery, don't use drops or water rinsing.
Don't put drops in when the ear hurts or there's pus or blood.
Don't use ear candling — there's no evidence, and burns and eardrum injuries have been reported.
Don't dig in children's ears. They injure far more easily than adults'.

plan.title: Stop the cotton buds — they're the cause
plan.why:
Cotton buds **don't scrape wax out; they push it in.** It's the most common reason wax clumps and blocks. Just wipe the ear opening with a towel.

It isn't rare to **injure the eardrum or cause a wound inside the ear that gets infected** while digging with an ear pick.

plan.title: Ear drops for 5 days — usually this gets it out
plan.why:
Putting in drops that soften wax **once or twice a day for 5 days** often lets it flow out by itself.

Of 10 trials pooled, only one (117 ears) compared directly with doing nothing. In that trial, **22 in 100 ears given drops for 5 days** cleared completely, versus **5 ears that had nothing** (low-quality evidence). And **no evidence showed a difference between oil-based (olive oil) and water-based (saline) drops** — meaning there's no reason to think the expensive one is better.

**How to use**: lie on your side with the blocked ear up, put in a few drops and **stay still for 5 minutes**. Then turn over the other way to let it drain.

plan.title: Still blocked — have it removed at an ear, nose and throat clinic
plan.why:
Hard, tightly packed wax **won't come out with drops.** An ear, nose and throat clinic removes it in a few minutes with suction or instruments, and you hear again on the spot.

**Don't rinse it out with water at home** — if you have a hole in your eardrum or have had middle ear infections, water getting in can make things much worse.

plan.title: Hearing aids make wax clump more
plan.why:
Hearing aids and earphones block the way out for wax. **Older people with hearing aids should have their earwax checked every few months.**

Many complaints of “my hearing aid suddenly isn't working well” aren't a fault but **earwax**.

notWorking.title: Still the same after 5 days
steps: **Have it removed at an ear, nose and throat clinic.** Suction takes a few minutes and you hear again on the spot.
If hearing is still poor after removal, get a **hearing test** — age-related hearing loss is often there too.
Sudden hearing loss in one ear may not be earwax. See “When to see a doctor” below.

faq.q: Don't I need to dig earwax out?
faq.a: No. Earwax **protects** the ear and works its way out by itself every time you move your jaw. Digging is what blocks it.

faq.q: Can I use olive oil?
faq.a: Yes. In an analysis pooling several studies, **no evidence showed a difference between oil-based and water-based drops.** But **if you have a hole in your eardrum, none of them are OK** — check that first.

faq.q: I also hear a ringing in my ear
faq.a: Sometimes it comes from the blockage and goes away once removed. If it continues after removal, it's **tinnitus** — that needs looking at separately.

earwax.clinic: At the clinic, **it's removed while looking directly** — with instruments or by rinsing with water. If it's hardened or stuck to the eardrum, this is far safer and quicker. **If you've had a hole in the eardrum or ear surgery, water rinsing isn't allowed, so be sure to say so beforehand.**
earwax.pharm: The only thing you can buy at the pharmacy is **ear drops that soften earwax**. If you put them in for three or four days, it often comes out by itself. **Cotton buds and ear picks actually push it further in.**

fatigue.lead: For tiredness, **there's no medicine that makes it go away.** It's a symptom where the order easily gets reversed, so this page puts **finding the cause** before medicine. Anaemia, low iron, thyroid, blood sugar, depression and sleep apnoea are common causes, and one blood test sorts out most of them. Pharmacy high-dose vitamin B is a medicine licensed for **physical fatigue**, but if 2 weeks of it changes nothing, it means you're not short of vitamins.
fatigue.planTitle: Tiredness and low energy — do this
fatigue.planLabel: Tired for weeks even after sleeping, with no energy
how: The real cause of tiredness is usually found in this order — sleep (7 hours, snoring, sleep apnoea), anaemia (periods, vegetarian diet), thyroid, blood sugar, depression and anxiety, medicines (blood-pressure medicine, antihistamines, sleeping pills), alcohol. One blood test beats ten energy drinks.
Energy drinks and caffeine are **borrowed energy**. Afternoon caffeine cuts your night's sleep and makes you more tired the next day, so one bottle a day, in the morning.
pharmacy: “I've been tired for weeks — one high-dose vitamin B from the pharmacy, please. Can you also check it doesn't overlap with the supplements I already take?”
Say **how many weeks it's been, whether you've lost weight, and whether you get breathless** — anaemia and thyroid problems aren't things to cover up with supplements.
selfcare: Iron is a medicine taken for 3–6 months **after a test confirms anaemia or low iron stores**. Don't take it long-term without testing (iron overload).
Tiredness from cutting back on sleep can't be fixed by medicine — going to bed and getting up at the same time comes first.
avoid: Doubling up several energy drinks and caffeine
Doubling up several vitamin B products (too much B6)
Taking iron long-term without a test
Getting by on less sleep
Using alcohol to fall asleep

plan.title: If you're tired for more than 2 weeks — sort out the cause first
plan.why: One blood test checks **anaemia, iron stores, thyroid and blood sugar**. **Even without anaemia, if iron stores are low**, iron supplements reduced tiredness (18 trials, 1,170 people). But actual exercise capacity didn't improve, so it's closer to 'feeling more energetic'. Sleep (snoring, sleep apnoea), depression and anxiety, medicines you take (blood-pressure medicine, antihistamines, sleeping pills) and alcohol are looked at too.

plan.title: High-dose vitamin B complex — try it for just 2 weeks
plan.why: A medicine licensed for **physical fatigue**. Take just one, try it for 2 weeks and judge. Supermarket vitamin B is a supplement with different strength standards.

plan.title: If your diet is poor — a multivitamin medicine
plan.why: It helps a little when meals are irregular. Just one, so the ingredients don't overlap with other supplements.

plan.title: To get through just today — tonic energy drink
plan.why: It's **borrowed energy**. 30 mg of caffeine, one bottle a day, preferably in the morning. Not for under-15s. Afternoon caffeine cuts night sleep and sets up a cycle of being more tired the next day.

plan.title: If a cause is found, that cause is treated
plan.why: If an underactive thyroid is confirmed, levothyroxine makes it better. Iron deficiency is treated with iron for 3–6 months; depression and anxiety with the right treatment. For **tiredness with no known reason for more than 4 weeks**, weight loss, fever and night sweats are checked for too.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Vitamin B for 2 weeks. If it continues for more than 4 weeks even with enough sleep, see a doctor (blood test).
Check sleep, alcohol and caffeine first → vitamin B for 2 weeks → over 4 weeks, tests (anaemia, thyroid, blood sugar) → if severe for more than 3 months, assessment for chronic fatigue.

faq.q: Can I drink a vitamin drink every day?
faq.a: Ones containing caffeine disturb sleep and make tiredness worse. For vitamin B, **just one product**; try it for 2 weeks and stop if nothing changes. Yellow urine is normal.

faq.q: Will iron tablets give me energy?
faq.a: Only if you're anaemic. Taking them long-term without testing builds up iron and damages the liver. If tiredness lasts more than 4 weeks, anaemia, thyroid and blood sugar tests come first.

faq.q: What kind of tiredness needs a doctor right away?
faq.a: Weight loss, fever or drenching night sweats, breathlessness, or severe tiredness that came on suddenly — don't wait; see a doctor.

fatigue.clinic: **Finding the cause comes first.** Blood tests check for anaemia, iron stores, thyroid and blood sugar, and sleep and mood are looked at too. If a cause is found, that cause is treated.
fatigue.pharm: **Pharmacy medicines only help a little.** Try a high-dose vitamin B product licensed for physical tiredness for 2 weeks; if nothing changes, it means vitamin shortage isn't the cause.

gumdisease.lead: Gum disease is caused by **bacteria living in tartar**, and tartar doesn't come off with a toothbrush. So **the real treatment is scaling and gum treatment**. In its 2016 re-evaluation, the Korean drug agency narrowed pharmacy gum medicines' indication to **'an aid after dental treatment'** — meaning they can't replace treatment.
gumdisease.planLabel: Gums bleed when brushing and feel loose
how: Diabetes makes gum disease more likely, and gum disease **makes blood sugar control worse** — they push each other. If you have diabetes, get scaling more often.
Smoking tightens the gum blood vessels and **stops them bleeding**. No bleeding doesn't mean it's fine — the warning sign is hidden.
A dry mouth speeds up gum disease — see [[symptom:drymouth|dry mouth]] too.
pharmacy: “My gums are swollen and bleeding. I've booked the dentist — something to use until then, please.”
“Could you help me choose the right size of interdental brush for the gaps between my teeth?”
selfcare: Brush **carefully**, not hard — angle the brush 45 degrees at the gumline and use small movements, for 2 minutes.

Use an interdental brush that fits the gap. Forcing it in damages the gums. In an analysis pooling 35 trials (3,929 people), **interdental brushes appeared to reduce gum inflammation a little more than floss** (low-quality evidence) — if you have gaps, go for interdental brushes.
Scaling once a year is covered by national health insurance in Korea. Don't put it off.
avoid: Taking gum medicine for a long time without seeing a dentist
Avoiding brushing because it bleeds — you actually need to brush more
Using chlorhexidine mouthwash for two months on end (staining)
Poking between teeth with a toothpick — the gums recede

plan.title: Benzydamine rinse — calms swelling and pain
plan.why:
A benzydamine mouth rinse. It's not a disinfectant but a medicine that **directly calms inflammation and pain**, so it's comfortable when gums are swollen and sore. Rinse with 15 mL 2–3 times a day and spit. As licensed, **don't keep using it for more than 7 days** — if it hasn't settled by then, it's time for the dentist.

**Avoid harsh alcohol-containing mouthwashes at this point.** The tingling may feel like disinfecting, but on swollen gums it only irritates.

plan.title: Anti-inflammatory tablets — for both swelling and pain
plan.why: Anti-inflammatory tablets genuinely help gum inflammation. Take them briefly on the few days it's swollen and throbbing. If your stomach is sensitive, keep famotidine alongside.

plan.title: Don't stop — gently, with a soft brush
plan.why:
Not brushing a spot because it bleeds makes it worse. Brush **gently with a soft brush, but don't skip it**. Bleeding eases within days.

Gum disease starts **between the teeth**, where the brush doesn't reach. Flossing or using an interdental brush just once a day makes a difference.

plan.title: When it's very swollen — chlorhexidine, up to ten days
plan.why: A gum-disinfecting ingredient that actually reduces inflammation. Rinse with 15 mL for 1 minute and spit, twice a day. **Long use stains teeth brown** and dulls taste, so usually no more than ten days. It and toothpaste cancel each other out, so use it 30 minutes after brushing.

plan.title: Gum tablets — see them as a helper at most
plan.why:
These are the gum tablets heavily advertised in Korea. In its 2016 re-evaluation, the Korean drug agency changed this group's indication to **'a medicine that helps after periodontal treatment'**. They aren't the main weapon against swelling — think of them as **a helper**.

The licence says if there's no change after a month, stop and see a dentist.

plan.title: Once it settles — sort out the cause at the dentist
plan.why:
It's not over when the swelling goes down. If hardened tartar remains below the gums, **the same spot swells again a few months later.** Scaling is covered by **Korean national health insurance once a year** from age 19, and gum treatment is covered too.

The bone around the teeth doesn't hurt while it's being lost, so by the time it hurts and you go, it may already be advanced.

plan.title: What happens at the dentist
plan.why: Antibiotics are added for swollen, infected spots. Gingivitis usually improves with scaling; for periodontitis, root planing scrapes below the gumline.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Floss or use interdental brushes for 2 weeks and see if the bleeding stops — with gingivitis, this alone is enough.
If it still bleeds or teeth are loose, it's **periodontitis**. That's for the dentist, not medicine.
As licensed, **stop gum tablets if there's no change after 1 month**.

faq.q: The gum medicine adverts say it makes gums stronger?
faq.a: In its 2016 re-evaluation, the Korean drug agency narrowed the indication to **an aid after dental treatment**. Medicine doesn't remove tartar. On medicine alone, the bone around your teeth melts away silently.

faq.q: Does frequent scaling damage teeth?
faq.a: No. It only removes tartar and doesn't harm teeth. Korean national health insurance covers it **once a year**, and with gum disease it's done more often. Sensitivity settles in a few days.

faq.q: My gums bleed when I floss — should I stop?
faq.a: The opposite. Where it bleeds is where the bacteria are, so **if you keep it up, the bleeding usually eases within 1–2 weeks**. If it still bleeds or teeth are loose, it's periodontitis — see a dentist.

gumdisease.clinic: Swelling and bleeding mean **inflammation in the gums**. An anti-inflammatory brings down swelling and pain, used with **an anti-inflammatory mouthwash such as benzydamine**. If there's pus, an antibiotic is added. Once it settles, the next step is having the dentist clear the cause (tartar and inflammation below the gums).
gumdisease.pharm: Bringing the swelling down with **an anti-inflammatory mouthwash (benzydamine) and an oral anti-inflammatory** comes first. If it's very swollen, add chlorhexidine briefly. **Avoid mouthwashes that sting at this point** — they can irritate. Don't stop brushing; **go gently with a soft brush**.

hairloss.lead:
For hair loss that thins **slowly over several years** at the crown or forehead (the inherited type), pharmacy **minoxidil applied to the scalp** has evidence. But **you need to apply it for four months to see a difference, and if you stop, the hair falls out again.**

On the other hand, if hair falls out **suddenly in round patches**, **in clumps all at once**, or **the scalp is itchy with oozing or crusts**, it's for **a skin clinic**, not pharmacy medicine.
hairloss.planTitle: Hair loss — look at it like this
hairloss.planLabel: First which kind of hair loss, then medicine
how: **In the first 1–2 weeks it may seem to fall out more.** New hairs are pushing the old ones out, and it usually stops. But **if it keeps getting worse beyond 2 weeks**, stop for now and talk to a pharmacist or doctor.
It takes **four months** to work, and **a year** to judge properly. Taking photos in the same spot and the same light makes comparing easier.
**If you stop, it goes back to how it was within a few months.** Start knowing it's a medicine you keep using.
pharmacy: Just describe how it's falling out, like **“my crown is slowly thinning”**.

**If you have high or low blood pressure or heart disease (rhythm problems, heart failure, angina), talk to a doctor before using it** — the leaflet says not to use it. Minoxidil was originally a blood pressure medicine, so if absorbed into the body it can cause dizziness or palpitations.
**If you're over 55**, the leaflet says its effect and safety haven't been confirmed in older people — talk to a pharmacist or doctor first.
selfcare: Hairstyles that **tie tightly or pull** cause hair loss in that spot. Keep them loose.
Losing 50–100 hairs a day is normal. Don't be alarmed just by what you see on your pillow or comb.
Evidence that shampoos or scalp products cure hair loss is weak. Money is better spent on **diagnosis and medicine**.
avoid: **Don't use minoxidil while pregnant or breastfeeding.**
If it runs onto your face or forehead, **fine hair can grow there**. Keep to the amount, and don't apply it right before bed.
Don't apply it when the scalp has wounds or inflammation — more is absorbed into the body.

plan.title: Thinning slowly, or falling out suddenly?
plan.why:
**The crown or forehead thinning over several years** is inherited hair loss, and that's what the pharmacy medicine is for.

**A round patch suddenly going bare** is alopecia areata; if **about three months ago you had a major illness, gave birth or crash-dieted**, it may be telogen effluvium, where hair sheds all at once. Telogen effluvium **usually recovers by itself.**

plan.title: Minoxidil on the scalp — twice a day, for four months
plan.why:
In an analysis pooling studies of female-pattern hair loss (47 trials, 5,290 people), the 6 minoxidil trials (1,148 people) together showed **“moderately improved or better” in 26 in 100** (14 with placebo), and in a trial of 352 men, **hair counts increased** at 16 weeks.

**For women there was no difference between 2% and 5%, and 5% products in Korea are for men** — women should use **2–3% products**. Apply to a **completely dry scalp**, and at night apply it **2–4 hours before bed**. Wash your hands right after.

plan.title: For men — a tablet (finasteride)
plan.why: For male-pattern hair loss, adding a tablet increases the effect. It needs a prescription. **In women it was no different from placebo, and women who could become pregnant should avoid even touching it.**

notWorking.title: Still the same after four months
steps: **Have a skin clinic look at the cause again.** Thyroid problems, anaemia or hormones are sometimes involved.
For men, discuss adding **a tablet**.
If nothing changes after a year, this medicine doesn't suit you. There's no need to keep buying it.

faq.q: What strength of minoxidil should I buy?
faq.a: **For women there was no difference between 2% and 5%** (pooled analysis of 4 trials, 1,006 people). Start with the lower strength. Men often use 5%.

faq.q: What about supplements (biotin and so on)?
faq.a: **There's no evidence they help people who aren't deficient.** If you're low on iron, topping up iron may help — that's why **testing comes first**.

faq.q: It fell out a lot after a stressful time.
faq.a: After a major illness, surgery, giving birth or severe stress, it's common for hair to fall out **all at once two to three months later** (telogen effluvium). It **usually recovers by itself within 6 months.** If it continues past six months, see a skin clinic.

hairloss.clinic: At the clinic, **thyroid and anaemia (iron) tests** look for other causes first. For male-pattern hair loss, **a tablet (finasteride)** is added, and for alopecia areata, **injections or steroids** are used.
hairloss.pharm: At the pharmacy you can buy **minoxidil applied to the scalp**. Apply twice a day to a dry scalp. **You need to use it for four months** before you can judge.

ibs.lead: Irritable bowel syndrome means **tummy pain and bowel habits that swing back and forth** while tests show nothing wrong. The gut isn't broken — **the signals between gut and brain have become oversensitive** — so rather than a cure, the aim is **finding ways to make it less of a struggle**. First check that you aren't losing weight and that there's no blood mixed in.
ibs.planLabel: Months of tummy pain, with diarrhoea and constipation taking turns
how: **A low-FODMAP diet** (cutting carbohydrates that ferment easily in the gut) and **probiotics** had the firmest evidence in a review that pooled 58 meta-analyses (still only moderate).
