Low-FODMAP means restricting for just 4–6 weeks with a dietitian, then adding foods back one at a time — don't do it alone for long.
Coffee, alcohol, fatty food, dairy and artificial sweeteners (sorbitol, xylitol) are common triggers. **Writing down** what sets it off is more useful than tests.
Stress and too little sleep make the gut more sensitive. Regular meals and walking are worth as much as medicine.
pharmacy: “My tummy often hurts and I get diarrhoea and constipation by turns. Tests were normal. What can I use from the pharmacy?”
“Peppermint oil in capsules that dissolve in the gut, please. I also have a bit of reflux — is that all right?”
selfcare: Don't skip meals; eat regularly. Large meals make the pain worse.
Increase soluble fibre (psyllium) little by little — raising it all at once makes the wind worse.
For just 2 weeks, note what you ate and when it hurt. The triggers show up.
avoid: Using antidiarrhoeals every day
Doing low-FODMAP alone for months (it leaves you short of nutrients)
Writing off weight loss as just irritable bowel
Taking stimulant laxatives every day out of habit

plan.title: Make sure it isn't one of these
plan.why: If **you're losing weight · there's blood in your stool · pain wakes you at night · it started for the first time after 50 · bowel cancer runs in your family**, don't write it off as irritable bowel. A colonoscopy comes first. If none of these apply, go on below.

plan.title: For cramping pain — an antispasmodic
plan.why: This relaxes the gut. **Trimebutine**, the most used in Korea, is sold in pharmacies and works for both the diarrhoea and the constipation type. Take it only when it hurts — no need to take it every day. The evidence is moderate: there aren't many large trials, but it's widely used and has few side effects.

plan.title: Peppermint oil — 1 in 4 people benefit (a health supplement in Korea)
plan.why: In an analysis pooling 1,030 people, overall symptoms improved in **1 in 4** and tummy pain in **1 in 7** (the quality of evidence was rated very low, and mild side effects such as heartburn were more common than with placebo). But in Korea there's no enteric-coated capsule licensed as a medicine, so you'll have to look for it as a health supplement or imported product, and pharmacies may not stock it. Always choose capsules that dissolve in the gut, 30 minutes before meals. Avoid it if you have reflux (heartburn, sour fluid coming up).

plan.title: Match it to your stool — antidiarrhoeal for diarrhoea type, bulking fibre for constipation type
plan.why: Use **loperamide** only on days the diarrhoea is bad, not every day. For the constipation type, soluble fibre such as **psyllium (plantain seed husk)** works better; insoluble fibre like wheat bran actually increases wind. If fibre isn't enough, a gentle laxative such as **magnesium oxide** can also be used.

plan.title: What happens at the clinic
plan.why: If lifestyle and pharmacy medicines aren't enough, doctors use prescription antispasmodics (otilonium, pinaverium), medicines specific to the diarrhoea type, and **low-dose tricyclic antidepressants** for pain control (far lower than the depression dose). In older people, tricyclics cause dry mouth, constipation and dizziness, so they're used with care.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Note trigger foods and eat regularly for 2–4 weeks → antispasmodic, peppermint → if it's still hard, a gut specialist.
If you're losing weight or there's blood in your stool, **don't wait** — get a colonoscopy.

faq.q: Do probiotics help?
faq.a: Some help, but it varies by product. Try one product for **4 weeks** and stop if it doesn't help (UK guideline advice). It isn't a cure.

faq.q: How do I do the low-FODMAP diet?
faq.a: Doing it alone for months leaves you short of nutrients. With a dietitian, the aim is to find trigger foods in the order **restrict for 4–6 weeks → add foods back one at a time**.

faq.q: Is it caused by stress?
faq.a: The signals between gut and brain have become oversensitive, so stress makes symptoms worse. There's evidence that cognitive behavioural therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy work as well as medicine. If you're struggling emotionally, see a doctor who'll look at that too.

ibs.clinic: **First doctors check there are no warning signs**, then use an antispasmodic for tummy pain and medicines suited to the diarrhoea or constipation type. If pain is severe, a low-dose tricyclic is sometimes used.
ibs.pharm: **An antispasmodic for cramping pain** (trimebutine) is the basis, then matched to your stool: an antidiarrhoeal for the diarrhoea type, soluble fibre for the constipation type.

meno.lead: For hot flushes, night sweats, sleep, mood, vaginal dryness and joint pain, **the treatment that works best** is **hormone therapy (prescription)**. Whether you can use it is for a gynaecologist to decide. Pharmacy herbal medicines and supplements are an option **when symptoms are mild or you want to avoid hormones**.
meno.planLabel: Sudden flushing, trouble sleeping, more irritable
how: If a pharmacist suggests a herbal medicine such as **Gami-soyo-san** — it's licensed for menopausal symptoms, but the effect varies a lot between people and the evidence is weak. It contains liquorice, so stop if you get swelling, rising blood pressure or weakness in hands and feet (especially if you take blood-pressure medicine). Rare liver problems have also been reported. If it's unchanged after a month, don't keep using it — move on to a doctor. Don't take it if you could be pregnant (contraindicated per the package insert).

Ingredients approved by the Korean drug agency for **'menopausal women's health'** (Japanese pagoda tree fruit, white swallow-wort root combinations, soy isoflavones, etc.) are **supplements, not medicines**, and their effect is small. With a history of breast cancer, discuss isoflavones with your doctor.
pharmacy: “Menopausal hot flushes and irritability are wearing me down — something from the pharmacy, please. I take blood-pressure medicine — is something with liquorice OK?”
Be sure to say **whether you've had breast cancer or blood clots**. It changes what you can choose.
selfcare: For vaginal dryness, painful sex and recurrent cystitis, vaginal moisturisers and **vaginal oestrogen (prescription)** work well and are relatively safe.
Bone density falls quickly in the 5 years after menopause — calcium 1,000–1,200 mg (including food), vitamin D, strength exercise, and a bone density test (at 65 or older, earlier if at risk).
avoid: Doubling up on several supplements
Long-term use of liquorice-containing herbal medicines without checking
Alcohol, spicy food and caffeine with hot flushes
Isoflavones or hormones without advice if you've had breast cancer

plan.title: Ask about hormone therapy first — prescription
plan.why: It's **the most effective treatment so far** for hot flushes and night sweats. It also helps sleep, mood and vaginal dryness. Started **within 10 years of menopause and under 60**, the benefits tend to outweigh the risks; it isn't used if you've had breast cancer or blood clots. Before holding out on pharmacy herbal medicines, check with a doctor at least once.

plan.title: Calcium (calcium carbonate + vitamin D)
plan.why: Not a medicine that eases menopausal symptoms but one that **protects bone, which thins quickly after menopause**. If food covers your daily needs, you don't need extra; top up only by what you're short. Absorption drops above 500 mg at once, so split doses, and keep the total including food under 2,000 mg a day.

plan.title: Vitamin E — when symptoms are mild
plan.why: Vitamin E — its licensed uses are **menopausal stiff shoulders and neck, and tingling or cold hands and feet**. Evidence that it reduces hot flushes is weak, and the North American Menopause Society (2023) didn't recommend supplements. Try it when symptoms are mild, but **if you take a blood thinner or an oestrogen contraceptive, check with a pharmacist or doctor first**. If it's unchanged after 4 weeks, move on to a doctor.

plan.title: If you can't or don't want to use hormones — other prescriptions
plan.why: If you've had breast cancer or blood clots, or want to avoid hormones, **antidepressant-type medicines** reduce hot flushes (at lower doses than for depression). For bone thinning, see the [[symptom:osteoporosis|osteoporosis page]] separately.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Holding out with pharmacy medicine is for mild symptoms. If hot flushes and sleeplessness make daily life hard, don't wait 4 weeks — go straight to a gynaecologist; hormone therapy works much better.

Lifestyle (layered clothing, staying cool, exercise, less alcohol) → pharmacy medicine for 4 weeks → gynaecologist (hormone therapy, non-hormonal prescriptions, bone density test). If daily life is hard, don't wait your turn — start with the gynaecologist.

faq.q: Does hormone therapy cause breast cancer?
faq.a: Using combined hormones (oestrogen + progestin) for more than a few years raises the risk slightly. Still, it's small — **fewer than 1 extra case per 1,000 women a year** — in a large US comparison trial (ages 50–79, average 5 years), it was 8 more per 10,000 women a year. It isn't used with a history of breast cancer, blood clots or liver disease, so weigh it up with your doctor.

faq.q: Does soy (isoflavones) work?
faq.a: Even when it works, the effect is small and slow (weeks to months). With a history of breast cancer, don't take it without advice. If hot flushes are keeping you from sleeping, don't wait — see a doctor.

faq.q: What should I do when a hot flush suddenly comes on?
faq.a: Taking off layers and moving somewhere cool helps in the moment — but there was no evidence that these, or 'slow breathing', reduce the hot flushes themselves (North American Menopause Society 2023). Non-hormonal methods with evidence are **cognitive behavioural therapy, clinical hypnosis**, and prescription medicines (antidepressant-type, gabapentin, newer drugs). If hot flushes are frequent, discuss it with a doctor.

faq.q: What about menopause products like pomegranate or black cohosh?
faq.a:
To be honest, **the evidence is weak.** In 2023 the North American Menopause Society sorted hot-flush treatments by level of evidence, and **supplements and herbal medicines were placed under 'not recommended'**. Soy and equol, yoga, meditation and exercise, and acupuncture were in the same box. What was recommended was **cognitive behavioural therapy, clinical hypnosis, antidepressant-type medicines, gabapentin and newer drugs**.

If you still want to use them, we won't stop you — they're not very harmful. But use them **knowing they may not work**, and if hot flushes keep you from sleeping, **don't wait — see a doctor**. If you've had breast cancer, discuss even herbal products first.

meno.clinic: **Hormone therapy works best for hot flushes.** Within 10 years of menopause and under 60, the benefit tends to be large. If you can't use it, antidepressant-type medicines reduce hot flushes.
meno.pharm: **Pharmacy medicines have clear limits.** Vitamin E shows a small effect at most. If nothing changes after 4 weeks, move on to a doctor.

numbness.lead: With tingling and numbness, **finding the cause comes before covering it with medicine**. Diabetes, a neck or back nerve, carpal tunnel, low vitamin B12, the thyroid — each cause has a different answer, and pharmacy products rarely solve it. Here we first sort out **where to look**.
numbness.planTitle: Tingling hands or feet — do this
numbness.planLabel: Tingling in the fingertips or toes, worse at night
how: Ordinary painkillers (paracetamol, anti-inflammatories) **don't work well for tingling that comes from a nerve**. Don't raise the dose because they aren't working.
If you have diabetes, **look at your feet every day**. When feeling dulls, you can get a wound without noticing — and that's how losing a foot begins.
Drinking often damages nerves in itself.
pharmacy: “Both my toes tingle. I have diabetes — will vitamins do, or should I see a doctor?”
“My hand tingles and wakes me at night — a wrist splint, please. How should I wear it?”
selfcare: For just 2 weeks, note where and when it tingles — it helps find which nerve much faster.
If you have diabetes, check your feet every day, soles included (a mirror helps).
If it tingles when you walk, see **whether it settles with rest**. That answer splits the diagnosis.
avoid: Taking only vitamins for a long time without looking for the cause
High-dose vitamin B6 for months (it can actually cause tingling)
Keeping on raising anti-inflammatory painkillers for tingling
Hot packs or heaters on feet with dulled feeling (you can burn without noticing)

plan.title: Which part tingles tells you half the answer
plan.why: **Both feet, from the toes up, like wearing socks** = peripheral nerves, such as diabetes or low B12. **Only the thumb, index and middle finger, worse at night and better when you shake the hand** = carpal tunnel. Tingling running down one leg = a slipped disc or spinal stenosis in the lower back. Tingling while walking that eases with rest = spinal stenosis or leg blood vessels. Note which fits and say it as is at your appointment. But the feeling alone doesn't pin down the diagnosis well — findings on examination are more accurate (Neurology 2005). Use your own sorting only as a note for the appointment.

plan.title: Check blood sugar and vitamin B12 with a blood test
plan.why: The basic tests recommended in a review of peripheral neuropathy (JAMA 2015) are **a blood count, metabolic tests, vitamin B12, and fasting blood sugar with a glucose tolerance test**. Among these, the **causes you can fix if found** are low B12 and diabetes. People who've taken stomach acid reducers or metformin for a long time, or who've been vegetarian for years, are especially prone to low B12. The thyroid is often checked too.

plan.title: Only if B12 is low — a vitamin B complex
plan.why: It's worth it **when a shortage is confirmed**. Taking high doses for a long time when you aren't short can actually **make tingling worse through too much vitamin B6** (above Korea's upper limit of 50 mg a day, for a long time — 2025 Korean Dietary Reference Intakes). Buying vitamins first for tingling is doing things the wrong way round.

plan.title: For carpal tunnel — a wrist splint at night
plan.why: Many people improve just by keeping the wrist from bending at night. You can buy one at the pharmacy, and it can take about **6 weeks** to help, so use it until then before judging. Look at your wrist angle at the computer and when driving too.

plan.title: What happens at the clinic
plan.why: After finding the cause, for the nerve pain itself doctors use **gabapentin or pregabalin**, or **duloxetine** (ordinary painkillers don't work well for nerve pain). In older people they start low and raise slowly because dizziness can cause falls. For spinal stenosis, limaprost is sometimes used, and for diabetic neuropathy, thioctic acid. Severe carpal tunnel clearly improves with surgery.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Note which part tingles → blood tests for sugar, B12 and thyroid → if still unclear, a neurologist (nerve conduction test).
If you're losing strength or your walking is unsteady, don't wait — see a doctor.

faq.q: How do I know if it's carpal tunnel syndrome?
faq.a: Suspect it if your **thumb, index and middle finger** tingle and wake you at night, and shaking the hand helps. A wrist splint at night is the first treatment; if the muscle wastes, discuss surgery.

faq.q: Who tends to get low vitamin B12?
faq.a: It's common with a vegetarian diet, after stomach surgery, in people who've taken **metformin (a diabetes medicine) or acid reducers for a long time**, and over 65. Topping up after a test can improve tingling. High-dose B6 without testing can actually cause tingling.

faq.q: Should I take a circulation supplement (ginkgo)?
faq.a: It doesn't treat the cause of tingling and the evidence is weak. Combined with blood thinners it can raise bleeding risk. Check the cause first (blood sugar, B12, thyroid, nerves).

numbness.clinic: **Where it tingles points to the cause.** Blood tests check sugar and vitamin B12, and for nerve pain itself, nerve-pain medicines are used rather than ordinary painkillers.
numbness.pharm: **There's no suitable medicine at the pharmacy.** Vitamin B is worth it **only when a shortage is confirmed**. For carpal tunnel, a wrist splint worn at night helps.

pms.lead: Premenstrual syndrome is a set of physical (swelling, breasts, headache, back) and emotional (irritability, low mood, appetite) symptoms that **repeat every month** from ovulation until your period starts, easing once the period begins. Keeping **a symptom diary** (app) for two or three cycles is both the diagnosis and the start of treatment.
pms.planLabel: Swollen, on edge, with headache or back pain for a few days before your period
how: For pain and headache, take an anti-inflammatory **starting a few days before your period**. For swelling, pamabrom — together with cutting back on salty food and coffee. Pamabrom combinations already contain acetaminophen, so don't double up with plain acetaminophen.

If mood symptoms are bad enough to wreck daily life and relationships (premenstrual dysphoric disorder), pharmacy medicine isn't enough — prescription medicines work well (which one is for the doctor to decide), and it's nothing to be ashamed of.
pharmacy: “Before my period I get swollen, irritable and headachy. A painkiller with pamabrom and naproxen, please — my stomach is fine. Would vitamin B6 or magnesium help too?”
Saying **your cycle and when the discomfort starts** helps decide when to take medicine.
selfcare: Regular exercise, sleep and cutting back on alcohol and caffeine have evidence behind them. For B6, Korea's upper limit is 50 mg a day, but Europe warns of numbness with long-term intake above 12 mg (2025 Korean Dietary Reference Intakes · European Food Safety Authority 2023). Calcium 1,000–1,200 mg (including food) also has a little evidence.
Keep a symptom diary for two or three cycles. 'Does it ease once the period starts?' is the key to the diagnosis.
Many people notice less swelling and breast tenderness if they cut back on salt, alcohol and caffeine just in the week before their period.
Walking and light exercise help mood symptoms. So does regular sleep.
avoid: Caffeine, alcohol and salty food before your period
High-dose B6 for a long time
Doubling up pamabrom with other water pills
Doubling up pamabrom combinations with plain acetaminophen
Holding out and taking painkillers late

plan.title: Headache, back and lower belly pain before a period — anti-inflammatory
plan.why: Prostaglandins play a big part in pain around periods, so acetaminophen alone often isn't enough and anti-inflammatories do better. Naproxen lasts a long time per dose: as the package insert says, **2 capsules (500 mg) first, then 1 capsule every 6–8 hours if it hurts**, no more than 5 capsules (1,250 mg) a day. You don't need to take it every time it hurts. To reduce heartburn, take it **with food**, and only on the few days you have symptoms.

plan.title: Adding — acetaminophen
plan.why: What doctors add when an anti-inflammatory alone isn't enough. In theory taking them at the same time isn't recommended (package insert), but they're sometimes used together and work better than either alone — keep each medicine's interval and daily total separately.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while on an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid**, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use the anti-inflammatory — if you have had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from your doctor is the surer option. Everyone else can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if the burning continues.

plan.title: Calcium — the best evidence of anything you can buy at a pharmacy
plan.why:
In a comparison trial (466 women) taking 1,200 mg a day steadily for three cycles, symptom scores **fell by 48%** (30% with a dummy pill). All four areas improved — mood, swelling, appetite and pain. It's not a medicine for when it hurts but **one to take every day**, and you can't tell after one cycle — **give it two or three cycles**.

Absorption drops if you take more than 500 mg at once, so split the dose. Including what you get from food, don't go over 2,000 mg a day.

plan.title: Magnesium as a medicine (muscle cramps, supplementation)
plan.why: There's a little evidence for swelling, headache and mood — the trials are small, so it's not certain. It's not a medicine for when it hurts; use it **steadily for one cycle** and then judge. Large amounts cause diarrhoea; if so, just take less.

plan.title: If you're swollen with sore breasts — combination with a diuretic ingredient
plan.why: Pamabrom, found in women's acetaminophen combination products, is the diuretic ingredient. **The evidence isn't strong**; think of it as something to try just on those few days when swelling and breast tenderness are the main symptoms.

plan.title: Vitamin B6 — not recommended
plan.why: It's been recommended for a long time, but the evidence is essentially **a single 1999 review**. That review said 'up to 100 mg a day is likely to help', but the authors themselves wrote that 'most trials were of low quality, limiting the conclusion', and no proper replication has followed. Gynaecology guidelines still list it among first options for mild symptoms. But **taking more than 50 mg a day (the 2025 Korean Dietary Reference Intakes upper limit) for a long time can cause numbness in hands and feet**, and the European Food Safety Authority set an even lower upper limit of 12 mg a day in 2023. If you use it, keep the dose low and the course short. For the same money, calcium has better evidence.

plan.title: What happens in the clinic
plan.why: Gynaecology guidelines put exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy and vitamin B6 at the first step together with **an oral contraceptive containing drospirenone** and **antidepressants (only in the 2 weeks before the period, or daily)**; if these don't work, the dose is raised or an oestradiol patch is used, and after that hormone injections that stop ovulation itself (gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues), among others. Anti-inflammatories for pain.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: Judge after two or three cycles. If mood symptoms are severe, go straight to a gynaecologist or psychiatrist.
Symptom diary → two cycles of anti-inflammatory, pamabrom, B6/magnesium → if still the same, a gynaecologist (tests; the doctor chooses the medicine).

faq.q: What is pamabrom?
faq.a: A mild diuretic. It's an ingredient used **for just a few days** for swelling and breast tenderness before a period, and doubled up with caffeine or other diuretics it can cause palpitations and dehydration. Many products combine it with acetaminophen, so don't double up with plain acetaminophen.

faq.q: I heard calcium helps?
faq.a:
**This one has evidence.** 466 women were split into two groups and took **calcium 1,200 mg** for three months; symptom scores **fell by 48%** (30% with a dummy pill). All four areas — swelling, appetite, pain and mood — improved.

1,200 mg a day can be largely covered by **milk, yoghurt, cheese and small dried anchovies**. If you take a supplement, don't take more than 500 mg at once — split it. **If you've had kidney stones**, ask before taking it.

faq.q: When should I start taking painkillers?
faq.a: **As soon as the pain starts.** Holding out and taking it late makes it work less well. Naproxen after food; you can start from the day before your period.

faq.q: The irritability and low mood are terrible.
faq.a: If daily life falls apart before every period, it may be **premenstrual dysphoric disorder**. Antidepressant-type medicines are prescriptions that work well (2013 combined analysis), and there's also the option of taking them only in the 2 weeks before your period. See a gynaecologist or psychiatrist.

pms.clinic: **The contraceptive pill or an antidepressant** deals with the hormonal swings that cause the symptoms. More people respond well than you'd expect.
pms.pharm: **When it hurts, an anti-inflammatory painkiller** comes first. Of what you can buy at the pharmacy, **calcium has the best evidence**, and you need to take it steadily for a month to see if it's worth it. Mood symptoms are hard to manage with pharmacy medicines.

smoking.lead:
Smoking is **much easier to quit with help than with willpower alone.** With nicotine patches or gum, **about 1.5 times as many** people quit, and the prescription stop-smoking medicine (varenicline) helped **more than twice as many** as placebo.

In Korea, this help **mostly comes at no cost** — public health centre stop-smoking clinics offer counselling plus patches and gum, and there's the quitline **1544-9030**.
smoking.planLabel: Don't just grit your teeth — get help
how: **Set a quit date.** That morning, put on a patch and clear away cigarettes, lighters and ashtrays.
The urge to smoke **usually passes within a few minutes.** Get through it with a glass of water, brushing your teeth or a short walk.
**Drinking sessions are the riskiest.** It's better to avoid them for the first few weeks.
One cigarette isn't failure. **Start again the next day** — many people quit after several attempts.
pharmacy: Ask: **“I smoke this many a day — which patch strength should I start on?”**
Mention if you take medicines for heart disease, blood pressure or diabetes. Quitting can **change blood sugar or how some medicines work**.
selfcare: Note **the times and places** you crave a cigarette (after meals, with coffee, driving) and decide in advance what you'll do instead at that moment.
After quitting, your appetite comes back and **gaining a little weight** is common. Start walking alongside.
Tell your family your quit date. **No one else smoking at home** is the biggest help.
avoid: **Don't smoke while wearing a patch.** Too much nicotine brings nausea, dizziness and palpitations.
**If you're pregnant**, be sure to discuss it before using nicotine products.

If you've had a heart attack or stroke in the last three months, or have angina with chest pain coming more and more often, or a serious heart rhythm problem, don't start nicotine products yourself — let a doctor decide (the product leaflet says not to use them).

plan.title: Public health centre stop-smoking clinic — counselling, patches and gum at no cost
plan.why:
In Korea, at your local **public health centre stop-smoking clinic**, a counsellor helps you one-to-one, and if needed gives you **nicotine patches and gum at no cost**.

If it's hard to go in person, you can get a 30-day programme from **the quitline 1544-9030** (weekdays 9 am–10 pm, weekends and holidays 9 am–6 pm).

plan.title: Patch — one a day, put on in the morning
plan.why:
It releases nicotine slowly to ease **withdrawal (irritability, poor concentration, sleep problems)**. In an analysis pooling 133 trials of nicotine products (64,640 people), looking only at the 51 patch trials (25,754 people), **1.6 times as many people quit** with the patch.

The starting strength depends on **how much you used to smoke a day** — tell the pharmacist. You step down over several weeks. If the patch site gets itchy and red, **change the spot every day.** If you have vivid dreams at night, **take it off before sleep.**

plan.title: Gum and lozenges — with the patch, right when you crave one
plan.why:
**Using gum or lozenges together with a patch** helped about 1.27 times as many people quit as using one alone (Cochrane 2023, 16 trials, 12,169 people). The patch gives a base level, and you use gum when the craving hits — work out the starting strength with the pharmacist.

Don't **chew the gum continuously like ordinary gum.** Chew a few times until it tingles, then **park it between your cheek and gum**; when the tingling fades, chew a few more times. Chewing nonstop means you swallow the nicotine and get **nausea and hiccups**.

It isn't absorbed well right after coffee or cola, so use it **about 15 minutes later**.

plan.title: Still hard — stop-smoking medicine (varenicline)
plan.why:
It isn't nicotine but **a prescription medicine that makes cigarettes less satisfying**. In 75 trials with 45,049 people, **2.3 times** as many quit as with placebo, and **1.25 times** as many as with a single nicotine product.

In Korea, you can get it for 8–12 weeks through **national health insurance support for quitting**. While taking it **you may feel sick, and rarely your mood may drop**, so it's used with a doctor keeping an eye on things.

notWorking.title: If several attempts haven't worked
steps: There's the option of **using two nicotine products together** (patch + gum). Discuss it with the pharmacist or a stop-smoking counsellor.
Get **stop-smoking medicine (varenicline)** from a doctor. Health insurance support applies in Korea.
If you smoke because of low mood or anxiety, getting that treated too helps you quit.

faq.q: Is it easier to quit by switching to e-cigarettes?
faq.a: In an analysis pooling several studies, **nicotine e-cigarettes helped 4 more people in 100 quit** than nicotine products. But **long-term safety isn't known yet.** It's a tool to use briefly while quitting, not something to keep using. Using cigarettes and e-cigarettes **together** gains you nothing.

faq.q: I have heart disease — can I use a patch?
faq.a: **In most cases it's far safer than smoking** — besides nicotine, cigarettes contain thousands of things that harm the heart. But **if you've had a heart attack or stroke in the last three months, or get chest pain often**, let a doctor decide.

faq.q: Can I cut down and then stop?
faq.a: Yes. Stopping all at once works a bit better, but **cutting down while using nicotine products and then setting a quit date** is also an option. Either way, **setting a quit date** is the key.

smoking.clinic: At the clinic, **stop-smoking medicine (varenicline)** is prescribed with counselling over 8–12 weeks. In Korea, **national health insurance support for quitting** keeps the cost low. If you've failed several times with nicotine products alone, this route is better.
smoking.pharm: At the pharmacy you can buy **nicotine patches, gum and lozenges**. Tell them how much you used to smoke a day and they'll pick the starting strength. But in Korea, **at a public health centre stop-smoking clinic you can get the same at no cost**.

tinnitus.lead:
A ringing or buzzing sound in the ears is called tinnitus. **Up to 1 in 5 adults** have it, and of those, 1–3 in 100 are badly troubled by it. **There's no pharmacy medicine that gets rid of tinnitus** — it's better to be honest about that. But **ways to be less bothered by the sound** have evidence, and the surest is **talking therapy that works on your thoughts (cognitive behavioural therapy)**.

**If it starts suddenly in one ear and you can't hear well on that side, it's an emergency** — go to an ear, nose and throat clinic the same day.
tinnitus.planLabel: There's no medicine to remove it, but you can be less bothered
how: **Avoid silent rooms.** At night, a very quiet background sound makes falling asleep easier.
**Caffeine, alcohol and smoking** make tinnitus louder for many people — cut down for just 2 weeks and see if it changes.
In noisy places (building sites, karaoke rooms), wear earplugs. Noise makes tinnitus worse.
“Not listening out for the sound” genuinely helps. The more you focus on it, the louder it gets.
If you can't sleep, work on **your sleep habits** first rather than reaching for sleeping pills.
pharmacy: **There's no pharmacy medicine that reliably reduces tinnitus.** Ginkgo products are sometimes used in clinics, but the effect isn't clear.
It's quicker to check **whether earwax is the cause** first. See whether the ear also feels blocked.
Show your list of medicines and ask **whether any of them can cause tinnitus**.
selfcare: **Silence is the enemy.** Set up a soft background sound.
Protect your ears from loud noise — a pair of earplugs is enough.
Cut caffeine and alcohol for just 2 weeks and see if it changes.
Nights when you can only focus on the tinnitus are hardest. Play the radio or an audiobook very quietly.
Don't bear it alone — when sleep and mood collapse, tinnitus gets louder.
avoid: Don't spend a lot on ginkgo, zinc or vitamin products. There's no solid evidence they reduce tinnitus.
Don't dig in your ears. A wound makes it worse.
Be wary of adverts for devices or procedures that “get rid of tinnitus”.
Don't listen to louder sounds to drown it out — noise makes tinnitus worse.
Don't put off sudden tinnitus in one ear with “let's wait a few days”.

plan.title: Check earwax and your medicines first
plan.why:
Here are two **fixable causes** of tinnitus.

One is **earwax**. Removing a blockage sometimes makes it go away.

The other is **the medicines you take**. High doses of aspirin, diuretics, some antibiotics and cancer medicines can cause tinnitus. **Don't stop medicines yourself** — tell your doctor “I've developed tinnitus”.

plan.title: Best evidence — talking therapy that works on your thoughts
plan.why:
It doesn't remove the sound itself, but it reduces **how much the sound shakes your life**.

Pooling 28 trials with 2,733 people, those who had the therapy saw **the impact of tinnitus on their life fall by about 11 points on a 100-point scale** (the threshold for a meaningful difference is 7 points, so it's a bigger change than that). There were almost no side effects.

This is compared with no treatment, and the evidence is low quality. One trial (42 people) also compared it with tinnitus retraining therapy using a sound generator, and the talking therapy did better.

plan.title: Avoid quiet places — with sound around, you hear it less
plan.why:
Tinnitus **sounds louder the quieter it is.** That's why nights are hardest.

A background sound such as a fan, a very quiet radio or rain sounds makes falling asleep easier. The evidence is weaker than for talking therapy, but it **does no harm and costs nothing.**

plan.title: If you also don't hear well — hearing aids
plan.why:
Many older people with tinnitus **also have hearing loss**. When hearing aids let outside sounds in well, **the tinnitus stands out less.**

Getting a hearing test once is also the start of dealing with tinnitus.

plan.title: What happens at the clinic
plan.why:
**There's still no medicine that removes tinnitus itself.** Ginkgo extract, zinc and vitamins have no solid evidence of reducing it either.

But when tinnitus **keeps you from sleeping or makes you low**, those are treated. When sleep and mood improve, tinnitus often becomes bearable too.

For sudden tinnitus and hearing loss in one ear, **starting steroids quickly** matters — after time passes it's hard to reverse.

notWorking.title: If it's hard to bear
steps: Get a **hearing test** — if you also have hearing loss, hearing aids reduce the tinnitus.
If tinnitus **stops you sleeping or brings your mood down**, get that treated too, alongside the ear, nose and throat clinic. That's also tinnitus treatment.
Ask where you can get **talking therapy that works on your thoughts (cognitive behavioural therapy)**. It has the best evidence.

faq.q: Does it get better?
faq.a: **Sometimes the sound goes away completely, and sometimes it stays.** But many people find it “bothers them less” over time. Talking therapy speeds up exactly that process.

faq.q: I heard ginkgo products are good?
faq.a: **There's no solid evidence they reduce tinnitus.** Of 12 trials (1,915 people) reviewed, only two (85 people) could be combined for tinnitus scores, and the difference was **1.35 points** out of 100 — and even that was rated “very low certainty”. It is safe — nothing serious such as bleeding or seizures occurred. But if you're going to spend money, a **hearing test and talking therapy** are far better value.

faq.q: Why does it get louder at night?
faq.a: The sound isn't louder — **the surroundings are quieter, so you hear it more**. That's why a very quiet background sound helps.

tinnitus.clinic: First **a hearing test** checks whether you're really not hearing well. If there's a cause, that's treated; if not, **sound therapy and talking therapy that changes your thinking** have the most evidence so far.
tinnitus.pharm: **There's still no medicine that reliably reduces tinnitus.** Ginkgo preparations are sometimes prescribed in clinics, but the effect isn't clear — we think it's honest to say so.

vaginitis.lead: Discharge and itching come in **three kinds**. ① White, lumpy discharge with intense itching = candida (thrush; pharmacy medicine exists) ② Grey, thin, with **a fishy smell** = bacterial vaginosis (prescription metronidazole) ③ Yellow, frothy, smelly and stinging = trichomonas (prescription; treat partners too). Pharmacy medicine works only for ①.
vaginitis.planTitle: Vaginal itching and discharge — do this
how: Get it checked by a doctor if it's the first time, it recurs 3 or more times a year, you're pregnant, have diabetes, have fever or lower belly pain, or abnormal bleeding. Studies show that **self-diagnosed thrush** is right only about one time in three — keep the threshold for seeing a doctor low.
Insert pessaries deep at bedtime; they work less well during a period, so use them after it ends. They weaken latex condoms and diaphragms, so use another contraceptive method for a few days.
pharmacy: “I have white discharge and itching, and it's not the first time. A clotrimazole pessary and a cream for outside, please — I'm not on my period now.”
**If it's the first time, you have a fever, or there's a foul smell**, you need to see a doctor before buying medicine.
selfcare: Habitually washing inside the vagina, scented products, tight clothes and staying in wet swimwear are triggers for recurrence, and thrush often follows antibiotics. Partners need treatment for thrush only if they have symptoms, but for trichomonas always.
Wear cotton underwear, and don't stay long in tight clothes or wet swimwear.
Washing inside the vagina actually upsets the balance — just rinse the outside gently with water.
Thrush often comes after antibiotics. If it recurs then, mention that to the pharmacist or doctor.
avoid: Don't use vaginal washes **as a habit**. They wash away good bacteria too and increase recurrences. The right way is to use them for a few days when you have symptoms, after talking to a pharmacist.
Habitual internal washing, scented washes, bubble baths
Pessaries during a period
Repeatedly self-treating with thrush medicine when there's a smell or froth
Repeated pessaries **for prevention** without symptoms

plan.title: If it's the first time — see a doctor first
plan.why:
Itching and discharge don't always mean fungus. Of 95 women who judged themselves to have thrush, **only one in three (32) actually had it**. If it's bacterial vaginosis or trichomonas, pessaries won't cure it, and it spreads while you waste time on the wrong medicine.

A look under the microscope at the clinic sorts it out straight away. If it isn't fungus, the next step is **an antibiotic (metronidazole)**.

**Being asked about sex may feel awkward.** But the medicine depends on the answer, so staff ask not to judge you but to choose the medicine. Going in prepared makes it much easier.

plan.title: If you've had the same diagnosis before — clotrimazole pessary
plan.why:
A medicine for when you've been diagnosed with fungal (candida) vaginitis before and **know it's the same symptoms**. **One 500 mg pessary once at bedtime** is simplest; 100 mg for 6 days or 200 mg for 3 days are also licensed. The effect is similar.

Don't use it during a period, and while using it condoms and diaphragms are weakened, so take care with contraception.

plan.title: If the outside (vulva) is itchy and swollen
plan.why: If it's the outside rather than inside that's itchy and red, apply a thin layer of cream with the same ingredient. You can use it with the pessary.

plan.title: Washing matters as much as medicine — but do it 'right'
plan.why:
**Don't wash inside the vagina.** It washes away good bacteria too and makes recurrences more frequent.

For the outside, **lukewarm water** or **a gentle product made for intimate washing**, once a day, is enough. Avoid soap, body wash and strongly scented products, and **dry completely** after washing. Wear cotton underwear and don't stay long in wet swimwear or tight clothes.

plan.title: In these cases, don't hold out with pharmacy medicine
plan.why:
**If you have a fever, lower belly pain, or symptoms so bad you can't sleep**, don't hold out with pessaries — see a doctor right away. It may not be fungus, and even if it is, a doctor can choose **an antifungal tablet (fluconazole, prescription)** or longer treatment. Tablets don't work faster than pessaries, but they're done in one go, which is convenient.

If you're pregnant, it recurs three or more times a year, or it's unchanged after finishing treatment, a doctor is also the answer.

plan.title: What happens in the clinic
plan.why: After identifying the type under the microscope: for fungus, an antifungal tablet or pessary; for bacterial vaginosis, metronidazole. For trichomonas, partners are treated too.

notWorking.title: If it isn't getting better
steps: After a pessary, it should start improving within 3 days and recover within 7. If not, see a doctor.
Check the type by the colour and smell of the discharge → if thrush, pessary + cream → if unchanged after 3 days, or there's a smell or froth, see a doctor (tests, metronidazole).

faq.q: Can I have sex while using pessaries?
faq.a: Avoid it during treatment. Clotrimazole **weakens condoms and diaphragms**, so contraception can fail. If your partner is itchy too, see a doctor together.

faq.q: Which is better, tablets or pessaries?
faq.a: **The rate of symptom relief is the same.** That's the result of pooling 26 trials with 5,007 women. Only the rate of clearing the fungus was slightly higher with tablets, and patients generally found tablets more convenient. The 'type' of side effect differs — **pessaries sting where inserted; tablets can upset the stomach or cause headache.** In pregnancy it's **pessaries**, and tablets (fluconazole) need a prescription.

faq.q: I'm pregnant — can I use pharmacy medicine?
faq.a: Topical and vaginal clotrimazole is commonly used in pregnancy, but **talk to your doctor first**. Antifungal tablets (fluconazole) are avoided in early pregnancy.

faq.q: Do yoghurt or probiotics help?
faq.a: The evidence is weak. If it recurs often, first review antibiotic use, blood sugar, tight clothing and internal washing habits, and if it recurs 3 or more times a year, you need to see a doctor.

vaginitis.clinic: **The type is told apart by the look and smell of the discharge** — the medicine is completely different for yeast, bacterial vaginosis or trichomonas. But it's often hard to tell by eye, so **if bacterial vaginosis is suspected, an antibiotic is sometimes tried first**. **If there's fever or symptoms are severe, an oral antifungal** is used promptly.
vaginitis.pharm: **If it's the first time you've had these symptoms, see a doctor before the pharmacy** — of people who judged it to be yeast themselves, only one in three were right. If you've been diagnosed with the same thing before and recognise the symptoms, a vaginal tablet may cure it. But in the same study, **even people diagnosed before weren't often right on their own**, so if it isn't better within 3 days, don't put off seeing a doctor.

acetaminophen.tagline: The basic painkiller and fever reducer, easiest on the stomach
acetaminophen.lead: This is the most basic medicine for pain and fever. It doesn't calm inflammation, but it's easier on the stomach, kidneys and heart than anti-inflammatory painkillers, so clinics lay it down first as the **base** of pain treatment. The thing to watch most is **the daily total**. If you add up the acetaminophen hidden in cold medicines and combination painkillers and go over 4 g a day, the liver gets damaged. If you drink more than three drinks every day or have liver problems, talk to a doctor or pharmacist first (leaflet).
sideEffects: Side effects are rare at normal doses
stop: Nausea and vomiting with pain in the upper right tummy, or yellowing of the eyes or skin (signs of liver damage)
A rash that spreads or blisters
tips: One of the few painkillers you can take on an empty stomach. With a glass of water.

Don't double the dose because it 'feels weak'. Taking it **at the same time as ibuprofen, a different type, isn't recommended in principle** (leaflet, UK guidance), but clinics sometimes use the two together or alternately if one isn't enough — keep each medicine's own interval and daily total. If you're pregnant, have a stomach ulcer or kidney disease, or take blood thinners, you may need to avoid ibuprofen.
Don't split or chew extended-release (8-hour) tablets.
If fever lasts more than 3 days or pain more than 10 days, don't increase the medicine — see a doctor.

faq.q: Is Tylenol the ingredient name?
faq.a: No — Tylenol is a brand name, and the ingredient is **acetaminophen**. Several other Korean brands contain the same ingredient, and many cold medicines and combination painkillers also contain 300–650 mg each. The ingredient list on the back of the box shows straight away whether they overlap.

faq.q: If the fever goes down, am I better?
faq.a: No. A fever reducer lowers fever for a while — it controls the symptom, it doesn't treat the cause. If fever lasts more than 3 days, goes down and comes back, or you feel very unwell, have the cause checked.

faq.q: Is three times a day OK?
faq.a: Yes. 1–2 tablets of 500 mg 30 minutes after breakfast, lunch and dinner, at least 4 hours apart. Even if you take extra when it hurts, don't go over 8 tablets (4 g) a day.

faq.q: I have a stomach ulcer — is it easier on the stomach than anti-inflammatories?
faq.a: In an overseas study (UK, 2001), under 2 g a day it didn't raise the risk of stomach bleeding and was easier on the stomach than anti-inflammatories, but above 2 g a day the risk of stomach bleeding rose 3.6 times. Korean leaflets say not to take it if you have an ulcer now, so talk to a doctor or pharmacist first.

acetaminophen.children: **500 mg tablets are from age 12** (Korean approval). For younger children, give **children's suspension or syrup** by body weight — don't split adult tablets for them. Syrup is from 4 months; under age 2, talk to a doctor.

ibuprofen.tagline: Among pharmacy anti-inflammatories, one of the easiest on the stomach
ibuprofen.lead: An anti-inflammatory painkiller that reduces pain by calming inflammation. Among the anti-inflammatories you can buy at a pharmacy, it's **one of the easiest on the stomach at low doses (up to 1,200 mg a day)**, and it works fast. It works better than acetaminophen for muscle and joint pain, period pain and toothache.
sideEffects: Swelling, higher blood pressure (high doses, long use)
stop: Black stools or vomiting blood (gastrointestinal bleeding)
Breathlessness, wheezing or a swelling face (allergic reaction)
Passing much less urine or swollen ankles

If a rash spreads over the body with fever, or there are blisters, peeling skin, sores in the mouth and eyes, or a swollen face with lumps in the neck, **stop at once and go to the emergency department** (severe skin reaction — usually within a month of starting)
If an allergy such as hives or face swelling comes with **chest tightness or chest pain, call 119 at once** (Kounis syndrome, where allergy tightens the heart's blood vessels)
tips: Right after a meal, or with milk or a snack. An empty stomach increases heartburn.
Hitting the pain firmly with 400 mg early and then continuing with 200–400 mg works better than taking little bits.

**If you're 65 or older, or take blood thinners or steroids,** keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use anti-inflammatories — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid suppressant at a clinic is surer. Others can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if it keeps burning.
With a glass of water. When you're dehydrated, the kidneys struggle.

faq.q: Are the different ibuprofen brands different medicines?
faq.a: Most contain the same ingredient, ibuprofen (some contain dexibuprofen). Even if the brand names differ, taking two with the same ingredient together is doubling up (strength and form can differ by product — if unsure, check with a pharmacist).

faq.q: Can I take it with acetaminophen?
faq.a: In principle taking them at the same time isn't recommended (leaflet, UK guidance), but clinics sometimes use them together or alternately when fever or pain isn't controlled. Together they work better than either alone — keep each medicine's own interval and daily total. But don't double up on two anti-inflammatories, such as ibuprofen + naproxen.

ibuprofen.children: From 6 months. Avoid during dehydration (vomiting, diarrhoea), when the strain on the kidneys is greater.

famotidine.tagline: The strongest acid suppressant you can buy at a pharmacy — only 10 mg is non-prescription
famotidine.lead: An H2 blocker that reduces stomach acid production. In Korea, strong acid suppressants such as omeprazole are prescription-only, so **the strongest acid suppressant you can buy at a pharmacy is famotidine 10 mg**. It's a medicine you can try first from the pharmacy when your stomach burns while taking anti-inflammatories or you're worried about the strain on your stomach (it's weaker than prescription acid suppressants). But it's **a medicine that reduces heartburn** — at this dose it hasn't been shown to prevent stomach bleeding or ulcers from anti-inflammatories; those studies used prescription doses (40–80 mg a day). It works later than antacids (30 minutes–1 hour) but lasts 10–12 hours. **Only 10 mg products are sold at pharmacies; 20 mg and above need a prescription.**
stop: Black stools, vomiting blood
Difficulty swallowing
tips: When buying it with an anti-inflammatory, just ask for “famotidine 10 mg”.
If heartburn is bad right now, an antacid first; famotidine for prevention and keeping it at bay.
If you need it for more than 14 days, don't increase it — see a doctor. If Helicobacter bacteria are the cause, there's separate treatment to get rid of them.

faq.q: Why buy it with an anti-inflammatory?
faq.a:
Anti-inflammatories also reduce the substances that protect the stomach lining, so they can cause heartburn and ulcers. Famotidine is the strongest acid suppressant you can buy at a pharmacy, so if you're 65 or older or take blood thinners or steroids, try taking it alongside **to ease heartburn** (up to 20 mg a day). If your stomach keeps burning or doesn't improve, see a doctor.

But it hasn't been shown that pharmacy doses prevent ulcers or bleeding from anti-inflammatories. The trial where famotidine reduced stomach ulcers used a prescription dose (80 mg a day), and at 40 mg a day the difference in ulcers wasn't clear. If you've had a stomach ulcer or need to take it long term, get a prescription acid suppressant from a clinic.

faq.q: How much less if my kidneys are poor?
faq.a: The dose is set by your doctor. For reference, the US label reduces it, even on prescription, to 20 mg every other day if the kidney function test (creatinine clearance) is under 30 mL per minute — half of taking pharmacy 10 mg twice a day.

naproxen.tagline: Long-lasting, and the anti-inflammatory least likely to raise heart attack and stroke risk — but harder on the stomach
naproxen.lead: A long-acting anti-inflammatory painkiller — one dose lasts 8–12 hours. In a 2013 pooled analysis of anti-inflammatory trials worldwide, it was **the only anti-inflammatory painkiller that didn't increase heart and blood vessel events**, so clinics often choose it for pain in people with high blood pressure or heart disease. But **naproxen, like other anti-inflammatories, roughly doubles the risk of heart failure (a weak heart causing swelling and breathlessness).** If you have heart failure or severe high blood pressure, don't take it — talk to a doctor. On the other hand, **its strain on the stomach is about twice that of ibuprofen**. For period pain, a loading dose of '2 capsules for the first dose' is approved.
sideEffects: Heartburn, indigestion (more common than with ibuprofen)
stop: Black stools, vomiting blood
Breathlessness or a swelling face
Passing less urine, swollen ankles

If a rash spreads over the body with fever, or there are blisters, peeling skin, sores in the mouth and eyes, or a swollen face with lumps in the neck, **stop at once and go to the emergency department** (severe skin reaction — usually within a month of starting)
tips: For period pain, hit it firmly with 2 capsules as the first dose as soon as it starts (or the day before), then 1 capsule every 6–8 hours regularly for 2–3 days.

Always after food. **If you're 65 or older, or take blood thinners or steroids,** keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use anti-inflammatories — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid suppressant at a clinic is surer. Others can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if it keeps burning.
Don't go over 1,250 mg (5 capsules) a day.

faq.q: I have heart disease — what if I need an anti-inflammatory?
faq.a: In the 2013 pooled analysis it was the only anti-inflammatory painkiller that didn't increase heart and blood vessel events, so clinics often choose it. But naproxen, like other anti-inflammatories, roughly doubles the risk of heart failure (a weak heart causing swelling and breathlessness). If you have heart failure or severe high blood pressure, don't take it — talk to a doctor. Its strain on the stomach is about twice that of ibuprofen, so always take it after food, and if you're 65 or older or take blood thinners or steroids, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside.

faq.q: How do I take it for period pain?
faq.a: As soon as it starts (or the day before), hit it firmly with 2 capsules as the first dose, then 1 capsule every 6–8 hours regularly for 2–3 days. Don't go over 5 capsules (1,250 mg) a day.

naproxen.children: Check each product's age limit. Some products can be used by teenagers (12 and over) with period pain.

trimebutine.tagline: Relaxes squeezing pain — the gentler choice for older people
trimebutine.lead: A medicine that calms hollow organs such as the gut or bladder when they **squeeze out of control**. What's unusual is that it doesn't push only one way — if they're moving too much it slows them, and if they're sluggish it speeds them up. So it can be used for both the diarrhoea and the constipation type. **It has no anticholinergic action**, so there's almost no dry mouth, glare or blocked urine, which makes it easier than butylscopolamine for older people. **It's sold at pharmacies.**
stop: If your skin turns yellow or urine gets dark, stop and see a doctor
If a rash or hives appear, stop
tips: It works best **30 minutes before a meal**.
A warm hot-water bottle on the sore spot helps the spasm settle faster along with the medicine.
If you're taking it for bladder pain, **drinking enough water and not holding in urine** matters as much as the medicine.

faq.q: Can I take this for cystitis?
faq.a:
Cystitis pain is spasm pain from **the bladder squeezing**, so adding an antispasmodic makes it much more comfortable. Clinics sometimes use tiropramide, and trimebutine can also help. But **this medicine doesn't kill bacteria** — cystitis is treated with prescription antibiotics, and holding out for days on painkillers and antispasmodics alone can let it reach the kidneys. Think of it as **a medicine to add while you're being treated**.

(Using it for bladder spasm isn't confirmed by large trials — it's **based on how it works and clinical experience**.)

faq.q: How is it different from butylscopolamine?
faq.a: Butylscopolamine is **an anticholinergic**, so it works well but can cause dry mouth, glare and difficulty passing urine. **If you have glaucoma or an enlarged prostate, avoid it altogether.** Trimebutine doesn't have that action, so it's easier on older people. On the other hand, butylscopolamine starts working a little faster.

trimebutine.children: For children, the dose is adjusted by weight using syrup. Talk to a paediatrician.

cetirizine.tagline: Once-a-day second-generation antihistamine — among the drowsier of its group, so take it at bedtime
cetirizine.lead: A second-generation antihistamine that works for 24 hours on one tablet a day for allergic rhinitis, hives and itching. It's the drowsiest of the second-generation group (3.5 times more drowsiness than loratadine in a large observational study), so the standard is to take it before bed.
stop: If you're too drowsy to work during the day, switch to another ingredient
If hives last more than 6 weeks, see a doctor
If your face or lips swell or you get breathless, go to the emergency department at once
tips: Taking it in the evening and sleeping reduces daytime drowsiness.
If your rhinitis is mainly a 'blocked nose', antihistamines alone aren't enough — a steroid nasal spray (prescription) is the first-line treatment.

faq.q: Will it make me drowsy if I take it during the day?
faq.a: It's the drowsiest of the second-generation group (3.5 times that of loratadine), so the standard is to take it before bed. Before driving or precise work, loratadine or fexofenadine is safer.

faq.q: Doesn't it work for a blocked nose?
faq.a: Antihistamines alone aren't enough. For rhinitis that's mainly a blocked nose, a steroid nasal spray (prescription) is the first-line treatment.

cetirizine.children: Tablets from age 6; syrup for younger children.

loratadine.tagline: Once a day with hardly any drowsiness — for daytime
loratadine.lead: A second-generation antihistamine that causes hardly any drowsiness (it was the baseline drug for drowsiness risk in a large cohort study). It starts working a little more slowly than cetirizine, but one tablet a day lasts 24 hours, and you can use it while driving or working.
stop: If hives last more than 6 weeks, see a doctor
If your face or lips swell or you get breathless, go to the emergency department at once
If drowsiness is bad, switch to another ingredient
tips: An antihistamine you can take in the morning.
If it feels too weak, switch to cetirizine (at bedtime).

faq.q: Can I take it in the morning?
faq.a: Yes. It causes hardly any drowsiness, so it's for daytime. If it feels too weak, switch to cetirizine (at bedtime).

faq.q: What if my liver isn't good?
faq.a: If liver function is reduced, it's taken every other day. Tell the pharmacist.

loratadine.children: **Tablets from age 6, syrup from age 2** (approved ages differ by form).

dexibuprofen.tagline: The 'active half' of ibuprofen — the same effect from a smaller amount
dexibuprofen.lead: Ibuprofen is a 50:50 mix of two mirror-image molecules, and dexibuprofen is just the one that actually relieves pain. So **300 mg has about the same effect as ibuprofen 400 mg**, and in crossover trials it started working a little sooner. Claims of 'fewer' stomach side effects are an assumption based on the total amount being half — there isn't yet enough independent comparative evidence.
stop: Black stools, vomiting blood
Breathlessness or a swelling face
Passing less urine

If a rash spreads over the body with fever, or there are blisters, peeling skin, sores in the mouth and eyes, or a swollen face with lumps in the neck, **stop at once and go to the emergency department** (severe skin reaction — usually within a month of starting)
If an allergy such as hives or face swelling comes with **chest tightness or chest pain, call 119 at once** (Kounis syndrome, where allergy tightens the heart's blood vessels)
tips: With food.
Brand names that sound stronger can make it seem like a stronger medicine, but it's in the same class as ibuprofen 400 mg.

faq.q: Is dexibuprofen 300 mg stronger than ibuprofen 400 mg?
faq.a: No, it's the same class. It's just the part of ibuprofen that actually relieves pain, so 300 mg has about the same effect as ibuprofen 400 mg. Brand names that sound stronger make it easy to mistake it for a stronger medicine.

faq.q: Is it gentler on the stomach?
faq.a: That's an assumption based on the total amount being half — there isn't yet enough independent comparative evidence. Take it with food, and don't double up with other anti-inflammatory painkillers.

diclofenac-topical.tagline: An anti-inflammatory you rub on for sprains and bruises — in trials, about 3 in 5 people who used it benefited
diclofenac-topical.lead: In an analysis pooling studies of fresh sprains and bruises, **diclofenac gel came out best in 2 trials (about 3 in 5 people who used it benefited).** But there's little data comparing topical medicines directly with each other. Side effects at the application site were similar to placebo. It was also shown to work for knee arthritis over 6–12 weeks. Unlike oral diclofenac, there's hardly any worry about the heart or stomach.
stop: Stop if the area turns red and itchy
If it's no better after a week, see a doctor
Stop if your stomach burns while using it together with an oral anti-inflammatory
tips: Rub it in until absorbed and wash your hands.
For a sprained ankle or wrist pain, this gel + a cold pack is clinics' first choice before tablets.

faq.q: I've sprained my ankle — is it better than tablets?
faq.a: About the same. In an analysis pooling several studies, topical anti-inflammatories seemed to reduce pain about as well as oral ones, and with diclofenac gel about 3 in 5 people benefited in 2 trials. Side effects at the application site were similar to placebo. This gel + a cold pack is clinics' first choice.

faq.q: How much do I apply?
faq.a: Rub in an amount the size of 1–2 cherries 3–4 times a day and wash your hands. Don't apply it to wounds or mucous membranes, and if you take anticoagulants, be careful with long-term use over large areas.

xylometazoline.tagline: Spray it and your nose clears within minutes — but the 3-day rule
xylometazoline.lead: It directly constricts the blood vessels in the nasal lining and clears the nose within minutes. Unlike oral decongestants it has little effect on blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure can use it briefly. The problem is that **using it for more than 3 days in a row causes rebound rhinitis — the nose gets more blocked when you stop**. Approved use: up to 3 times a day, not for 7 days in a row, and stop if it isn't better after 3 days.
stop: Using it for more than three days actually makes it more blocked — stop before then
Stop if you get frequent nosebleeds or sores inside the nose
Stop if your heart races
tips: For a blocked nose from a cold, using it at night for just 3 days and then stopping is the standard.
If your rhinitis comes back every season, a steroid nasal spray (prescription) is the answer — this one is for emergencies.

faq.q: How many days can I use it?
faq.a: Just 3 days. If you keep going longer, you get rebound rhinitis — the nose gets more blocked when you stop. The approved use is up to 3 times a day, not for 7 days in a row.

faq.q: My blood pressure is high — is it OK?
faq.a: Unlike oral decongestants it has little effect on blood pressure, so it can be used briefly. With high blood pressure or heart disease, talk to a pharmacist before using it, and don't use it if you have an enlarged prostate or angle-closure glaucoma (Korean leaflet).

xylometazoline.children: **Always check the strength.** 0.1% is for adults (12 and over), and **0.05% is for children from age 2 to under 12** (approved use — one spray at a time, 3 times a day, 8 hours apart). Don't spray the adult one in a child's nose.

fexofenadine.tagline: The least drowsy antihistamine — don't take it with fruit juice
fexofenadine.lead: It barely enters the brain, so it's the least drowsy even among second-generation antihistamines (on a par with loratadine or less). In Korea the 120 mg strength is sold without a prescription. Taken with orange, grapefruit or apple juice, or aluminium/magnesium antacids, much less is absorbed — take it with water.
stop: If hives last more than 6 weeks, see a doctor
If your face or lips swell or you get breathless, go to the emergency department at once
tips: The one to choose on days you absolutely mustn't be drowsy, like driving or exams.

faq.q: Can't I take it with juice?
faq.a: Taken with orange, grapefruit or apple juice, or aluminium/magnesium antacids, much less is absorbed. Take it before meals with water.

faq.q: Is it the least drowsy one?
faq.a: It barely enters the brain, so it's the least drowsy even among second-generation antihistamines. The one to choose on days you absolutely mustn't be drowsy, like driving or exams.

ors.tagline: The real hero of treating gastroenteritis — this comes before anti-diarrhoeals
ors.lead: It's water **matched to the ratio the body absorbs best** to replace the water, salt and sugar lost through diarrhoea and vomiting. Gut cells have channels that carry salt and glucose **together**, and water follows them in. So water with only salt, or a drink with only sugar, can't do this job — **both have to be there together**. It's the centre of treating sudden gastroenteritis; anti-diarrhoeals are a side dish. The composition the World Health Organization recommends **reduced** the salt and sugar per litre compared with the old one, and compared with the old composition it **shortened diarrhoea by about a quarter of a day (roughly 7 hours)**, with fewer people needing a drip in hospital.
sideEffects: The salty taste can make it hard to drink (chilling it helps)
stop: If you pass no urine for half a day or more, or are too dizzy to stand, see a doctor straight away
If you vomit and can't keep down a single sip, you need a drip — don't hold out
If you have kidney or heart problems, don't decide the amount yourself — check
tips: Chilled and sipped little by little, it goes down much more easily.

Most oral rehydration solutions sold at Korean pharmacies are **approved as 'electrolyte supplement foods', not as 'medicines'**. That doesn't mean they don't work — they just can't state benefits like a medicine. When choosing, look for products that say they **follow the World Health Organization composition**.
In an emergency at home, you can make something similar with 1 L of water + 6 teaspoons of sugar + 1/2 teaspoon of salt. But inaccurate measuring is dangerous, so use a pharmacy product if you can.
Sports drinks have a lot of sugar and little sodium, so they fall short as a substitute. If you use one, dilute it half and half with water.

After sweating a lot in the heat, it's better than plain water. In a small trial of 10 people who lost 2% of their body weight in sweat in a hot room, those who replaced it with plain water only tended to cramp more easily, and those who used oral rehydration solution tended to cramp less.

faq.q: Can't I use a sports drink instead?
faq.a: It falls short. Sports drinks have **a lot of sugar and little sodium**, which can make diarrhoea worse. If you must, dilute it half and half with water, and use a pharmacy oral rehydration solution if you can.

faq.q: I heard it's good for hangovers?
faq.a: **There's no evidence for hangovers.** Where oral rehydration solution has proven itself is 'water and salt lost through diarrhoea and vomiting'. In studies of hangovers, neither electrolytes, blood sugar nor the hormones that indicate dehydration were related to how bad the hangover was, and neither was how much water people drank after it started. But **if you vomited all night**, that's real dehydration, and then it's right.

faq.q: Can't I just drink lots of plain water?
faq.a: When diarrhoea and vomiting have also drained your salt, drinking lots of plain water **dilutes the salt in your body further**. It's especially dangerous for children and older people. Water is absorbed properly only when salt and sugar are in it together.

faq.q: Where do I find it at the pharmacy? I can't see a product name
faq.a: **It isn't in the Korean drug agency's medicine list** — most are approved as 'electrolyte supplement foods', so they don't come up when you search by medicine name. They're near the pharmacy counter or in the chilled display as powder or liquid; just ask the pharmacist for 'oral rehydration solution'.

ors.children: The most important treatment for children's gastroenteritis. Give a little by spoon every 5 minutes.

magnesium-oxide.tagline: A gentle osmotic laxative you can use every day — not if your kidneys are poor
magnesium-oxide.lead:
It draws water into the bowel to soften stools. It's less habit-forming, so it's the basic medicine for long-standing constipation (guideline: conditional recommendation), and it also has an antacid effect. In Korea, the most familiar **tablet brand contains magnesium hydroxide 500 mg**, while **its 'S' version contains magnesium oxide 250 mg** — the names are similar but the ingredient and number of tablets differ. If your kidneys are poor, magnesium builds up and becomes dangerous, so avoid it.

What they do is the same (draw water into the bowel to soften stools). Because the strengths differ, don't simply carry the number of tablets across — **follow the directions on the box**.
stop: Muscle weakness, nausea, a slow pulse (signs of high magnesium)
If you've taken it for a week and still haven't passed a stool, don't increase it — see a doctor; there may be another cause
If your kidneys aren't good, this medicine builds up in the body. Be sure to mention it at your appointment
tips: It works only if you drink enough water.
Adjust by reducing the number of tablets if stools are too soft, and increasing if they're hard.

faq.q: Can I take it every day?
faq.a: It's less habit-forming, so it's the basic medicine for long-standing constipation. It works only if you drink enough water; if stools are too soft, take fewer tablets. If you're over 65, check your kidney function and start low.

faq.q: What if my kidneys aren't good?
faq.a: Avoid it. Magnesium builds up and becomes dangerous. Keep it 2 hours apart from other medicines.

magnesium-oxide.children: Check children's doses with a pharmacist.

fusidic-acid.tagline: A topical antibiotic — only for infected wounds, not needed for simple scrapes
fusidic-acid.lead: An antibiotic you apply to wounds and impetigo infected with bacteria (especially Staphylococcus aureus). In an analysis pooling several studies, it worked as well as mupirocin. But **simple wounds without signs of infection (pus, spreading redness, warmth) don't need it**, and using it out of habit only breeds resistance. Rinsing the wound under running water and a moist dressing come first.
stop: If it isn't healing after a week, stop and see a doctor
Stop if the area gets redder and oozes more
If you get a fever and the area spreads, see a doctor straight away
tips: Without signs of infection, petroleum jelly or a moist dressing is also better for scarring.

faq.q: Do I need to put it on every scrape?
faq.a: No. Only when there are signs of infection such as pus, spreading redness or warmth. For simple wounds, rinse under running water and use a moist dressing first; using it out of habit only breeds resistance.

faq.q: How much do I apply?
faq.a: Thinly, once or twice a day, for up to 1 week. If it doesn't improve, see a doctor. Don't apply it around the eyes.

mupirocin.tagline: A topical antibiotic as effective as fusidic acid — some products need a prescription
mupirocin.lead: An antibiotic you apply to wounds with pus or spreading redness; in an analysis pooling several studies it worked as well as fusidic acid. But **in Korea some products need a prescription**, so check whether you can buy it straight from the pharmacy. If you want to buy one straight away, fusidic acid is the sure option. Using it to clear bacteria inside the nose is prescription-only.
stop: If it isn't healing after a week, stop and see a doctor
If the area spreads and you get a fever, see a doctor straight away
tips: **Only when there are signs of infection** such as pus or spreading redness. Applying it out of habit to clean wounds only increases resistance.
Thinly 2–3 times a day, **no longer than 10 days**. If it isn't better after 3 days, see a doctor.
Applying it inside the nose (to clear bacteria there) is prescription-only.

faq.q: How is it different from fusidic acid?
faq.a: In an analysis pooling several studies, they worked equally well. The difference is **how you can buy it**. Fusidic acid can be bought straight from the pharmacy, while some mupirocin products need a prescription.

faq.q: For how many days do I apply it?
faq.a: Thinly 2–3 times a day, no longer than 10 days. If it isn't better after 3 days, see a doctor. Applying it inside the nose is prescription-only.

ketoprofen.tagline: An anti-inflammatory patch — works well, but 'avoid sunlight for 2 weeks'
ketoprofen.lead: It delivers an anti-inflammatory through the skin to the spot. For sudden muscle and joint pain, the evidence for ketoprofen gel is solid: about 2 in 5 people who use it benefit (pooled analysis of several studies). But because of **a reaction where the skin flares up in sunlight** (photosensitivity), in 2010 the Korean drug agency made it mandatory to state 'not for under 15s, and keep the patched area out of sunlight for 2 weeks even after removing it'.
stop: Blisters or a bad rash where applied
**Keep the area covered from sunlight for up to 2 weeks** after removing it — sunlight can cause a severe rash
If you have asthma or have been breathless after an anti-inflammatory, it's safer to avoid patches too
tips: For pain in one area like a knee or shoulder, a patch is a good first choice over tablets, without the strain on the stomach or heart.
In summer, piroxicam, diclofenac or loxoprofen patches carry less photosensitivity worry than ketoprofen.
The sunlight rash usually appears after you've taken the patch off, so it's easy to miss that the patch caused it.

faq.q: Why keep the patched area out of the sun?
faq.a: Because of photosensitivity, in 2010 the Korean drug agency made it mandatory to state 'not for under 15s, and keep the area out of sunlight for 2 weeks even after removing it'. In summer, piroxicam, diclofenac or loxoprofen patches are less of a worry.

faq.q: Can I use it with an oral anti-inflammatory?
faq.a: For pain in one area, the patch comes first. Using it over a large area for a long time on top of an oral anti-inflammatory can add to what's absorbed into the whole body.

relax-combo.tagline: A pharmacy combination muscle relaxant for tight muscles
relax-combo.lead: A muscle relaxant ingredient (chlorzoxazone) + a salicylate pain reliever (ethenzamide) + caffeine. A non-prescription medicine used briefly for a crick or tight muscles. An older product that combined it with acetaminophen was discontinued in 2023. Be careful about drowsiness and alcohol; not for under 15s.
stop: Stop if you nearly fell from drowsiness
If your eyes turn yellow or your urine gets dark, stop at once and see a doctor (liver)
If you've been taking it for more than 2 weeks, see a doctor
tips: Ask for 'a non-prescription medicine with a muscle relaxant' and you'll get this type.

faq.q: Do I really need a muscle relaxant?
faq.a: A muscle relaxant can help when tightness is clear, but the effect is small and it makes you drowsy. According to its leaflet, this medicine isn't taken with other fever reducers or anti-inflammatory painkillers — choose **only one of the two** with an oral anti-inflammatory. If you feel you must take both, talk to a pharmacist (they're sometimes used together when needed). If there's no tightness, you can leave it out. If you need a prescription muscle relaxant (eperisone), see a doctor.

eperisone.tagline: Korea's most prescribed muscle relaxant — relatively less drowsy
eperisone.lead: The muscle relaxant most often added to prescriptions for musculoskeletal pain by orthopaedic and internal medicine clinics in Korea. It causes less drowsiness than other centrally acting muscle relaxants, so it's easier to use during the day. It needs a prescription, and the usual clinic combination is **an anti-inflammatory + eperisone + a stomach protector (+ acetaminophen)**.
stop: If you nearly fell from drowsiness or dizziness, stop and tell your doctor
Stop if you feel drained and can't put strength into your body
Rarely, if hives spread over the body and you get breathless, go to the emergency department at once
tips: It isn't sold at pharmacies. If a crick doesn't ease in 3 days, it's quicker to see a doctor and get this combination prescribed.

faq.q: Can I buy it at a pharmacy?
faq.a: No. It needs a prescription. If a crick doesn't ease in 3 days, it's quicker to see a doctor and get the anti-inflammatory + eperisone + stomach protector combination prescribed.

faq.q: Does it make you drowsy?
faq.a: It causes less drowsiness than other centrally acting muscle relaxants, so it's easier to use during the day. It can still make you feel weak, so be careful driving, and if you're over 65, take care not to fall.

butylscopolamine.tagline: For a cramping tummy, from the pharmacy — older people, check conditions first
butylscopolamine.lead: A pharmacy medicine that quickly stops hollow organs like the gut or womb from **squeezing**. It's often used for cramping tummy pain, and **added** to an anti-inflammatory painkiller for period pain. But it's **an anticholinergic**, so it can cause dry mouth, glare and difficulty passing urine. **If you have glaucoma or an enlarged prostate, you should avoid it.**
stop: If your eye suddenly hurts, goes cloudy and you see rainbows, see an eye doctor at once (acute glaucoma)
If you can't pass urine at all and your lower tummy is tight, see a doctor at once
tips: A warm hot-water bottle on the sore spot makes it ease much faster.
For period pain, using it **together with** an anti-inflammatory painkiller (such as naproxen) tackles two different kinds of pain separately.
If you keep needing it for more than a few days, have the cause checked at least once.

faq.q: Does it work for cystitis pain?
faq.a: It's the same kind of squeezing pain, so it may help, but **it isn't recommended for men with an enlarged prostate or people with glaucoma** — urine can be blocked completely. In those cases, **trimebutine**, which has no anticholinergic action, or **tiropramide** from a clinic is easier (tell them if you have glaucoma). And for cystitis, either way, **antibiotics come first**.

butylscopolamine.children: The Korean leaflet gives adult directions only. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before giving it to a child.

benzydamine.tagline: Straight to the sore spot — a mouthwash for mouth ulcers and sore throats, sold at pharmacies
benzydamine.lead: A mouthwash and spray that calms inflammation while **reducing the feeling of pain, a little like numbing it**. It's widely used for mouth ulcers, sore throats, after tonsil surgery, and mouth pain from cancer treatment or radiotherapy. It isn't swallowed but touches the sore spot directly, so there's little strain on the whole body. **It's sold at Korean pharmacies** (as mouthwash and spray products).
for: Mouth sores from cancer treatment or radiotherapy
sideEffects: Tingling or stinging in the mouth
